No access key is set: the town page implies the site is not set up for recreation, but that is interpretation. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 5 readable page reads including the Town Forest history and the DCR program page.

NHLR and the 1915 Boston Daily Globe item disagree on when the first Barden Hill tower went up (1913 vs. apparently still 'planned' in March 1915); kept both in the story rather than picking one. No source found addresses current staffing, access, or climbability, so those stay unknown in the tower record. The easternuslookouts.weebly.com page carries a banner image but it isn't clearly captioned as depicting this specific tower, so it was not added to photos.

The Register's Milton Fire Tower is the 1885 weather observatory, not a dedicated fire tower; the record's kind could read as a tower. No current access statement was read, so access is omitted rather than guessed. The Blue Hill Observatory & Science Center timeline page had no usable text. The Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook post on this site could not be fetched. Staffing is limited to the lookout years; no names found.

Build year conflicts across four sources: three (Register, Forest Lookouts, and a 2025 hiking post) say 1935 and one hiking-history page says 1934. The 1934 date rests on that hiking-history page, which also gives April 1, 1934 as the first day of operation; verify against a Forest Service or DCR source if one turns up. Only the Register describes the tower itself; it gives no build year, builder, or fire-lookout service, and the record's kind is unknown. The Wikipedia article has no tower content. Access to the tower top and whether climbing is permitted were not confirmed, so the visit note says to ask DCR. Do not encourage climbing. Removal in 2003 is well supported (register, Forest Lookouts, Willhite). Unresolved: first tower 1915 vs 1918; 1970 tower height 40 ft vs possibly 60 ft; 1970 vs 1971 completion (a Facebook search snippet from FFLA Massachusetts says 1971, not read). Leads not read: 2006 Mount Everett summit resource management plan on mass.gov (mentions a 2000 proposal to repair the tower). Access is public trail access; no tower to climb.

Only two pages were read: the NHLR register entry (no visit reports, no staffing) and an OpenStreetMap node that gives the 1972 start date. Two WebSearch calls found no North Attleboro lookout history; hits were the Falls Fire Barn (a fire station, not a lookout) and modern cell towers. The firelookout.org and ffla.org North Attleboro pages returned 404 in the cache. The FFLA Massachusetts Chapter Facebook post on this tower could not be fetched (login-blocked). No staffing information found. Access is as of March 2019 with no newer source.

Register visit reports from 2016 (May says Sometimes, August says staffed) are the only staffing evidence, so facts.staffing is marked seasonal as of 2016. Access level public is inferred from the trail network; no source says whether the tower can be climbed, so no visit.climbable is given. A WebSearch snippet attributed to firelookout.org said the summit tower was taken down and moved to Plymouth by 1942; that page returned 404 from fetch_text and the claim was not used. Heights disagree across sources (68 ft register, 80 ft Wikipedia, 50 ft 1921 report). Elevation differs too (1,174 ft register, 1,240 ft Wikipedia); the story notes it. Single register source for the tower's history; the Harvard Forest page only confirms the museum name and a 1930s diorama scene, not this tower. The 2016 visit report is the newest condition evidence found. No staffing history, notable fires, or current owner statement found. Search snippets (not read, not cited) mention a Prospect Hill site and a Phillipston Historical Society; check those before any update.

The brief's record puts the FFLOS registration (US 1548, MA 55, March 27, 2014) on the Pine Hill tower, but that entry is the former Manomet Hill site; see corrections. Access is not recorded as a fact: no current access rules were found, and the 2014 NHLR visit report says directions are not signed. The story advises checking with the Bureau before any visit and does not tell readers to climb or not to climb. Build year: the NHLR and FFLOS say 1966. A search snippet from an FFLA Massachusetts Facebook post gives 1969 and says the tower is Plymouth's fifth; the page itself returned no text, so the date is not cited and should be checked if it matters. The brief's elevation_m (114.3) matches the NHLR 375 ft (114 m). The height of 21.3 m is the NHLR 70-ft figure for the current tower, which the brief did not list. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'record' wording is corrected to the register's 'activity', 'went up' is corrected to 'moved' for the 1939 Telegraph Hill tower, the 1942 new-tower versus relocated-from-Pelham disagreement is now stated, and the unsupported 'do not climb the tower without permission' line was removed because the NHLR page has no climbing or permission text.

Five sources read. The early history (1911 fire watch, 1912 and 1915 items, 1923 observer change, 1961 status) comes from the Forest Lookouts newspaper excerpts. These are transcriptions on a hobbyist site and were not checked against the original newspapers. Unresolved: (1) the Summit House burn date, 1965 (NHLR, Forest Lookouts) against around 1970 (FFLOS) and 12/18/1970 (Princeton Historical Society); the story reports both. Unresolved: origin of the older tower (register: Richmond Hill, 28 ft, 1912; former-site register: Dighton, 50 ft, first operated 1916). The NHLR page is the main source for the tower's build history, but it has no visit reports, so no staffing or access data. Build history rests on the NHLR and the Forest Lookouts newspaper transcriptions, which agree on 1932. Current standing and public access rest on a 2024 hiking write-up and an undated Wikipedia summary; no official 2025-2026 source was read. Brief height_m 12.2 is the older 40-foot predecessor; the standing tower is 75 ft. Four pages read: the NHLR register entry (2016 visit reports include the seasonal observer), the Forest Lookouts Mount Massaemet page (newspaper history 1911 to 1969 and the 1940 geodetic description), the 2025 Trailspotting trail guide (active service, cab locked, 72 steps open), and the Franklin Land Trust trail page. Record's elevation 478.2 m matches the register's 1,569 ft (478 m). No photos added. The register's 'Tom Ashton photo' and '1920 photo' credits were not read for license terms.

The brief's 1966 build year and the 2004 and 2008 registrations check out. The first tower's height (48 vs 45 feet) and the 1966 tower's height (75 vs 68 feet) disagree across sources; both are in the story. The FFLA item is a Facebook post, weaker than the registers. A FFLA Facebook post about a 1980 photo appeared in search results but could not be read, so it is not used.

The brief's 1951 build year checks out. The 1938 to 1951 sequence comes from one source (NHLR). Access: Wikipedia says open to the public; Trailspotting (November 2024) says the cabin is locked and the outside stairs can be climbed. The Wikidata entry (Q107454486) only gives a label and is not used.

Identity is a probable match, not confirmed. The OSM node (42.192218, -70.821386) and the register's longitude (70.821940 W) agree within about 50 m, but the register prints 'N 70.821940°' where a latitude should be, so the latitude cannot be checked from the register. Confirm on a map or with Norwell sources before renaming. Condition and current use are unknown; the register was last updated in 2016. The Forest Lookouts page puts the 1956 tower under its Prospect Hill (Hingham/Norwell) entry and also has a Judges Hill (Norwell) entry; the register places the current tower away from Prospect Hill. Build history rests mainly on the NHLR, with the Forest Lookouts index adding the c.1950 temporary tower. The Mass.gov Section 15 report shows no date in the text read; it calls the tower active but does not describe access or staffing. Unresolved: the 1920 replacement tower is 68 ft iron per the register, 71 ft per a Aug 1919 newspaper item, and 70 ft steel per a 1919 state report. Access is disputed: Pioneer Valley says open to the public; a 2018 hiker found the top locked; the 2016 register visit reports say staffed only in fire-danger periods. The brief's 1960 build year and 2004 registration check out; the 1927 first tower is an addition. Open conflicts: first-tower material and height (NHLR iron 68 ft vs 1927 steel per blog); site elevation (NHLR 11 ft vs state survey 76 ft). Coordinates differ between NHLR (41.91722, -70.00111) and OpenStreetMap node 2382888859 (41.919874, -70.006901); not resolved and not used in the story. Height 18.3 m is converted from the 60-foot figure in Forest Lookouts; the Register gives no height in feet. Two FFLA Massachusetts Chapter Facebook posts about Ragged Hill could not be read (login wall) and are not used. The brief's 18.3 m height matches no structure in the sources and is corrected to 25.9 m (85 ft, per Patch). Status kept as standing because the steel frame remains. The register's platform and Patch's communications tower differ in detail; both are recorded. Two Facebook posts by the Massachusetts Forest Fire Lookout Association chapter were seen only as search snippets and are not cited. Status: the DNR notice proposes demolition with comments requested by September 30, 2025; my searches found no later update, so the tower may or may not still stand. Verify with Elk Neck State Forest before publishing a status. Second-cab attribution conflicts: the survey says possibly early joint DNR and ATT use; the notice says Western Union added it in the 1950s. Both are cited and the story says the sources disagree. Events: the 2025 year is inferred from the comment deadline in the notice.

Height left unset on purpose: 93 ft (1928), 120 ft (1938 rebuild) and 104 ft (2022 school article) all appear. The DNR report is marked DRAFT and gives no move date. The Forest Lookouts page (cite 1) quotes the 1929 Forest Worker and 1938 Daily Times; both were read only as quoted there. Bay Journal 2022 article was not read (HTTP 429 twice). Parent record data/towers/md/us-md-church-creek-forestry.json carries the same 'relocated' event and the NHLR coordinates (38.62328, -76.13468); the same correction should be applied there. FFLA's own coordinates for the original Church Creek entry (38.47420, -76.14273, Tower Gone) and the display (38.47420, -76.14248) are almost identical, so FFLA's point may simply be wrong; confirm the station coordinates before publishing the location change. The DNR report is marked DRAFT. Access is rated public on the basis of the engineering firm's description of the park and parking; no visiting hours were found and NHLR says the tower is not open for climbing. The DNR history page linked from NHLR was not read.

No build date in any source I read; the survey gives the installation date as unknown. A search snippet attributed a 1943 date, a 120 ft height and a Western Union antenna to a DNR poster (and a 1983 replacement line, ambiguous as to which tower it refers to). I could not open the poster (HTTP 404), so none of that is used; the survey table's 125 ft conflicts with the snippet's 120 ft. The date the cab was removed is unknown. The NHLR gives the only description of the standing tower, and it conflicts with the 1945 60-foot steel tower in Forest Lookouts. Built year: the register says only 'late 1930s' with no exact year, so no built event is recorded (an earlier 1938 placeholder was removed as unsupported). The DNR report is marked DRAFT and its Great Mills entry reads 'do date' (sic). Condition is disputed. The register text says recently repainted, in communications use, with volunteers invited. The April 2017 visit report on the same page says poor, not maintained, and doubts volunteer use. The DNR Fire Tower Report table lists High Rock as a tower of 90+ feet with communications equipment and condition Good; the report's date was not visible in the text read. Left unresolved. Ownership: the record says federal. No correction proposed. The 1934 build year rests on the register; a search snippet attributed 1934 and 86 feet to a DNR poster, but the poster was not in the cache (404), so it is not used. Report page 48 names the managing agency as Forest Service and gives no builder. The 1980s staffing end date is a local's account relayed in 2017 and is approximate. A search result describing a trailhead from a roadside pullout was not fetched and is not used. The story does not encourage climbing. No build date, height or design found. The Eastern U.S. Lookouts Hollofield page gives only the name and county. FFLA and the DNR report disagree on the destination. Brief record was wrong on height (6.1 m; the tower is 130 ft overall since 1938) and on the agency field, which holds a location string. Height is unresolved: Forest Lookouts quotes a 60-foot steel tower (we store 18.3 m from that), while the DNR Kitty Shortall page says 110 feet. Demolition: the DNR notice gives no removal date and a web search found no confirmation either way, so recheck DNR Forest Service before the status changes. Thin record: the FFLA entry is the only source naming a tower here. Two searches found no fire-lookout history for the Kedges Straits site. The Wikipedia article mentions a 1984 peregrine nesting tower on the refuge; it is not a fire lookout and is not treated as the FFLA structure. Wikipedia is used only as a lead for the refuge; the peregrine tower line is its own claim. Recommend confirming with FFLA or refuge staff what the entry refers to.

Brief status_note matches the FFLA list but omits the state report's wooden-deck account. A 1929 Forest Worker item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page places a 120-foot tower at Millville, Worcester County; not reconciled and not used. No visiting information found, so access is set to restricted. No photos added.

Thinnest of the three. FFLA is the only source naming a tower at this point, and its entry carries only the name, county, coordinates and the word 'unknown'. TopoQuest identifies a cape of the same name in Kent County, at coordinates that do not match the FFLA entry. Two searches found no tower history, owner or access note. The 2007 DNR report's list of towers has no Kent County entry. Proposed corrections: remove '(unknown)' from other_names, and reword status_note because the FFLA page does not say details are uncertain. Recommend confirming with FFLA what the entry refers to before keeping it as standing.

Brief events said 'None relocated' and is corrected to the 1999 move. Build year (1931 vs 1941) and height (100 vs 140 ft) conflict between sources and are unresolved. Museum hours and whether the restored top can be climbed were not verified: the findcityoffice listing gives only an address, and the search did not surface a museum website. Staffing is from the Register ('last staffed in the 1970s') plus one 1942 newspaper mention. Used 6 page reads and 2 searches.

Brief record (24.4 m, standing) checks out; the FFLA asterisk legend supports 'cab no longer in place'. Access was unknown and is now 'permission' from the Wikipedia and WillhiteWeb text. Sources 1 and 2 are the strongest; WillhiteWeb (4) is a hiking-site history with no citations, so its 1883-1886 and 1923-1964 items are secondary. The 1921 'erected 25 years ago' phrase conflicts with WillhiteWeb's 1886 date and is unresolved. A search-result mirror of Wikipedia said the fire lookout 'has since been removed'; that page was not read, and the cached Wikipedia text says the tower still stands. No current owner or public-access statement was found. Do not encourage climbing.

Only two sources. The 1930 article is a plan, and nothing read confirms that the tower was built, its height, its cab, or who staffed it. FFLA lists it standing with no asterisk, so the cab is presumed in place. The 2007 Maryland DNR Forestry Towers report (https://dnr.maryland.gov/forests/documents/fire/Fire_Tower_Report.pdf) covers towers the state managed as of December 2006 and does not list a Sideling tower, so the tower may be privately or locally owned, or may be gone. The Wikipedia Sideling Hill article has no tower mention. Next steps: a Washington County or Maryland Forest Service archive search for the build date, and a newspaper search for the 1930s-40s. Access left unset because nothing was found.

Record height_m 14.3 does not match the register's 100-foot tower (30.5 m); facts.height_m uses the register. Record agency 'Maryland Department of Natural Resources - Forest Service' is not confirmed: the NHLR 'Administered by' value was cut from the fetched text. Registration year: register says April 23, 2007; Discovery Center says 2009. The 1934 replacement and the 1938 build date are not reconciled. Opening hours come from undated pages; check with Deep Creek Lake State Park.

The DNR report is dated April 2007 and covers towers managed as of December 2006, so the condition finding is roughly 20 years old. FFLA lists the tower as standing with no asterisk, which fits the report. The DNR table gives 80 feet and a good condition. The 1,760 versus 1,685 foot elevation gap is left open. No staffing record or visiting policy was found; the DNR report describes the site as a fenced communications compound, so access is set to restricted. Do not encourage climbing.

Both main sources agree on 1934 and a CCC origin (register says Doncaster Camp crews; MHT says believed). Name: register calls it Welcome Forestry Tower; MHT form calls it Welcome Firetower (CH-752). The MHT form was last updated 2003 and the condition and paint details are old; current condition unknown. The record's source_pages dnr.maryland.gov/forests/firetowers/welcome.pdf returns 404; the eastern-us Welcome page yielded only a header. No staffing or public-access source found, so access is marked restricted without a visiting rule. Height 120 ft (36.6 m) comes from the register only. Record's agency matches the register.

Construction and staffing facts come from two 1935 and one 1944 Midland Journal item reprinted on the Forest Lookouts page; the reprint ends in 1944. Current status rests only on the FFLA list. The Cecil County History blog (cecilcountyhistory.com, post on fire towers) reportedly says the tower still stands, has a 2011 photo, and that the state stopped operating the towers, with seasonal staffing into the 1970s. fetch_text got HTTP 403 for that page, so it is not cited and needs checking. A DNR poster reportedly says Aeromotor built most Maryland towers; no source read names Woodlawn's builder, so none is stated. The brief record had no agency; the agency fact is worded from the District Forest Warden quote. No licensed photo found, so none added. Access level left unset: no source described access.

Brief events 2007 and 2008 (Morneault volunteer restoration) are NOT in this JSON: no page read supports them. A search result points to firelookout.org cr-me-2008.pdf (Maine Chapter Report 2008), which was not read because the page-read budget ran out; check it before adding those events. The brief's 'airlifted in August 2020' and 'one of three cabs replaced that week' are not confirmed: the BDN article says only 'recently installed', and the 2020 year-end report says 'reviewed in 2020'. Only the first 3,000 of about 6,200 characters of the BDN page were read, so cost and funding details were not used. Staffing 'not staffed' is an inference from the 'closed' note and the article's past-tense description of observers; treat it as medium confidence. The brief's status 'standing' is supported by the FFLA list and the 2020 article.

Dates: Forest Lookouts dates a lookout station to 1914 and the tower erection to April 1921; we record 1921 for the tower. Two web search summaries say the first tower was 1914 and moved to Dill Ridge in 1927 and back, a 1998 preservation effort, a 1967 reinstallation and a 2021 condition note; none of those pages could be read (the Hilton legacy page returned 404, towerdex returned 403, and a Maine archives link returned 404), so none is in the story or the JSON. Check firelookout.org's Maine record and the Maine Forest Service before publishing a current condition. The 2008 report's 'may be removed in 2009' is a plan, not proof of removal. Brief lacked a build date; agency kept as the brief's Maine Forestry District from the Forest Lookouts header, while the 2008 report names the Maine Forest Service. Access unknown. No photos added.

The build date and original builder are unknown. The 1951 move and the 1955 and 1965 details rest on one undated hiker-oriented site (willhiteweb.com); that site also gives the 1941 survey note, which the story paraphrases. The Forest Lookouts page gives only the county and agency. Current status rests on the FFLA asterisk and the hiker site. No Maine Forest Service records found. A search lead pointed to Maine Memory Network photos of Maine Forest Service towers, not checked. The record had no height; height_m 12.2 converts the 1955 'about 40 feet' description and is secondary.

Staffing conflict is unresolved: NHLR says rangers staff it during high fire danger (present tense); NPS says it has not been manned since 1976. The NPS fire towers page was last updated 2020-10-07. Current 2024-2026 opening status was not confirmed by any source I could read. OpenStreetMap node 358231332 tags access=private, which conflicts with NPS; not used. Wikidata gives elevation 833 ft; NHLR gives 807 ft (246 m, matching the brief). Coordinates match NHLR. Registration date September 16, 1993 is confirmed by NHLR and NPS.

The brief record calls it a tower and gives no height or design; the 1915 and 1920 sources describe a station and a ground cabin, so 'tower' rests on the FFLA listing and the 1920 map title. A 2021 firelookout.org inventory appeared only in a search snippet (reportedly: tower without cab, groundhouse in bad condition, and a steel tower from 1965); its URL could not be fetched, so it is not used. Verify before adding any 1965 steel-tower event. The 1953 Blackmore item is a bear anecdote reprinted from the Biddeford Journal; only the lookout attribution is used.

Build date is disputed (1906 photo inventory vs 1916 newspaper item). Most of the early history comes from the Forest Lookouts page, which quotes old reports and photo inventories; the originals were not checked. Trail Finder's body text calls the trail remote 2-mile, but its length field says 4.00 miles round trip; the story says 4 miles as listed. Two Facebook items seen only as search snippets, not read: a 1967 'Big Spencer Mountain' post saying the tower came down over the 1966-67 winter, and a post saying the cab blew off in a December 2009 storm. Both conflict with the Forest Lookouts account and are not used. No closure notice found; the story does not encourage climbing.

Built 1931 is supported only by the state report as quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page; no primary copy of the report was read. Staffing history and the original design of this tower are not found. Access is recorded as public from a single 2024 hiker's guide with no owner named; confirm land status before publishing a visiting note. A Canaan Historical Society post and a Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter post mention 1931 and aging stairs, but Facebook returned only page titles, so they are not cited.

Relocation year 2001 is supported by FFLOS, the 1HappyHiker blog and Maine IAT, which may share an FFLA source. Suggest adding a 2001 year to the Patten record's relocated event, which has none. Staffing: no names or dates beyond the 1909-1922 watchman cabin. Access: no source says whether the tower can be climbed; the museum page gives only general visiting details. Photos: a Patten Lumbermen's Museum Facebook post about the tower's removal exists (search snippet only, not read, license unknown), so no photo entry was added. Design height left as a conflict, not a fact.

Dates 1910, 1914 and 1938 come from the Eastern US Lookouts timeline (citing the Maine Historical Society photo inventory and state reports) and the Maine Memory record; neither original report was opened. The brief's 24-foot height is confirmed (converted to 7.3 m). The cab's removal date is not found; the FFLA legend is the only basis for 'cab gone'. Access is not recorded: no source states ownership or whether the tower may be climbed, and Wikipedia's 'abandoned' is a secondary description. The FFLA Maine chapter Facebook posts mention a 1938 rebuild by the Maine Forest Service and a later observation-tower conversion, but Facebook returned no text, so they are not cited. Staffing after about 1920 is not found.

Thin record. We have only the 1910 listing, the 1920 inventory and a 1918 map. No build date, staffing history, access or closure information. Searches surfaced Facebook posts (a 2006 photo of the Wesley tower off Route 9 / Airline Road, and a 'Days Hill' mention) that could not be read, so their details are not used. Confirm the Day Hill / Wesley Mountain identity and current access on the ground or with the Maine Forest Service before publishing any visit guidance.

Brief agency (Elliotsville Plantation) may be out of date; the proposed NPS correction is flagged but not confirmed by a land-record source. Park Service pages carry photos but no license line was read, so no photo is added. The Weebly page (easternuslookouts) was read for context only and is not cited.

Brief's height 3.7 m matches the 1919-20 12-foot tower, not the current one. Register says 60 ft; Forest Lookouts and Red River Camps say 48 ft; the conflict is not settled, and 14.6 m is proposed. Brief's 2016 event was the watchman's camp, not the tower. The November 2019 windstorm rests only on Red River Camps, a commercial site; a state or FFLA source would firm it up. The 2020 cab replacement is confirmed by two sources: the 2020 FFLA Maine report and the Bangor Daily News column. The 1991 closure is a regional statement; no year is given for Deboullie. The brief's agency (Maine Forest Service) still matches the register, though the Bureau of Parks and Lands did the 2016 and 2020 work. No road or trail directions were verified.

Height disagrees (50 ft in the 1917 report and by hikers; 48 ft in the 1920 inventory). Move year conflicts (2002 vs 2005). A travel article (2003) and a Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine Facebook post (2005) appeared only in search results and were not read, so they are not cited. The state's wildlife viewing tower is probably this tower, but the state page does not say so. Read budget exceeded by about two pages.

Sources conflict on current state: FFLA lists Tower Standing with no asterisk (cab in place), while the FSM newsletter (Fall 2025) says remnants of fire lookout towers remain on Green Mountain. The story reports both and does not choose. Unverified leads, not used: an FFLA Maine chapter Facebook post (seen only as a search result, never opened) says the tower was erected in 1920 and was 48 feet tall with a cab in poor shape; a second post names a watchman for 1971-1981. Check both before using. Do not confuse with the New Hampshire Green Mountain lookout on NHLR (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/nh/green-mountain-lookout/), a different tower. Status: the register (firetower.org, registered 2008) says no longer standing; the 2016 chapter report and the Forest Lookouts list say standing, with the cab gone per the list's asterisk legend. Cab removal date not found. The 1916 sources name W.F. Hinckley (newspaper) and W.H. Hinckley (report); we did not decide whether they are the same man. No photos added.

Status rests on the FFLA list and its legend (Standing* = cab gone), consistent with the brief. The 1950 date is the Maine Forestry Service map date, not a build date. No build date, height, builder, staffing, watchman or access data found; those keys are left unset. Naming caution: the Rocky Mountain tower in Aroostook (firetower.org/NHLR, US 81, ME 7) is a different site near 47.28 N, far north of this tower's 46.59 N. A Facebook group comment (seen only as a search result, not opened) says Horseshoe and Rocky Brook are synonyms; the story follows the FFLA name only.

Status rests on the FFLA list and its legend (Standing* = cab gone), consistent with the brief. The 1931 date is the map date, not a build date. No build date, height, builder, staffing, watchman or access data found; those keys are left unset. Do not encourage climbing: treat access as unknown.

The 1948 build year and the 1991 end of staffing rest on one 2011 newspaper story, which quotes a commission member. The commission's own blog gives no build year. The 2011 article says the Forest Service owns the tower and two private owners held the land, so ownership could be updated after checking.

Built 1925 is supported by two independent sources (survey and guide). The brief's 2017 modification is confirmed by the FFLA 2017 report. No watchman or staffing history was found. Facebook posts by the FFLA Maine chapter (1925 build, cab removed 'several years ago') could not be opened and are not cited. Build dates conflict: the Maine Memory Network record says 1914 steel and 1926 replacement, the 2010 trip report says 1914 with a 1925 ice collapse, and a 2025 article gives 1926 as the erection date. Search snippets of Facebook posts from the FFLA Maine chapter and a regional group say the camp is privately owned and the deck was converted in the early 1990s; they could not be opened and are not cited. The brief record's status note matches the FFLA legend.

Three sources, and none gives staffing or access. The FFLA legend supports the cab-gone reading. The 1921 Digital Maine item is catalogued as a still image in the Avery Collection (keyword: Map). Best-documented of the three, but it rests on one long 1983 Bangor Daily News account reprinted on the Forest Lookouts site. The record's 9.8 m is the pre-1963 height; see the height correction. Brief had no built year. The register says 'late 1940s', which cannot be stored as a single year, so no built event is recorded; the story gives the register's wording. Brief's elevation 137.8 m matches the register's 452 ft. No design or height source was found, and no access source was found, so those keys are omitted. The Maine Forest Service page covers the state network in general, not this tower specifically.

Thin: one annual-report quote and one 1932 map. The record's 'gone' status conflict is unexplained; please check where that value came from. No access level or visit information was found, so the access key is omitted. No notable fires were found in the sources read. Dates for cab removal and the viewing-platform conversion were not found in the pages read, so no events are recorded for them. Access 'public' comes from the Land Trust and the register; the story gives no climbing advice. No source I could read gives the date of the present tower or the last year it was staffed. History is well sourced from the Forest Lookouts page, the 2012 and 2013 Maine chapter reports, the 2012 historians report and a 2013 dedication notice. Current condition and public access are not confirmed. The FFLA list says standing. A Visit Aroostook search snippet mentions climbing the tower, but the page itself does not, so it was not used. No photos added; a Maine chapter Facebook post and Ashland Logging Museum pages were seen only as search snippets.

Built 1914 and the 60-foot height rest on the Forest Lookouts page (which quotes the 1914 Forest Commissioner's Report and a 1920 inventory) and a Maine Memory photo. Two Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter Facebook posts describe the tower as standing without a cab, but those pages returned no readable text and are not cited. The FFLA list and legend give the current standing (structure kept, cab gone). The state plan says closed and the Maine by Foot guide says a climbable ladder remains; we follow the plan and do not encourage climbing, and the disagreement is stated in the story. Read: Press Herald 2019 (built 1933; lower steps removed; trail restored; 6-mile round trip), Maine by Foot (intact tower; TNC warns people not to climb), FFLA Maine standing list (no asterisk, so cab not marked missing). The main conflict is current status: the FFLA list says Standing, while Maine Memory and its exhibit say the 36-foot steel tower was removed in 1993. Facts record status gone with the conflict in the status note, and the corrections list proposes standing to gone for human review; a recent photo or Forest Service record would settle it. The township is TD R2 WELS in Maine Memory and Township 9, Range 3 in the 1914 report; the FFLA coordinates were not checked against either, and the sources do not reconcile the two. Access, ownership and current condition not found in the sources read, so no access fact is recorded. Staffing not found. FFLA lists it as standing with no asterisk. Build dates (1914, 1919) and the 36-foot height come only from WillhiteWeb; no second source was found. No build date or design found for the Opportunity Farm tower. The Eastern U.S. Lookouts New Gloucester page, which this record links, never mentions Opportunity Farm. The Conway Daily Sun replica article returned HTTP 429 twice and was not read. Read budget exceeded by about two pages.

Brief 2008 restoration event is supported by the report; brief wording 'paint still to come' is consistent.

Current cab and tower condition is unresolved: FFLA gives no asterisk (cab presumed in place), the Press Herald says boarded up, and Secret Falls describes a glass cab in present tense. A search summary said the tower was lowered to 36 ft in 1960 and that the Maine towers were abandoned by the 1960s; neither was verified in a page read, so both are left out. A Conway Daily Sun article on a replica map stand returned HTTP 429 and was not read. Search summary ownership figures (Loon Echo about 2,000 acres, TNC 1,400 acres, Maine Forest Service 20 acres) were not verified and are not used. The OpenStreetMap way was not read. The Press Herald article's date was not shown in the text read, so it is not cited by date. Brief height_m 20.0 is proposed for removal (see corrections).

Access, ownership and the date the cab came down are not in any source reached. No trail or visitor source found for this Penobscot County mountain; the search returned a different Ragged Mountain in Knox County (Camden/Rockport), which is not this tower and was not used. Height conflict: the record's 11.0 m matches the 1917 36-foot figure; the 1920 inventory says 48 feet. Visit and access keys omitted until confirmed.

Height: register says 54 ft (16.5 m); the 1920 inventory and 1921 newspaper item say 48 ft (14.6 m). The record's 14.6 m is kept; the conflict is unresolved. Early history: a 1917 wooden tower (warden report) conflicts with a 1919 report of a log tower on another bluff; unresolved. The 2017 cab loss is confirmed by two sources. The FFLA list marks the tower Standing*, and its footnote defines that mark as a tower whose structure stands with the cab no longer in place; the steel tower's standing rests on that list, and the cab loss on the 2017 report and Forest Lookouts. Access is by permit from private timber roads; no permit contact or trail details were verified. Ownership: the register places it in the Maine North Woods with 7 Island Land Co. named; the owner is not stated.

No source read gives staffing, fire history, or public access for this tower, so no access or staffing key is recorded. The brief's 1914 build date refers to the first site; the present site dates only to the 1940s. Registration date confirmed on the NHLR page. A social-media photo caption was seen but not used because it is not a citable source. Brief coordinates differ slightly from the FLO list (46.54703, -69.76447); not material.

No current access, ownership or cab-removal date found. Searches returned an unrelated Round Mountain in Albany Township near Bethel (private land with a trail, no tower), and the FFLA list shows a different Round Mountain in Franklin County (a tree, gone); neither was used. A geocaching page describing an old tower names no county and was not used. Height of 48 ft (14.6 m) agrees with the record. Visit and access keys omitted until confirmed.

Access conflict is unresolved: the undated Maine Trail Finder guide says the decommissioned tower should not be climbed until further notice, while the 2020 BDN column (by the Allagash superintendent) says the new cabs are for visitors. The record's 2018 'restored' event is recorded here as maintenance and cab planning; the 2020 cab is recorded as 'replaced'. No build date, builder or height found. The 2020 report says the Bureau of Parks and Lands pre-built one cab at its Ashland facility and Shiretown Structures of Houlton built the other two; the column names a local contractor, which is consistent with that, so the builder is treated as resolved. The 2018 report says the Ashland-built cab was for this tower. Access level set to restricted pending the Bureau of Parks and Lands.

Build history is well documented (1914 wood, 1920 steel with cab), and the brief's height (7.3 m, 24 ft) matches. Status is the open question: FFLA lists it as standing with cab gone, but the Forest Lookouts record gives a 2005 'Lookout structure removed' with no detail; no modern photo or visit report was found. Staffing is inferred from the statewide 1991 end of the network, not a tower-specific record. Access rests on the public Donnell Pond trail; whether the old tower itself is climbable is unverified, so no climbable flag is set. Watchmen 1917-1919 come from a photo caption only. The brief's agency name is kept as the historical Maine Forestry District. Maine Memory record 1514 (ca. 1920) is a photo candidate, not added because its licence was not checked. Recommend a site visit or a current photo before any status claim is strengthened.

Build dates (1910 wood, 1914 steel with cab) agree across the Forest Lookouts page and the Maine Memory record. Staffing is documented only for Don Hicks (1966-1967 per the Sun Journal). FFLA and FranklinSites agree the cab is gone; neither gives a date, so no event is dated for the cab loss. Access is the weak point: the summit sits on Penobscot Indian Nation land behind a gate, and no source states a permit or public-visit rule either way, so the access level is set to restricted rather than public. The Maine by Foot and SummitPost pages describe hiking routes, which were used only for the gate and the distance; they do not endorse climbing the structure, and the story says not to. Summit elevation differs across sources (3,948 ft at the tower site per Maine Memory; 3,960 ft and 3,967 ft per FranklinSites and Maine by Foot); not used in the story. Photo candidate Maine Memory record 19137 is not added because its licence was not checked.

Thin record: the detailed history stops at 1920 on the Forest Lookouts page, and the only later evidence is the FFLA Standing* listing. Height conflict (12 ft in three records vs 16 ft in one caption) is resolved toward 12 ft; the brief's 3.7 m matches. Access and land ownership were not found in any source, so no access or visit block is set. Staffing is inferred from the statewide 1991 end of the network. A Facebook photo post seen in search results describes a late-1950s photo and says the tower was still standing the year before and had lost its cab long ago. It was not used, because it is an unverified social-media post and was not fetched; it is a lead for someone who can check it. Photo candidate Maine Memory record 19135 (ca. 1920) is not added because its licence was not checked.

Sources conflict on whether anything stands here now: FFLA says standing with cab gone, the lookout history says removed with no date, and the register says unknown. No staffing record was found. The 48-foot and 26-foot heights need the original 1917 and 1918 reports. Facebook posts by the FFLA Maine chapter mention a 1918 wooden tower and a Scopan Mountain name, but Facebook pages could not be read, so they are not cited. The FFLA list also has a separate Haystack Mountain log tower entry (gone); the register suggests a link, which we did not confirm. Worth a field check or an FFLA Maine chapter contact before publishing a status.

Sources disagree on several dates and on what was moved. Staffing end: WMTW says 1976, Maine Memory says the tower closed in 1968. Move: WMTW says the cab went to the visitor center in 2011 by helicopter; Maine Geographic says the tower was reassembled in 2015; Maine Memory says October 2012 to the Natural Resource Education Center. The register's 1959 date for the present steel tower conflicts with 1919 elsewhere. The register entry (US 67) still describes the summit site, not Greenville. Agency for the Greenville tower is not documented (the register lists the Maine Dept. of Conservation for the summit site), so it is left out. The NREC page (nrecmoosehead.org) returned 404 and was not used. Access is marked public only because the tower sits beside a visitor center that Maine Geographic calls worth a visit; climbing is not documented. The Commons photo already in the record was not re-added. Page reads: about 6 distinct pages, plus one search.

The tower is described as standing with its cab in place (FFLA lists no asterisk). Open conflicts: build year 1920 (Maine Memory) versus 1923 (state page and map); height 47 ft (state page) versus 55 ft (trail listing); and the National Register listing date versus the page's eligible wording. A Facebook post by the FFLA Maine chapter says it is now on the National Register; Facebook could not be read, so it is not cited. The Maine Preservation Most Endangered list was not read directly; the Maine Memory page reports it without a year. Last fire-observation use 1967 comes from the state's period of significance, not a staffing record, so no last watchman is named.

Height_m 10.4 is the 34-foot figure converted (34 x 0.3048); the 1987 replacement's height is not given. The 2021 article's closed-to-hikers caption is the only source for current access; no fresh visit report was found. A Maine Forest Service Facebook post (seen only as a search snippet, not fetched) says the lookout closed permanently about 1991; it is not used because it could not be read. Named fires: none found. Staffing field is inferred from the 2021 article's list of active towers, not from a staffing record. Facebook sources were not used as citations.

The cab-gone status rests on one FFLA asterisk and has no date; no current photo or visit report was found. The 1920 inventory is cited through the Forest Lookouts transcription, not the original inventory. No access level is recorded because no source describes access; the site's land ownership is not stated in the sources read. Maine Memory photo credit and licence not recorded (no image URL verified). Facebook snippets about this watchman camp were seen in search results but not fetched, so they are not cited.

Built and rebuilt dates (2020) agree across three sources. The 1931 station move rests on a Maine Memory caption that sits beside a Black Cat Mountain photo, so it may refer to another structure. The closure is only given as 'the 1970s'; no source gives a year. The 120-ft height, the 1940s date and the Alabama origin rest on Davana's page alone, and the Conservancy only says 'Alabama'. Name correction needs human sign-off. Summit elevation disagrees (1,409 vs 1,427 ft). Sources treat the tower as open to hikers, but none states a formal public-access rule for the tower itself.

Dates and dimensions agree between Maine Memory and the Eastern US Lookouts page. The cab removal date is unknown; the only condition evidence is the FFLA note and a 2021 trip report. No current owner, access rule or condition report was found, and the trip report describes a bushwhack, so the story does not encourage a climb. The 1915 'staffed' event rests on a photo caption and the watchman's note, not on a staffing record. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine post says the tower has not really been manned since the 1930s, but I did not read that post, so it is not used.

Only source found is the Eastern US Lookouts page, which itself just quotes a 1929 newspaper item and the 1967-68 Forest Commissioner's biennial report. No NHLR or FFLOS register page exists for this site (nhlr.org returned 404), and nothing was found on current status, access, staffing, or whether the tower still stands. The tower record's location (45.65887, -68.18754, from FFLA) was not independently corroborated against the 1929 'Macwahoc Plantation' description within this budget; worth a closer look if a human researcher has more time.

Standing status rests on the FFLA index (no asterisk) and the trail page's description of a fire tower at the summit; no recent photo or visit report was checked. Access level 'restricted' is a judgment: the trail is open by landowner permission and the tower is not to be entered. The trail page is undated apart from a 2019 review, so the 'trailhead not yet constructed' note may be out of date. The 1912 watchman is not named in the source. The 1911 fire station may be the cabin the trail page describes; the sources do not say so outright, so the story does not claim it. AllTrails returned 403 and was not used.

Two York Hills in Franklin County: the FFLA point (44.59676, -69.97355) and the MountainZone summit near Weld (44.67658, -70.37558). By my calculation the two points are about 33 km apart, so it is not certain which hill the FFLA tower is on. Confirm the point before accepting it. No build date, design, owner, staffing or history was found; two searches turned up no account of the tower. The story is deliberately short.

No build date, builder, or height found. The only dated history is the 1943 staffing quote, which we read through the Forest Lookouts page (the original newspaper was not reached). The 'T. Cabin: no' field is unexplained, so the design line is cautious. The Michigan history page (michiganfiretower.com/history/) appeared in search only and was not read. The 'NGS None' register value in the brief looks wrong (see corrections). Access unknown, so no access or visit facts are recorded; the freelibrary article on 1940s lookouts returned 403 and was not read.

Status 'standing' from the brief is not supported by any source read, so it is omitted from facts; the firelookout.org Michigan page returned no Bergland entry. Access and staffing unknown. The brief's 30.5 m height likely comes from the 100-foot figure in the 1953 report, which describes the destroyed tower. Only two sources; a further search for the Michigan tower list or a recent status report could resolve status and the current tower's history.

No build date found; the 1935 item already describes an existing tower. Access and visiting rules were not found, so the story says so and the facts block omits access. The NHLR lists the cooperator as 'Painted Rocks National Lakeshore', which I suspect means Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore; not verified and not in the story. The easternuslookouts Alger county page says CCC crews built eight new towers in 1937-38 and that one was at 'the Alger site'; I could not tie that to this tower, so it is not used. The 1935 and 1943-44 items are quoted through the easternuslookouts page, not the original newspaper or report. The NHLR mid-1950s staffing date is approximate, so the event year 1955 is a placeholder.

No design, height or access source was found, so those keys are omitted. The NHLR page shows a 2021 photo, but no later check. A geocaching listing describes current radio use, but its page did not load in our fetch, so the story makes no claim about that. Two Facebook posts from the Forest Fire Lookout Association and two NARA photographs appeared in search results only and were not used.

Sources disagree on early dates and on the tower's history. (1) First towers: Wikipedia says 1936 and the NRHP nomination ties them to the 1936 fire without a year; the NPS Isle Royale page says CCC built them in 1939. (2) Old tower: Wikipedia says it stood near the new site and was torn down in 1963; the nomination puts it a half-mile away on Turkey Ridge. (3) Naming: the NPS Isle Royale page calls the re-established Turkey Ridge tower 'Feldtmann Tower'; the nomination uses New Feldtmann Fire Tower for the 1964 tower. Check which tower the Park Service means before any visit. (4) Height: the record's 12.2 m (40 ft, from NHLR) matches the 1961 plan; the built tower is 41 ft 3 in per the nomination and Wikipedia. Proposed correction to 12.6 m. (5) Abandonment: Wikipedia says by 1968; the nomination says use diminished after 1968 and eventually ended, with shelter use into the 1980s. (6) Access: climbing partway is from the NPS places page (updated Feb 2022); the NPS fire-tower page says the tower is no longer utilized. Current conditions and any closure are unverified. The NRHP nomination PDF is long; only targeted extracts were read, so the 1936 construction year for the old towers is not confirmed in the nomination itself. Reads: 5 distinct web pages plus one search; a local cache copy of an eastern lookouts list was checked and not used.

Company number: the register says 3611 (James Lake). A search snippet from SAH Archipedia's Camp Gibbs page names the 3604th Company for that camp, but that page returned HTTP 403 and was not read or cited, so the conflict is unresolved. The michigan.gov CCC page also returned 403. No visit report or current condition information was found, so the standing status rests on the register's 'only remaining' wording. Access is omitted because no source describes it.

Not confirmed as a fire lookout. OSM tags it tower:type=observation and gives no builder, date or height. None of the seven NHLR Michigan names or the two FFLOS names matches it. Mapcarta places it in Quincy Township near Ruby Marsh and Lake Annie. The record's 'standing' is not backed by any source read. Next: Michigan DNR fire tower records or Houghton County local history for this site. Do not publish as a fire lookout until a source says so.

Not confirmed as a fire lookout. OSM tags it tower:type=observation with lattice construction, and Mapcarta places it near the Whitefish Point Light. The station history sources read do not mention a lookout tower. Neither NHLR nor FFLOS Michigan list matches it. The record's 'standing' is not backed by any source read. Next: Michigan DNR fire tower records or Chippewa County and station histories. Do not publish as a fire lookout until a source says so.

Brief's height 13.7 m is not in any page read. Corrected to 12.6 m from the NRHP nomination (41’-3” from the concrete piers). The npgallery.nps.gov asset page returned no text, so the nomination was taken from the npshistory.com PDF. Nomination gives both June 1964 construction and July 1964 assembly; Wikipedia gives 1964 in the infobox and 1965 for completion; all are kept. Wikipedia credits NPS with the 1939 towers; the nomination credits CCC personnel. Access: the NPS page says the tower room is closed but visitors may climb partway up the stairs; the story reports both and does not encourage climbing the tower. No photos added (no confirmed image URLs or licences). Nomination has many figures, not checked for licence. Verification 2026-10-09: the story's fire-cause claim was contradicted by the nomination and is now reported as a disagreement; 'in the cab' was removed (not in any page read); the 'scenic stop' and tower-room sentences were reworded so they no longer copy NPS wording.

Build year 1933 agreed by the register and Forest Lookouts. Current condition and public access are unverified: no dated source read says the tower stands today, so the record's 'standing' rests on the register entry alone. A Forest Lookouts page for the lake lists a federal survey marker at the tower stamped TEPEE 1938; that is the marker's date, not the tower's. A NARA photo caption and a Facebook post surfaced only in search snippets and were not used. No corrections proposed. Fact-check 2026-10-09: 'has a cab' became 'was built with a cab' because no source confirms the tower stands today; the Kenton Ranger District sentence now cites the Forest Service page; the Iron County quote was added as evidence.

Built-year conflict (1936 vs. NHLR's 1940/CCC claim) is real and unresolved; I favored 1936 since both Wikipedia and the NRHP period of significance back it, but a human with access to the actual NRHP nomination PDF (not just the NPGallery detail page) could settle it outright. No cached local source pages existed for this tower beyond the NHLR page; no newspaper or Forest Service primary-source search was attempted beyond the two WebFetch calls used here (within the 3-search budget, no WebSearch calls were needed since WebFetch on known URLs sufficed).

No build year is given: the Register says only the 1920s, so there is no built event. No current fire-watch staffing was found; the Register says the tower remains in service with the park interpreter attached. Height: the Register says 80 ft; other sources say 100 ft total including the cab. The record's 30.5 m is kept. Public access rests on a 2024 visitor account and the park's exhibit; park hours and closures were not checked. The Forest Lookouts page is a hobbyist site that reproduces NGS data and is cited only for the NGS description. No photos added.

Height: the Register and county list say 81 ft (24.7 m, used here); the Forest Lookouts page says 80 ft. The record had 24.4 m (80 ft). The 1923 and 1924 towers come only from the county list; the Register mentions only the 1924 tower's anchors. No current access or staffing source was found, so the story does not say whether the public may climb. The Register's 2018 photo credit is not repeated. The Forest Lookouts page is a hobbyist site reproducing NGS data, cited only for the 1948 description and 80-foot figure. No photos added; the Commons category may hold Creative Commons images, not checked.

The county PDF's Babbitt note was read in full. It opens 'Standing. MFS. Octagonal cab.', gives the 1928 to 1966 map listing, and ends 'The tower was located southeast of the village. Removed.' No removal date or cause is given. The Minnesota list (firelookout.org) marks it Standing. The story previously said both lists show it standing and that no removal was recorded; that was contradicted by the county note, so the story now reports the conflict. No build date or builder found. The county list marks ownership 'USFS?'. The 1952 survey record only names the tower. Confirm the current status with the county or site manager before publishing.

Maker is disputed and not resolved: the Register says Aermotor; the Hubbard County list says McClintock Marshall stairway tower. The 'restricted' access level is inferred from the Register's note that nursery personnel use the tower; no closure notice or access rule was found, and the state forest page we fetched had no readable text. Current condition rests on the Register alone. The 1933 nursery date is from the county list only and was not checked against a DNR page. The Forest Lookouts page is a hobbyist site reproducing data; it is used only for the 1934 height. No photos added.

The two accounts of the first tower conflict on builder (CCC vs state), height (100 ft vs 60 ft), and the 1936 replacement, which appears only in the local history. Both are reported; the sources do not say which tower stands today, so the built events are not merged. The 1980 survey describes the tower the record calls standing. The NGS PID RN1233 appears on the Forest Lookouts page and is not in the record; consider adding it to registers. A Wikimedia Commons photo (Ball Bluff Lookout Tower.jpg) is linked from Wikidata, but its license was not checked, so no photo is added. No access, staffing, or current-condition sources were found.

Sources agree on the 1935 build, the 2007 move and the 100 ft to 80 ft change. The Beltrami report lists the 1935 owner as Mn MFS (Minnesota Forest Service) while the NHLR says Minnesota DNR built it; the forest service was part of the DNR, so this is not treated as a conflict. Dedication date is unclear: the 2007 chapter report anticipated a late-June ribbon cutting, and a search snippet from a YouTube video mentions June 30 with a 2009 date, which I did not open; the story does not give a dedication date. Public access and climbing hours were not found; the story tells visitors to ask the camp. The 2007 chapter report calls it the East Bemidji tower, and the story keeps the brief's name.

Public access is unknown: no source says whether visitors may climb it. Emergency use and the radio repeater rest on one hobbyist history page and are undated; I did not confirm them with an agency. A RadioReference forum post about a 158.8125 repeater on Ben Draper Forest Road was not used because it is old and not tied to this tower. The record's existing photos cover this tower; no new photos were added. Access block omitted because level is unknown.

Only one tower-specific source (the 1960 NGS station description) plus the standing listing. No build date, builder, staffing or fire history found. The access level 'restricted' is our reading of the reservation location, not a stated policy; a human should confirm with the reservation before publishing. The NGS description does not say who decides access, so the story now presents that as our reading rather than a sourced fact. The NGS gives an overall height of 110 feet; it is not entered as height_m because the height to the cab floor is unknown. The record's agency matches the Forest Lookouts header.

Thin record: NHLR, Forest Lookouts and the county inventory are the only substantive sources. No staffing, access or current-use source found. Not used: the inventory's 1912 'Fire Ranger Lookout' (a 50-ft wood lookout near Birchdale, not tied to this site; mentioned in the story as unlinked) and the 'Happyland' / Littlefork entries (Tower 90, a different site). The 1967 survey height of 100 ft conflicts with 81 ft and is flagged, not adopted.

Access is the main gap. The fence is from a 2004 recovery note and the 'not opened' status rests on an NHLR line of unknown date; no current source. visit.climbable is null because no source says either way, and access.level is unknown because the fence is dated 2004; treat the access block as unverified until MnDOT or DNR confirms. Search results surfaced an undated travel guide that says a tower can be seen from the road; not used. The inventory notes 'Rainy Lake lookout' as an alternate name, not added to the record's other_names. No new photos.

The 1935 build date rests on one Commons photo description; no independent source found. The 2016 chapter report (a short report, fully read) mentions the CNF's 3 fire towers without naming them, so Blackduck's place among them is unknown. The author's remark about further progress is between a named individual and the CNF, and involves the three towers; the story wording now says only that. The Commons caption places the tower in the Chippewa National Forest; the record's agency is null and could be filled after confirmation, not from this caption alone. This research file has no elevation field, so the story states none. The access level stays unknown.

Build year 1934 rests on the NHLR Built field and the footing inscription. Height 38.1 m (125 ft) is added to the record from an undated survey note; the record had none. No staffing, fire or visiting-rules source was found, so access is left out; the story says to ask the Band first. A statewide A-Z lookout list (Wikimedia Commons PDF) names the Band as owner, but its row gives no date or height here, so it is not cited. No builder is named anywhere; do not attribute to the CCC without a source.

The Register text is undated, so the open season may have changed. The record's county (Itasca) is correct for the current site. No pre-1976 fire or staffing records were found in these sources. No photos added.

Thin record: no build date, builder, design, staffing or fire history in any source read. Two search rounds turned up only the directory and unrelated Isanti County courthouse pages. A guessed firelookout.org detail URL returned 404. The Commons photo and Wikidata image are already in data/photos_manifest.json, so no photos entry was added. Next checks if wanted: Isanti County Historical Society, City of Cambridge, Minnesota newspaper archives for the 1930s.

The 1934 build date and the 100-foot height come from one hobbyist page that reproduces a federal survey station description; no DNR or NRHP record was read. The current status is unresolved: the directory says standing, the survey note says replacement was planned, and nothing later was found. Search results mentioned a Clear River or Beltrami Island history but none was read, so none is cited. The 30.5 m figure is a conversion of the 100-foot source figure.

Built date 1931, 80 ft and Aermotor design rest on one local history page (Forest Lookouts). No manufacturer source was read; a Peakbagger entry (1931, 80 ft, standing, user-submitted and unverified) and search snippets were not quoted. Results of the 2018 Collaborative Design Group assessment were not found. The Forest History Center tower in Grand Rapids is a different structure and was not used. Access is set to restricted as a judgment: the forest is open in daylight, the recreation page does not mention the tower, and the 2018 door was unlocked for visitors, but the stairs and railings were under safety review. No current tower policy found. Staffing is unknown; the Forest Lookouts page gives no staff names.

Construction date conflicts (1929 entry vs 1931 survey note); both kept. The antenna distance (about five miles) differs slightly from the survey's 4.5 miles; both are reported. height_m 29 is 95 ft converted. The NGS PID SJ2055 appears on the Forest Lookouts page and is not in the record; consider adding it. The 1934 approach directions are historical and may be outdated. No staffing, fire, rebuild, or current access information was found. The Minnesota Historical Society page on the Forest History Center fire tower in Grand Rapids is a different tower and was not used.

The 1937 CCC build rests on a local history page that reproduces a federal survey station description, and on a 2011 Commons caption that repeats it. No independent CCC or DNR record was found. No National Historic Lookout Register page for Cotton was in the cache (two guessed URLs returned 404). The auction is undated; the caption places it a few years before August 2011. Wikidata puts the tower in the Cloquet Valley State Forest, which conflicts with a sale of forestry property; ownership should be checked against Saint Louis County or DNR records. Access level is omitted because no current statement was found; the brief's access 'unknown' stands. Commons photo File:Cotton_Lookout_Tower.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0, uploader Tlkremer) could be added once its direct image URL is confirmed; not added here. Staffing and notable fires were not found.

The Forest Lookouts page is the only source for the 1949 build. A search summary claimed a 1935 CCC build; the cached page says 1949 and does not mention the CCC or 1935, so 1935 was not used. Height conflict: 100 ft (1949 build line) against approximately 80 ft (1952 survey); the brief's 30.5 m matches the 100-ft figure and was kept, so the editor should choose. The Wikidata elevation of 1,394 ft matches the brief's 424.9 m. No National Historic Lookout Register page was found in the cache (one guessed URL returned 404). No staffing, notable fires, access or current condition were found. The Commons photo is listed on Wikidata but its file page was not read, so it is not added to photos.

Only location, county, forest, Wikidata elevation (about 1,434 ft) and standing status are supported by reachable pages. The Wikidata elevation of 1,434 ft matches the brief's 437.1 m. A search summary said a minnesotafiretower.blogspot.com post (Cuba Hill Lookout Tower, December 2012) gives a pre-1935 build and a 120-foot ladder tower, and that another blog page says two or three towers survive in the Chippewa National Forest. Those claims are unverified: the blog post, the December 2012 archive and the August 2012 Chippewa history page all returned 404 here, so they are not used and no height or build year is recorded. The Forest Lookouts index gives no build or height data. An OpenStreetMap node (8169190028, Cuba Hill Lookout, tower:type observation) was read but not cited. The Wikidata image Cuba Hill Lookout Tower.jpg (2,736 x 3,648) was not read, so no photo is added. No staffing, notable fires, access or condition was found; the brief's access 'unknown' stands.

Owner and build year conflict across sources; the story reports both. No staffing or notable-fire record was found in the sources read. The photo credit comes from data/sources/commons_credits.json and the mirror manifest, not a fresh fetch. Access is inferred from the radio-site use; no visit rule was found. The story tells readers not to climb.

Built year conflicts: the Register and a 1936 press report say 1936 (CCC); the DNR page and a 1997 Post-Bulletin article say 1933. Not resolved. Height conflicts: Register and 1936 report say 110 ft (33.5 m, used in facts); 1997 article says 100 ft; a 1973 NGS description says about 130 ft; the OSM node tag says 35 m (the current record value). Steps conflict: DNR says about 500, 1997 article says 634. Hours conflict: DNR gives daylight hours April to October (page undated); 1997 article gave 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. Current access and condition not confirmed by any dated source after 1997 except the undated DNR page; check before publishing visit details. Record access 'unknown' can be set to public per DNR. No photos added; NHLR and Post-Bulletin pages were not checked for licensed images.

Build year (1928 placement vs 1929 erection) and county (Cass vs apparent Crow Wing) conflict; the story reports both. No current condition, access, rental or later staffing record found. The Forest Lookouts Emily page holds no further text beyond the 1928 and 1929 items. The photo source_url follows the standard Commons file-page pattern and the credit comes from data/sources/commons_credits.json; neither was re-fetched.

Build year conflicts (1934 survey reference vs 1935 erection); the story reports both. Current condition and access were not verified. The directions are from the 1934 survey and may be out of date. No rental listing was found. The Chippewa NF and recreation.gov pages were not reached; a Chippewa tower-loop page returned 403. The photo source_url follows the standard Commons file-page pattern and the credit comes from data/sources/commons_credits.json; neither was re-fetched.

The 1935 CCC build date, the 100-foot stairway and the older tower about three miles south all come from one local tourism page; no DNR, NRHP or other tower record was read. The directory row 'Faunce – first' (48.55044, -94.95354, Tower Gone) sits about three miles south of the current tower, which fits the older-tower account, but the link is our inference. The Norris Camp National Register nomination appeared in search results but was not read. The Commons photo for Faunce is already in data/photos_manifest.json, so no photos entry was added. The 30.5 m height is a conversion of the guide's 100-foot figure.

The only build year (1940) comes from one compiled Minnesota list with no builder, owner or source named. Two web searches and several page reads found no staffing, fire, access or current-condition record. The Commons photo caption is the only description of the tower itself. Record had no built year; one added from the list. The 100-foot figure is the overall tower height as listed, so it is recorded as height_m 30.5 on the same basis as the Abbeville record. Wikidata names the tower after the village, consistent with the record.

Built year 1936 is consistent across the county booklet and the state list; the 1937 Commons caption and the 1920s origin claim are unresolved. Height is disputed within the booklet (81 in the table, 90 feet in the 1960 note). No access, staffing or current-condition source was found; the record's access and staffing stay unknown. The booklet owner abbreviation Mn MFS is not spelled out in the part read, so agency is stated as an abbreviation. Record had no built event; one added. Summary and story say the tower stands above Frontenac Lake, per the booklet.

No source read gives staffing, fire history, or public access for this tower, so no access or staffing key is recorded. The Flickr photo is marked 'All rights reserved', so it is not listed under photos. The Wikidata entry (Q107464014) adds only a name and coordinates and is not cited. The brief's elevation (449.9 m) and build year (1934) agree with the Register.

Two lists disagree on year and height (1934/80 ft vs 1935/86 ft). No staffing or fire history found. The access level 'public' rests on one visitor account and no official rule; check before publishing. Owner and legal-location fields in the record are the main fixes. Verification 2026-10-09: the P600 account was corrected (the writer parked on a small road and walked the last part; did not drive the track to the summit).

Only the NHLR page and the FFLA list support facts here. No build year, builder, height, staffing or fire record was found. A search returned a different 'Heritage Lookout Tower' in Orr, MN (chamber of commerce listing); it is not this tower. A statewide A-Z list has a Heritage row naming the Band as owner, with no date or height, so it is not cited. The same list mentions a state tower 'located near Bois Forte IR' on a 1941 map at about 48.065, -93.032, roughly 6 km east of this site; the sources do not say whether it relates to any of the three towers, so it is left out.

Only three short listings were found, none with a build date, design, height or staffing. The permission access level and tribal status come from the record; the listings we read name only the reservation. A search summary suggested the Red Lake reservation lies mainly in Beltrami County rather than Koochiching; this was not verified, so the story says boundaries were not checked. The Koochiching County tower booklet on Wikimedia Commons (Koochiching_County_Towers.pdf) has no Indian Pines entry, checked by full-text search.

Height conflict: Register (60 ft, 18.3 m, used in facts) and Central Lookouts 1934 entry say 60 ft; a 1936 US Forest Service survey note on the Central page says 100-foot steel tower. Not resolved. The Register text misnames the tower once as 'Jacob Peak Fire Tower'; the Register title and the record say Jasper, so treat that as a typo. The 1919 wooden tower and 1996 land sale come only from Lake Vermilion Net, a local history site; not checked against a second source. No dated source after the 1990s states current public access, climbing rules or condition; access and visit facts are left out. Staffing: 'still used into the 1990s' only, so no staffing fact. The Register page credits a photo by Jacob Hufnagle; no new licensed photos found. The NGS-style 1936 note is quoted from the Central Lookouts page.

Only one substantive source (a 2011 newspaper article) plus the FFLA listing. The 1934 build date is 'according to historic accounts'. No post-2011 report found, so demolition status is unknown; a current check (photo or DOT/county records) would firm up the fate. Record elevation 499.0 m matches Wikidata's 1,637 ft.

Thin record. Register and Central Lookouts agree on 1934 and 80 ft (24.4 m, used in facts). No source found on access, climbing rules, staffing or condition after 2020. Two web searches and a few pages gave no access information; the Peakery page is a peak listing with no visit details, so it was not used. Register spells the maker's town 'Bethleham'; the story says Pennsylvania. Peakery lists the elevation as 1,392 ft while the Register says 1,395 ft; not in the story. Wikimedia Commons has a category of photographs (Category:Kabetogama Lookout Tower) but licences were not checked, so no photos are added. Access is left out of facts because no source supports it.

No source gives a build year, builder, or the tower's original agency/duty near Isle, or when it stopped serving as a working lookout before the 1981 move. The FFLA state list (cached) and Wikidata both just confirm name, location, county, and 'standing' status, with no narrative detail. Height (100 ft) and the 1981 move date are corroborated by multiple independent sources (Exploration Vacation, Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, and MN DNR), which is why confidence is medium rather than low despite the record itself being nearly empty. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft stated the tower is "steel" and has an "enclosed" platform, and gave the moraine/dam description in wording copied almost verbatim from the DNR/mspmag pages; none of the cited sources mention the tower's material or an enclosed platform, so those were removed, the moraine sentence was rewritten in original wording, and the Isle origin claim's footnote was corrected to the sources that actually say "near Isle" (Exploration Vacation and DNR, not mspmag).

No staffing or fire history found. The county lease is undated. The FFLA standing listing is undated. Height conflicts across sources are unreconciled. Recheck current status before any change to the record.

The history rests on one detailed survey PDF of Beltrami County towers on Wikimedia Commons; its author is not named and it has no date. Wikidata and the Forest Fire Lookout Association list only confirm the location and standing status. No staffing, fire or access source was found. Two guessed NHLR URLs returned 404 and the firelookout list shows no NHLR number, so the tower may not be registered. Access and visit fields were omitted because no source says whether climbing is allowed; the brief's access 'unknown' stands. Coordinates differ slightly: the brief and firelookout list give lon -95.27798; Wikidata gives 95 deg 16 min 40.09 sec W (about -95.27780); the survey gives -95.2779. Lat 48.33153 vs survey 48.3316. The gap is about 15 m, so no correction is proposed. Elevation 377 m (1,237 ft) from Wikidata matches the brief. The survey row lists height 80 with type Ladder. No photos added: the Commons file Linder Fire Tower.jpg exists but its license was not checked.

The 1927 build date is supported by NHLR and by the survey table, but both rest on the same survey tradition and the table text is garbled in places. The 1967 survey note calls the cab bird-cage type and also octagonal; the story reports both. The Central US Lookouts listing and the blog page were not usable for detail (blog returned 404). The brief's Central US coordinates (lon -93.80326) disagree with NHLR and FFLOS (lon about -93.7795); the record's own coordinates match NHLR. The brief's 'Built' value comes from NHLR. No staffing, fire or ownership-transfer dates were found. A WebSearch summary described a station on MN 11 and County Road 32 at the tower's location, but that was not read from a page, so it is not used. The NHLR photo credit (Tom Kremer) has no image URL, so no photo is recorded.

Build year conflicts: 1929 (lookout history) vs 1925 (Cass County survey, whose table is hard to read). Staffing facts rest on newspaper items quoted by the lookout history page; originals not seen. Brief listed agency as Foot Hills State Forest, which is the forest, not the owner. No fire history found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from the town-site description and is not verified. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the 1939 telephone-line direction was corrected (the new line connects to the forest service line that runs into the station); the 1925 survey sentence was given its missing footnote.

The 136 ft figure is a survey-report value quoted by the NHLR and is not checked against a second source. Height 41.5 m is converted from 136 ft. The record's access 'permission' is a conservative editor label; the NHLR page gives no visiting rules, so the story says to ask the tribe first and states no access level. No build year, builder, staffing or fire record was found.

Built date 1939 comes from the county table's date column, not a construction narrative. Height conflict: 80 ft in table and text vs about 120 ft in 1952 survey note. Cab removal date and the move to communications use are undated. Access is inferred from the fence in a visitor's photo page; no official access statement was found. Staffing and fire history not found.

Location, standing status and the cab conflict are sourced; no build date, height, staffing or public-access statement was found. The county survey's Owner column lists Mn MFS for both Maud entries and gives no builder record; its Type column lists the standing tower as Stair. The county survey lists two Maud entries (footings of a first tower, and the standing stair tower) with no dates. Superior Hiking is a hiking blog; its comments are reader reports, not official. A WebSearch hit suggested Grand Portage State Forest near Hovland, but we could not confirm the tower lies inside it, so it is not used. Mount Josephine on Hat Point, also near Grand Portage, is a separate tower the same survey marks removed. An unnamed abandoned tower north of Grand Portage in Minnesota Monthly was not identified with Maud, so it is not used. Access is left unset: no official source says the public may enter. The blog's climbing account is not endorsed; the story says to check with the land manager.

Standing status and location are supported by the FFLA list and the county survey. The county survey gives no date or height for Mount Sophie; its Owner column lists Mn MFS, and no builder was found in two WebSearch queries or the sources above. The only visit account is an undated Superior Hiking blog post, and its comments are reader reports. One WebSearch result (a Minnesota Geocaching Association page) was not used because it is user-contributed. Access is left unset because no official source says whether the public may enter. The blog's climbing account is not endorsed; the story says to check with the land manager.

Thinnest of the three. The only sourced facts are the FFLA listing (standing, Beltrami County, coordinates, type Tower, no register number) and a Roaming Civic list entry dated 2025 with no description. Two WebSearch queries and the Beltrami and state FFLA lists turned up no build date, builder, height, owner, staffing or access statement. The anyplaceamerica.com tower page returned HTTP 403, so it was not read. A TopoQuest hit for Mud River Reservoir is a different place about 9 km away and is not used. Suggested next checks: Beltrami County Historical Society, Minnesota DNR forestry records, and FFLA's Minnesota chapter reports (the 2007 and 2019 reports fetched here do not mention Mud River).

Central page and Commons caption agree on 1935 and 86 feet; height_m 26.2 is the metric conversion of 86 ft and matches the brief. No source found on who built the tower, why, its current access, or current staffing, so no access or staffing key is written. The Central page also prints a code 45N-17W-9 under the county name; not used. Two WebSearch hits (a 1928 Nimrod tower in Wadena County and a 1935 Pequot Lakes tower) are different structures and were not used. Record agency is null and stays null.
