Brief checked: the 420 m elevation and the May 14, 1997 registration match the NHLR. Height 94 ft is converted to 28.7 m. A 1981 survey note in the Wadena list says about 100 ft; the story reports the conflict. The blog cited in the brief (minnesotafiretower.blogspot.com, 2012) returned 404 and is not used. No source read names a specific fire the tower helped catch. Access: NPR (2021) describes one northern Minnesota tower as reserved for lookouts only; the article's Nimrod passage follows that line, so the story treats it as probably this tower, and no public visiting rules were found. No photos added. The NPR staffing claim is from 2021 and is the newest staffing evidence found.

The 1934 build year rests on one 2008 state list, which also marks the tower scheduled for disposal, while FFLA still shows it standing. Confirm current status and any disposal with Minnesota DNR Forestry before publishing a fate. Norris Camp (NRHP 94001080) is a separate CCC-era district; no source links it to the tower. The 2008 list has a Forestry footnote about historic buildings at Norris Camp, which does not mention the tower; the story reports it. No access or staffing record found. No photos found.

Build year is disputed (1934 NHLR vs 1935 nomination and county). Current access comes from a 2026 visitor guide and was not checked on site. Staffing status rests on a 2019 article. The NRHP listing date was not confirmed.

Relocation year 2011 is supported by the county report, the DNR virtual tour and the IFalls guide. Suggest adding year 2011 to the record's relocated event, which has none. One aggregator page (Grokipedia) gives 1995 for the move; it was not used because the county report and DNR both give 2011. The DNR's 1930s-fires sentence refers to towers at Big Bog, not to this one. Waymarking (not read) gives spring 2011 for the move, which would fit. Photos: no verified photo found with a licence; a Minnesota DNR webcam view exists but was not added.

No build date, maker or design statement was found in the sources read, so the story has no build section and says so. The Pioneer gives 80 ft to the platform and 90 ft to the roof top; height_m uses the platform figure. The Pioneer article's year is not shown and the fair dates are left out. The first draft missed the Pioneer's by-appointment access from May 1 to Oct. 1; the story and access note now include it. Quam's 2019 report and the FFLA list agree on the 2004 move and the Tower Gone / Tower Standing entries. The Quam history page (Page336) has no Pinewood entry. Budget: two WebSearch calls; about five distinct pages read, with the FFLA list and the Pioneer article each read a second time with a narrower grep. A 2007 chapter report snippet also gives the 2004 move, but it was not read and is not cited.

Only one build-date source (the Kanabec County survey). No staffing or fire history found. Access level omitted: no source describes public access or the current owner. The survey places the tower under the Moose Lake Forestry Station, which may mean restricted access; not verified. The visit account reports decayed stair treads, so the story advises against climbing. Height converted from 95 ft (28.96 m, shown as 29.0). The FFLA index shows no NHLR number for this tower. Photo already in photos_manifest, so none added. Fact-check 2026-10-09: story said 'worn stairs'; the source says decay, so the story now says decaying stair treads.

Thin record. Only the FFLA list places the tower; no build date, design, owner, staffing or access record was found in any source read. Searches did not confirm whether Ponemah lies within the Red Lake reservation (Wikipedia's navigation box lists the reservation but the article text does not say so). Ownership of the land and the tower is unknown; Red Lake Nation or Beltrami County history sources would be the next step. No photos found.

The 1963 date rests on one site. The Commons caption (the photographer's own description) says the tower was previously the Peet tower about 30 miles south, but gives no date for the move and no source found for the Peet tower. A search for the Peet tower returned nothing relevant, so no relocated event is written (year unknown). The story says the 1963 date may or may not refer to the current site. Record agency 163N-33-19 is printed in the Central page header as a bare code with no agency named; it looks like a land-survey location code. Not changed here; editor to check. No access or staffing source found.

Build year 1929 comes from the Aitkin County survey alone; no conflicting date found. Ownership of the tower is unclear: the mountain is now a townhouse property per the association, and no source says who controls the tower or whether visitors are allowed, so no access level is recorded. Staffing and fire history not found. Design and height were not in the brief; added from the survey. Photo already in photos_manifest, so none added. Fact-check 2026-10-09: no factual errors; the townhouse page was added as evidence for the Aitkin County and Hill City location in the first sentence.

Only one source reached. Two web searches gave no build date, builder, design, staffing or fire history. The list agrees with the record on name, county, coordinates and standing status. A search surfaced the Faunce tower in the same county; it is a separate record (us-mn-faunce) and was not used here. The record's Wikidata item (Q107507037) was not fetched. Worth checking against a Minnesota DNR or state fire-tower catalog, and the access and visit fields are still unknown.

The 2008 state list has a fire tower whose only location name is 'River' (built 1928, scheduled for disposal). The list has no county or coordinate column, so it may or may not be this tower; it is mentioned in the story as unmatched. The FFLA coordinates were not checked against WMA boundaries. The DNR WMA page does not mention a fire tower. Records to check: Roseau County Historical Society, Minnesota DNR Forestry. No photos found.

Only one source reached. Two web searches gave no build date, builder, design, staffing or name origin. The list agrees with the record on county, coordinates and standing status. Search snippets mention a Rushseba Township in Chisago County (Minnesota Board of Appraisers docket pages on mba.state.mn.us); the name resemblance is an unconfirmed lead, not used in the story. Worth checking with the Chisago County Historical Society and the state fire-tower catalog linked from firelookout.org. Access and visit fields remain unknown.

Built year (1947), height and design rest on one inventory page (Forest Lookouts, Minnesota section); the FFLA list confirms only location and standing. The Komoot visitor listing is the only source for the probable fire use and the no-climb note; both are unverified and worded that way in the story. Two DNR Sand Dunes pages were read and did not mention the tower. The agency value 34N-27-22 looks like a survey location code, so a correction is proposed. The visitor listing places the tower in the Uncas Dunes SNA, which the editor may want to confirm against the DNR's SNA description.

Staffing, early use, fires and current hours are not in any source read, so none are given. The record's agency (Minnesota Dept. of Natural Resources) is not confirmed by the pages read: they name the Minnesota Division of Forestry as builder in 1933 and place the tower in Savanna State Forest, but none states the current manager, so facts.agency keeps the builder. Wikidata (Q107541658) lists 1933 and Aitkin County; its linked blog returns HTTP 404 and was not used. Access rests on one chamber page; confirm hours with the managing agency.

Two text sources agree on 1934 and a 100-foot steel stairway tower. The A-Z table height column reads 86, which is not explained. The A-Z entry's 1959 survey notes (120 and 125 feet) appear to belong to the neighbouring Savage entry, so they are not used. No staffing, fire history or current access statement was found. The 2019 significance study is named but its report was not located. An AllTrails trail page (saying the tower is closed to the public) returned 403 and was not used. The brief's record values (agency, height 30.5, standing) are consistent with the sources.

Almost all detail comes from one compiled list (the A-Z PDF). Wikidata's 1932 date and 100 ft height show no references on the page, so they do not independently confirm the A-Z list. The A-Z list credits the CCC, which ran from 1933 to 1942, so the CCC credit and the 1932 date conflict. The story says so; the sources do not resolve it. The 1936 survey note (80 ft, station about 16 miles north of Chisholm) sits in the Side Lake row of the A-Z PDF, checked against the PDF text layout, so its attribution holds. The Wikidata link to a minnesotafiretower.blogspot.com post returned 404. No access, staffing or fire information was found. The brief's record (standing, 100 ft, 1932 built) is supported, and its agency field is left general.

The 1926 date appears on the Central page and in the Commons caption; both are short and may share an origin. No source reached explains the term windmill tower or who built it. No height, access, or staffing source found. A second WebSearch returned nothing on this tower. Record agency 140N-37W-15 is a bare code like Prosper's and looks like a land-survey location code; not changed here, editor to check.

Aermotor rests on one source (Forest Lookouts); the NRHP calls it a standard 100-foot steel tower and does not name a maker. Build year is disputed (1936 vs 1937). The seasonal closure comes from a guest column, not a DNR notice, so confirm current park hours before relying on it. The 1948 item is quoted by Forest Lookouts and was not checked against the newspaper. The 'record' 1936 build year is supported by two sources but not the DNR page. Wikidata (inception 1930s) was not used.

Sources disagree on the build year: the county list text says 1928, while the county table and the Central US page give 1938. They also disagree on height: 94 feet in the text and table, about 100 feet in a 1941 survey note. The 1941 note sits in the Summit row of the PDF, but the identical wording also sits in the LaSalle row, so its attribution to Summit is doubtful; the story says so. facts.height_m is 28.7 m (94 ft) per the text and table. The Central US page gives no height. No access, staffing or fire information was found.

Built date (1934 vs 1935) and height (100 ft in 1964 notes vs 86 ft in the county table) are unresolved; no height_m recorded. Newest on-site description is 1964; current status and public access are unverified, so no access key was set. No NHLR or FFLOS registration was found. Wikidata elevation and the Commons photo are already in the record, so nothing new was added to photos.

Thin record: no staffing, fire, access or rental sources were found. The Minnesota fire-tower index at kjackson.us had no match for this lookout. Wikidata's linked blog post was not read. The register's photo (August 2016, credit Jacob Hufnagle) has no URL or licence in the text, so no photo was added. The brief's record matches the sources, so no corrections are proposed. Staffing and access are omitted because no source gives them. The forest is disputed: Wikidata gives Kabetogama State Forest and Forest Lookouts gives Superior National Forest; the story reports both without choosing.

Standing rests on the FFLA list alone; no current photo or owner contact was found. The county report gives no date for the sale or the move, only that the tower was sold and stood near Bemidji by the 1966 survey note. 'Mn MFS' is read as the Minnesota Forest Service; the report does not spell it out in the text we read. The us-mn-waskish record's agency field holds '154N-30W-8', a township/range/section location rather than an agency, and its height (30.5 m) differs slightly from the county table (30.4 m). Searches: 1 WebSearch; about 4 distinct pages read.

Height conflict (94 ft tower vs 100 ft overall in 1960 notes) is unresolved; facts use 94 ft. Newest on-site description is 1960; the Aitkin PDF has no date for its status, and the FFLA list has none either, so current condition and public access are unverified and no access key was set. The Commons photo already in the record was not re-added. No NHLR or FFLOS registration was found. The statewide A-Z list (upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/A-Z_List-Towers.pdf) has the same 1933 and 94 ft figures but was not cited.

Brief checked: county, agency and the 1935 build year match the NHLR. The 2026 condition and the Camp Willow company number come only from onX, a commercial trail-map page whose history section reports a February 2026 visit and a March 2026 documentation; treat it as secondary. The onX text says the cab and stair projects 'had since been completed' but describes the bottom stair flight as 'being re-constructed', so the story reports the stairs as in progress at the visit. The NHLR entry dates from 2010 and says the tower is in need of restoration; the story gives both dates. The 'unstaffed as of 2010' reading is inferred from 'No longer used'. The OpenStreetMap node (358066399) has no history and is not cited. No fire is named in any source read. Access is restricted by the closed gate and the day-use rule; no source says whether the tower may be climbed. No photos added.

Two sources only: the Register and the Forest Lookouts page. The year conflict (1936 vs 1938) and the older district name are reported, not settled. Access is left out because neither source says whether visitors may climb it, and the schema has no unknown value. The staffing as_of date is the Register's registration date, not a dated staffing check. Brief values confirmed: 1938 build, 30.5 m (100 ft), agency, and the June 28, 2026 registration. The Register has a photo caption but no image URL, so no photo was added. Living New Deal returned 403 and was not used; an Instagram post and the Forest Service history page had nothing usable.

Height conflict: 60 feet (Register, Forest Lookouts) vs 80 feet (MDC current page). The story flags it and keeps 60 feet. The MDC page is undated, so the 'standing' and public-access status reflects what it said when fetched on 2026-10-09. The brief's 'standing' is now supported by MDC. A 2018 MDC Central Region towersites plan PDF mentions the Camdenton towersite; I saw it only in a search snippet and did not read it. It may settle the height and condition. Staffing today is not stated by any source; the towerman quote is a 1941 plan. No rental listing found. No photos added.

Fact-check 2026-10-09: the Register and Forest Lookouts pages were searched for 'rebuil', 'wood' and '1967' and show no rebuild, so the story keeps the onX account as unconfirmed. The 1940 build date and the 68-foot steel tower agree across the Register and Forest Lookouts. The wood-then-steel rebuild in 1967 rests on one trail-app listing that cites MDC; I could not reach MDC's own page on it, so it is marked unconfirmed. Access is 'restricted' based on a trail listing that says the gate is likely closed and locked; no official visiting rule was found. No tower-specific staffing record was found, and the MDC magazine's staffing lines are general to its towers. The brief's 20.4 m height is corrected to 20.7 m (68 ft). The NGS 1962 station note calls the overall height approximately 80 feet; I left that out of the story because it conflicts with every other source. Missouri Life (403) and Living New Deal (not read) were not used. The Facebook post in search results was not read. No photos added.

Build year 1926 is the register's figure with no source; the 1930 press item is the earliest found. Height disagrees (85 ft vs about 100 ft in 1962). Climbing status is unconfirmed: the Semissourian and Missouri Life articles returned 403 and were not read, so the access level is public area, climbing unknown. Staffing record stops at 1951. About 6 page reads used.

Brief's 1958 build year is the start of the register's 1958-1959 range (correction applied in story 2026-10-09). The 1985 tornado and rebuild come only from the Forest Lookouts site, which gives no rebuild date. The MDC closure notice is undated. Not read: the Eminence Towersites plan PDF on archive.org (timed out twice); Facebook posts (tornado damage, lower steps removed to prevent climbing) appeared only as search snippets and are not used. A separate 'Doniphan Water Tower' entry appears in the Forest Lookouts index and was not checked. About 4 page reads used.

Only two sources, and the register itself says resources are extremely limited. Build year is 'allegedly' 1937. Closure date unknown. No Forest Service page found; the News-Leader 2018 article returned 403 and was not read. Staffing omitted (no record found). Visit note treats the tower as closed. About 3 page reads and 2 searches used.

Two conflicts are left open. Height: the Register says 100 ft; the 1943 annual report quoted on Central Lookouts says 50 ft. The brief's height_m 15.2 is the 50-ft figure, so it is left out of facts for the editor to decide. County: the brief and the Register say Texas County; the Central Lookouts list and page say Shannon County. The Central page's annual-report entries describe a 1943 steel tower, then later steel towers replacing temporary wooden ones in 1957-58 and 1962; the story reports this without choosing. The Register's land and erection dates are attributed to online resources, and the story says so. The brief's agency name follows the Register; the Central site uses 'Missouri Conservation Commission' for the same agency's earlier name. No staffing or fire data was found in any source read. Visiting rules are not stated. A Facebook group snippet mentioning the Angeline Conservation Area was not used. No photos added.

Two disputes left open. Build year: the register says 'likely' 1939 (Bartlett CCC camp); Forest Lookouts gives 1934 with no source; both are shown. County: the register says Shannon County, Forest Lookouts says Carter County (27N-2W-31); the story avoids naming a county. No current visiting or rental information was found; the register says restoration is planned. Two Facebook items (Shannon County Museum, Ozarks History Archives) appeared only in search snippets and were not used. Confidence is medium because of the unresolved county and build year. Fact-check 2026-10-09: two story sentences that closely copied register wording were reworded, and the summary now says restoration is planned pending approvals and that staffing was intermittent.

Built year (1950), 100-foot height and the Conservation-owned site agree across the Register, Forest Lookouts and the 2025 blog. Unresolved: the 1962 Coast and Geodetic Survey description (wooden, about 50 ft) disagrees on material and height; flagged in the story. Access: the Register (2025) says climbing is signed and the cab is inaccessible; the 2025 blog found no fencing, after earlier posts said fenced off. No staffing or fire history appears in the Register or the Forest Lookouts annual-report extracts, so none is stated. Condition and access after March 2025 are unverified; re-check before publishing any visit guidance. No photos added. The Register credits a photo to Rick Brown, AICP, but no image URL was captured.

Built year (1960) agrees across both sources. Current status and public access are unverified: the 2015 plan has no access statement for the Houston site (its Cabool appendix says that tower is closed to the public, which is not this tower). OpenStreetMap node 12729567032 tags access=yes and fee=no; that is a volunteer tag, not an authority statement, so no access key was set. The Facebook posts by Missouri Conservation History and Equipment mention an Aermotor MC-39 design and directions, but the fetch returned no readable text, so they are not cited. A 2018 local news item in the Central US Lookouts page concerns a private individual and is left out.

Height is unresolved. Sources give 90 ft (Aug 1927, under construction), 73 ft to the deck plus a 9 ft steel room (Sept 1927), 72 ft (Apr 1928), 80 ft (Dec 1935) and 85 ft (1939-41 annual report and NHLR). The record's height_m 25.9 equals 85 ft and is kept as the NHLR and annual-report figure. The guide's cab-floor measure is closest to the September 1927 figure of 73 ft to the deck (about 22.3 m), so the editor should decide which measure the record carries. Built 1927 is supported by NHLR and by the September 1927 completion clipping. Status 'standing' rests on the NHLR description, which is undated. Access level 'public' refers to the conservation area; no source read confirms the tower is open to climb today, and the 2019 article is the latest visitor description read. Staffing 'seasonal' rests on the 1935 clipping alone. The 2019 Conservationist article gives the area as 13,005 acres; the MDC page gives 13,503, which the story uses. The nature.mdc.mo.gov page returned 404 and was not used. No photos added; the record's existing NHLR photo is unchanged.

Built date is not established. The record has none. The only dated construction fact is the November 22, 1934 newspaper item that the foundation was being dug; the 1936 completion date appears in a web search summary citing the Living New Deal database, but livingnewdeal.org returned 403 to our reader, so it is not used and needs a manual check. Height: record height_m 33.5 equals the 1939 survey's 'about 110 feet'. The 1934 cab-floor figure (99 ft 9 in, about 30.4 m) is a plan, not a measured height. The editor should decide which measure the record should carry. Status 'standing' rests on the Salem News description in the present tense and the NPS page, which invites visits; no source read states the tower's condition in 2025 or 2026. Access level 'public' refers to Forest Service land with free parking; climbing is not confirmed. The NHLR entry says 'Nominated by Admin'. The NHLR photo set was not added to the record. Staffing is not stated in any source read; the Salem News credits CCC Company 732, not a lookout crew, with construction.

Built 1949 matches the register; the 1947-48 land acquisition precedes it and is consistent. The register's "100' Aermotor" does not say whether the height is to the cab floor, so height_m 30.5 is the stated tower height and the editor should confirm. Status and staffing rest on MDC's towersite page, which is undated but describes the tower in present tense as used by MDC staff to spot wildfires. The 1959 towerman death is in the story without his name; the JSON quotes avoid the name too. The acreage difference (80 acres in the late 1940s, 26.8 acres now) is unexplained. A web search summary tied the 1949 date to a different tower in a Missouri Life article; it was not used. No photos added.

History and register facts agree with the record (built c.1965, standing, registered 2026, coordinates). Height 100 ft is taken from the 2021 report's cab-entrance height and converted to 30.5 m. Access is set to restricted: the 2018 plan gives the picnic area limited public use, and the tower is closed to climbing. Staffing is recorded as unknown because no source says whether the tower is staffed. The newest firsthand detail is the July 2021 newspaper; no 2024-26 visit or photo was found. The 1980 event year marks a decade, since the Register gives no year. A Facebook post by Missouri Conservation History (in search results only, not read) mentions a 2023 deed agreement; not used.

Only three readable sources. No height was found in them, so none is recorded. The 2023 visit is the newest condition report. The agency question is unresolved: the River Hills column is undated in the text read, and the 1953 land purchase claimed on a geocache page (GC4AMAQ) was not readable, so it is not used. Built date 1953-54 agrees across sources. No corrections to the record. Status note is included because the cab is in poor shape; the tower is otherwise standing.

Current condition is not verified. The newest dated evidence is a 2014 headline (the article is paywalled, so only the headline was read) and a 2018 photo credit; no 2024-26 visit or report was found. Unverified leads, not used in the story: a USAspending contract record in search results mentions tornado repair at the Roby Tower site, but that page is script-only and the bid page returned 403; a Facebook snippet says built 1937, which conflicts with 1934 from the Register and Forest Lookouts. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m; it is not a cab-floor measurement. Access is left unknown because no source states it. No corrections to the record.

Which 1949 tower went to Runge is unclear. Forest Lookouts says a new steel tower was erected at Rocky Mount in fiscal 1968-69 and that a tower was moved in 2000, without saying which. The Runge caption says the tower there was formerly at Rocky Mount; no source read confirms the upper portion was re-erected or the tower's condition today, so 'standing' rests on the register's location. Heights for Runge found only in search snippets (72 ft, 55 ft, 77 ft at Rocky Mount) were not used. The register spells the site 'Rocky Mountain' once. The Waymarking page and a Missouri Life article were not readable through fetch_text. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the story no longer says the Commission put the tower up, since no source names who erected it; the 2000 move is now attributed to 'a tower' with the ambiguity stated; the Miller County footnote now sits on the sentence that states it.

No source read gives a build year; the July 1935 article is the earliest mention. A search snippet from AllTrails says the CCC built the tower in 1936, but the page returned HTTP 403, so it is not cited and the 1936 date conflicts with the 1935 article. Missouri Life and The Prospect pages (both HTTP 403) reportedly say the tower is still used to spot smoke; not verified, not cited. Record access was 'unknown'; set to public for the park, climbing not confirmed. Staffing as_of 1958 is the last staffing mention found. Fact-check 2026-10-09: facts.status changed from 'standing' to 'unknown', because no source read confirms the tower's present condition.

The record id spells the name 'stegrall'; both sources spell it Stegall Mountain, so the id is left as is. The 1962 event comes from a source that reads 'FY 1962-03', apparently a typo for the 1962-64 biennium; the report's own title reads 7/1962 to 6/1964. The 70 ft figure is an 'about' from the 1963 survey. Search snippets (not fetched) claim a 100 ft height and an Aermotor MC-39 design; not cited. Hiking-site snippets suggest the tower is still reached on foot; the MDC page is the cited source. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the story now says the tower 'appears to still stand' from the MDC page's hike description, and the 'no lookout named' point is limited to the reports read.

Most of the history (1948-1981) comes from newspaper and annual-report extracts transcribed on Forest Lookouts; the quotes were checked against that cached page, not the original papers. No fire events are named in any source read, so none are stated. Height disagrees across sources (60, 72 and 85 ft); facts use the Register's 72 ft. The brief's height_m of 235.3 is unsupported and is corrected. Access: no closure notice found; the state park page does not mention the tower, so public access rests on park status and the 2025 blog visit. The Wikidata entry lists the Missouri Department of Conservation as operator and names a Commons photo, 'View from Taum Sauk Mountain Lookout Tower.JPG', which was not checked for licence and is not added. Nothing after the 1980s is documented apart from the 1991 park, the 1997 registration and the 2025 visit.

Unverified leads, not used in the story: a Missouri Conservation History Facebook post (https://www.facebook.com/MCC1010/posts/thomasville-fire-lookout-tower-this-tower-and-the-surrounding-40-acres-was-sold-/770545715109867/) appears in search snippets to say the tower and 40 acres were sold on GovDeals; the post and the GovDeals listing (https://www.govdeals.com/asset/16/11790) returned 403 or only a title, so the sale is unconfirmed. A second post in search snippets describes a 68-foot Aermotor MC-39 tower northeast of Eminence; it may be a different tower. A search snippet gives a 1951 build year, but the fetched NHLR page says 1957; the fetched page is used. Missing from record: removal date and access level; no source gave either. The brief record's other_names 'Thomasville (Federal)' comes from the Forest Lookouts list.

No height, design or fire history found in the readable sources. The NHLR detail page gives only elevation (1,387 ft, 423 m). The News-Leader article returned HTTP 403, so it was not read. Forest Lookouts is a hobbyist site that quotes a 1936 Gazette item. The MDC plan dates from 2015, so current staffing and fence status are not verified. The removal of the dwelling buildings is a range (late 1960s or early 1970s), so no event year is recorded for it. Site directions in the plan were left out because the site is closed to the public. Brief's 'standing' and 'access unknown' were checked: standing per NHLR; access is closed per NHLR and the 2015 plan. Check 2026-10-09: all 18 quotes were found on the first run; three footnoted claims were corrected (a missing footnote on the dwelling sentence, the 1935 'seeing it' detail, and the undated 'Today' access claim, now dated to the 2015 plan and the NHLR's undated 'currently').

Record id is us-mo-unnamed, but the sources call this the Cabool fire tower; id left as is. Build year and height agree across two sources. The Cabool towersite is in Texas County, and the record's Texas County is correct. The MDC towersite page gives the directions 'From Cabool, take Route M north 2 miles' and public-use hours for the area; both are now cited. A Facebook post (not fetched; search snippet only) says the same directions; not cited. The sources read do not say which side of the site holds the tower or what happens to it after the July 2026 action; a follow-up could check the MDC towersite map or a later Commission action. Fact-check 2026-10-09: facts.status changed from 'standing' to 'unknown' and access.level from 'restricted' to 'unknown', because the 2015 plan is the last physical description and its locked-gate note is dated.

Unresolved date conflict: a Living New Deal page (https://livingnewdeal.org/sites/desoto-national-forest-airey-work-center-mchenry-ms/) says construction of the Airey Work Center began in 1935 under the CCC. The fetch returned 403, and the WebFetch paraphrase cannot be quote-checked, so the story does not use it. The NHLR 1934 date is used for the tower. A blog (https://thedirtymule.com/trails/desoto-national-forest-airey-lake-fire-tower-circuit/) also returned 403 and was not read. Access level not found in any source readable here, so it is omitted. Record change: the brief's record had no build event; 1934 added from NHLR.

Build year unknown in every readable source (NHLR says Unknown). The 1948 report is read only through the Forest Lookouts page, which quotes the Clarion-Ledger; the newspaper itself was not read. A second search returned FCC tower #1042132 'Kosciusko, MS (Dismantled)', which is a cellular structure, not this lookout, and was not used. An Attala Historical Society history page (https://sites.rootsweb.com/~msahs/history.html) returned 403 and was not read. Access level omitted: no source readable here states public access. The brief record's access 'unknown' stays.

Only the NHLR entry and one family obituary profile were read; the Weebly Barge page is a name-and-county stub. The brief says status standing, but no page read states the tower's current condition, so facts.status is unknown. The register's agency name differs from the 1985 company name (Barge Forest Products Co.); kept as NHLR wrote it. Two searches found no construction history or staffing record. The obituary profile does not mention a tower: a full-text check for lookout, tower, watch, fire and observation found no matches. Re-checked 2026-10-09: NHLR shows Elevation 586 ft (179 m), Built Unknown, and Administered by C.A. Barge Forest Products. The story's advice about visiting or climbing the tower was not supported by any source and was removed.

Agency: NHLR lists U.S. Fish & Wildlife under 'Administered by' and the Mississippi Forestry Commission under 'Cooperators'. This supersedes the earlier draft's reading that the Forestry Commission was the agency. Build date unknown after three searches. The 2023 standing note and the NGS datasheet text come from a secondary copy on the Forest Lookouts page; the original datasheet was not fetched. Goose Overlook (Wikipedia) and the Webster overlook in the refuge trail brochure are different structures and were not used. No access or visit rules were found.

Only the NHLR detail page and the 2020 Secretary of State public lands list were read. Two web searches and the Forest Fire Lookout Association Mississippi page found nothing local; that FFLA page says its Mississippi data is still under construction. The cdispatch.com article returned HTTP 410 and was not used. The register does not say outright that the tower is standing, so status is recorded as unknown; neither the register description nor the 2020 list confirms it. The access level private rests only on the register note. The conflict is open: the register says private property, while the state list places a Clay County Tower under the Forestry Commission. The state list may refer to a different site or the land may have changed hands, but neither is verified. Suggested next step: ask the Mississippi Forestry Commission about the tower and its owner, and check Clay County parcel records.

The register's history of the eight Bienville towers is detailed and gives the build range for this tower. The register's 1934 start for the towers conflicts with Wikipedia's June 15, 1936 establishment date for the forest; left unresolved. A search snippet attributed to a National Park Service nomination gave March 26, 1934 for the forest's start; that source was not read and is not cited. The Moore NRHP nomination (npgallery def15102) was read and its cached text has no mention of Clear Springs. Not found: staffing, fires watched, access status, or any current condition beyond the register's remains standing line. Two web searches and the Bienville Wikipedia article were the only other sources read. The 2020 Secretary of State state land list has a Smith County Tower under Forestry Commission; that is a state site, not this Forest Service tower. Suggested next steps: Bienville ranger district office in Forest, and Mississippi Department of Archives and History.

Only the NHLR detail page and the 2020 Secretary of State public lands list were read. Two web searches and the Conehatta Wikipedia article (no tower mention) found nothing local. The maker and the 120 ft height come from a register writer who says they could not find a makers label, so both are hedged in the story and should be treated as unverified. The register's own line 'It stands 120ft tall' is the only direct statement of standing; the 2023 site visit findings are not stated and the 2020 state list gives no condition. The record's access field was left unknown because no source gives public access status. Not used: a TowerDex directory of Mississippi Forestry Commission structures, which has no Conehatta entry, and the absence there does not rule out a shorter tower. Suggested next step: ask the Mississippi Forestry Commission for the tower's manufacturer, height, build date and current status.

Almost every tower-specific fact rests on the one NHLR detail page, which is written by a volunteer register contributor. Two searches found nothing else about this tower; the Sanders family's name and the 1991 sale appear only there. The Aermotor and MFC pages are Wikipedia, used for context only; the Aermotor article's 7x7 claim is not tied to this tower. The brief's access 'unknown' is now 'private' from the register's 'Private Property' line. No build date, staffing history or current-condition report was found. The register gives the sale price and the 1991 year with no citation of its own, so treat them as the register's account.

Only the NHLR detail page supplies tower facts. Two searches and a topo page (anyplaceamerica.com, HTTP 403) added nothing about this tower. The register lists the MFC as administering the site but also says the MFC no longer uses it; the owner today is unknown, so access is 'unknown' rather than guessed. Current status rests on the July 2022 site visit. The 'missing bottom flights' note is the register writer's, from 2022. The Aermotor page is context only and does not identify this tower's model.

Single source: the NHLR entry. The Forest Lookouts page for Energy names only the site and county. Two searches found no construction, staffing or fire history, and no Forestry Commission tower record for Energy. The brief's coordinates and elevation match NHLR. The condition quote contains the source's typo 'i a' and is kept as written. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against the NHLR page: Elevation 526 ft (160 m), Built Unknown, Administered by Mississippi Forestry Commission. The story now uses 'administers' rather than 'in connection with', and the two search-based statements no longer carry a page footnote.

Thin record: the NHLR page is the only substantive source. The Forest Lookouts Fairview page has only a header (Mississippi Lookouts, Fairview, Itawamba County) and no text, so it is not cited. Searches on the Mississippi Forestry Commission and the Itawamba Historical Society archives returned no tower history. Build date, staffing, fire history, and current condition and access are not in any source read. The brief's elevation (167.6 m) matches the Register's 168 m. The brief had no height; the 100 ft figure comes from the Register's description. No photos added. Story is at the 120-word floor because the record is thin; the Register's next-entry link is the only added detail.

Identity unconfirmed. The OSM point is 2.7 km from the Maben register coordinates and about 9.9 km from Oktibbeha, so it may be a mis-placed duplicate of one of them, or a different structure. The 2020 state list has no Fire Tower entry for Oktibbeha County. The story may not be worth publishing as a lookout history until someone confirms the point. Searches: 2 WebSearch. Page reads: 4 distinct.

The NHLR page is the only tower-specific source. Two searches turned up Flintkote Company well records and land-patent pages for Kemper County, but nothing ties them to this tower, so they are not used. The '(II)' suffix suggests an earlier Flintkote tower; the NHLR previous-lookout link points to Kemper (De Kalb), US 1667, not to a Flintkote tower, and this was not investigated. The brief's agency (MFC) conflicts with the description's timber-company owner; the correction is proposed for a human decision. Current owner name, condition and visitor access were not found.

Two sources only. Linking the register's Gauley tower to the Gauley Mountain tower in the 1935-36 account is an inference from the shared name; the register does not mention the CCC. The msgw.org https certificate has expired, so the page was read and cited over http. The record's material 'steel' is not in the register, which says only Aermotor; consider null. Facebook posts about the tower came up in search but were not read. Do not confuse with the Gauley Mountain tower site in West Virginia (FFLOS).

No build date, staffing or fire history in the register, the Forest Lookouts entry or the agency home page. The register's no-longer-in-use note is undated. Possible next steps: MFC records or Alcorn County newspaper archives. The record's agency spelling is a typo; correction proposed. Access level 'permission' is a judgment from agency administration and no public access information.

Only the register and OpenStreetMap were read. The Forest Lookouts page guessed at glenville.html returned 404, so no Forest Lookouts entry was found for this tower. No build date, staffing or fire history found. Access level 'permission' is a judgment from agency administration, not a stated rule.

Probable duplicate: the Greenwood (US 1774) and Leflore (US 1737) entries sit about 10 m apart in Leflore County, but the register does not say they are one tower and the nominators differ (Mike Lyon vs Jason Johns). The story keeps them separate and says so. Only two register pages found for this site after two searches each; the local-history searches turned up nothing. The Leflore entry's MFC administration and 120-ft Aermotor are not attributed to the Greenwood record in facts.

Only the register and OpenStreetMap were read. No build date, staffing or fire history found. The Raymond name may refer to the town rather than a site name. A search turned up an unrelated OSHA report on a 1997 TV antenna tower collapse in Raymond, Mississippi; not used. Access level 'restricted' is a judgment from the register's still-in-use note, not a stated rule.

Only the NHLR entry, the Forest Lookouts index (name and county only) and the Aermotor history were usable. Two WebSearch queries and several page reads turned up no local history, staffing, fire, build or fate information. The register's Hopewell visit note is undated. Status is 'listed' only: the register's present-tense description is not a dated check, so the story says the current condition is not confirmed. height_m is converted from the register's 100 ft. No access key set because the sources give no access level. No photos found.

Single source (NHLR) after two searches and a check of the Kemper County history page, which had nothing on the tower. The access level is left unknown: the removed treads suggest the stair cannot be climbed as it stands, but no source says whether the site is open or closed. Only the NHLR entry and the Forest Lookouts index (name and county only) were usable. The register gives a site visit noted as 2/5/22 and no narrative beyond the tower type. Two WebSearch queries found only a 1911 map mention of Kincaid and an unrelated 2005 antenna structure at Gore Springs, which are not used. The Gore Springs = Kincaid link is not supported: the register does not mention Gore Springs and the Gore Springs page does not mention Kincaid, so the story makes no such claim. height_m is converted from the register's 100 ft. No access key set. No staffing, fire or fate information found. No photos found.

Only one substantive source, the NHLR register entry, plus Wikipedia for the county seat. The 1957 build year is the register's Built field; the description beside it is undated and refers to Forest Service employees 'last week', so the wording may come from an old newspaper report, which is not confirmed. The 100 ft height comes from that same description and is converted to 30.5 m. No staffing, fire, rental or current-condition information was found in two searches and a few page reads; the Mississippi Forestry Commission or Mississippi Digital Library may hold older records. The record's photo already exists (credit Jennifer Payne), so no new photos were added. Status 'standing' is proposed as 'unknown' in corrections.

Thin record: only the NHLR entry, the Forest Lookouts index (name and county only) and the OSM node were usable after two searches. No build date, staffing, fire history, access or visit information found. height_m is converted from the register's 80 ft. No access key set because no source gives access. Grokipedia and anyplaceamerica appeared in search results and were not used.

Only the NHLR entry, the OpenStreetMap point and the Aermotor history were usable. Two WebSearch queries found nothing local about this tower. Coordinates were compared directly: the register's N 33.526580, W 090.263410 and the OSM point 33.5265960, -90.2634276 are within a few metres. height_m is converted from 120 ft. No access key set. Identity is the open question. The 1936 notices (quoted on Forest Lookouts from The Lexington Advertiser) describe a CCC-built steel tower on the poor house property north of Lexington. Thin record. The only sources are the NHLR detail page, the July 2020 state public-lands list, and the county wildfire plan, which mentions the E911 and cell towers but no fire lookout. The brief lists status standing; I have set it to unknown because no visit or condition report was found, though the register describes it in the present tense. No build date is given. A search result named a Forestry Commission-registered structure in Brookhaven (170.6 ft, built 1994) on towerdex; it is an antenna registry entry, not checked, and not used. Search snippets about other Lincoln County towers were not used.

Single source (NHLR). Two searches turned up no build date, builder, staffing or condition history. Map sites list a 'Winston Lookout Tower' and a 'Tombigbee Lookout Tower' in Winston County; those were search snippets only, not fetched, and nothing says whether either is this tower, so neither is used. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from the active MFC offices on the site, not from an access statement. The register's Louisville name is the only one confirmed.

Thin record. Sources are the NHLR detail page (2022 site visit, build date unknown) and the July 2020 state public-lands list, which shows a Maben Tower under the Forestry Commission. Status is standing on the strength of the 2022 visit note, not a later survey. Two search results were not used: a Columbus Dispatch article describing an idle tower with rotted stairs (the URL now returns 410 Gone, so its quotes cannot be checked), and a Towerdex record for a 379.9 ft Natchez Trace Parkway antenna in Maben, which looks like a communications structure. The article's condition description conflicts in tone with the 2022 note about replaced boards; an editor may want to confirm current condition with the Forestry Commission.

Single source (NHLR). Two searches found nothing else on this tower. The date the MFC vacated the site and the current owner are unknown; the 'private' access level rests on the Register's 'possibly owned by a timber company' wording. The 'standing' status rests only on the July 2022 visit. The Register's own admin and vacated statements conflict in tone (administered by MFC, yet vacated by MFC), so the story states both.

Thin record: the register page is the only source with dates and agency; Wikipedia and OSM only confirm location and a lattice design tag. The 2021 imagery line is the latest condition evidence; no 2024-2026 check found. Access roads were locked at the 2023 visit, but no public-access statement appears in any source, so access level is recorded as unknown rather than restricted. Thin record: register page gives registration, agency, elevation, the 100 ft LS-40 design and the 2023 visit; build date is Unknown in the register and no other source found. Access is not described in any source, so no access fact is written.

No 2024-2026 report on condition, climbing rules or closure was found after two searches. Access was left out because no source supports a level. Standing is inferred from the Register's 2023 site visit and present-tense description, not from a condition report. The build year is only a range, 1935-1940. Single source: the NHLR register page. The eastern_us_lookouts page cached for this tower holds only a title and a Mississippi lookouts heading, so it is not cited. The record's status 'standing' is not stated by the register; the 2022 visit is the latest evidence. No Wikipedia article for the place was found (404). The only detailed source is the 2022 NHLR entry, so the story has almost no build or fire history. Two searches and four page reads found no build date, staffing or fire record. The register entry is short and undated, and it is the only detailed source; the story says so. Its agency line reads 'Privately Owned' while the description says the site was an MFC county work center, which is why a correction is proposed. The 100 ft height is converted to 30.5 m. The MC-39 description rests on the register plus one general article on Aermotor models, not on documents about this tower.

The NHLR entry is short and undated and the only source on this tower's status. The register's administrator line and its no-longer-used line conflict, and the story reports both rather than choosing one. The LS-40 stair detail comes from a general article on Aermotor models, not from documents about this tower. The 100 ft height is converted to 30.5 m. No build date, staffing or fire history was found after two searches and about four page reads. The register gives no build date and no staffing or access information. Only the NHLR register page describes this tower. Two searches found no history, builder, staffing or dates. The register is the only source for the 1934 CCC build by a New Jersey crew and for the 100-ft height; two searches and the cached pages found no corroboration. Only the NHLR detail page was read. Two searches returned only NHLR and directory pages, with nothing on construction, ownership changes or condition. Only the NHLR detail page and the MFC homepage were read. Two searches found nothing on the tower's ownership change, and the Wikipedia article for Poplar Creek only repeats that the tower is on the register. Only two sources were usable: the NHLR register page and the OSM node. Two web searches found no staffing, fire or current-status information. One usable source only. The register gives the location, elevation (512 ft / 156 m), a 100 ft Aermotor description, build date unknown, registration details and the agency, and nothing else. height_m 30.5 is the register's 100 ft converted. Two register-level sources plus one town article. The register is the only source for the tower itself: location, elevation, 100 ft LS-40 description, build date unknown, a 7/8/22 site visit, stairs removed, and the MFC-to-county handover. The county conflict is real: the register and the record say Issaquena; Forest Lookouts says Sharkey, and the town of Rolling Fork is in Sharkey. The Wikipedia article was cached as wikitext; only the two tornado sentences are used, and no source says the tower was damaged. No access key set: no source gives an access level, and the register's stairs note and county-use note are not a public-access statement. No staffing, fire history or build date found. Forest Lookouts' Rolling Fork page gives no more detail than county and agency. Story length is set by these thin sources.

One usable source. Only the NHLR register page and the OSM node were usable. Two web searches found nothing on the tower's history or staffing. Sparse record. Build date, staffing, fires, condition and access are not documented in any source read. Only the NHLR entry, the Forest Lookouts index (name and county only) and the OSM node were usable after two searches. Two sources agree on the 1922 cabin, the 1934 or 1930s L-4 tower, and the 1962 cab. Staffing and the active-service status are undated, so the current status is medium confidence. Built dates 1931, 1940 and 1965 agree across NHLR, firelookout.com and the Weebly history. Trail access is public; nothing supports climbing the tower and the story says so.

Reasonably well documented for a rental-program lookout: two independent narrative sources (National Forest Foundation, Western News) corroborate the NHLR/firelookout.com build history. The 1980s retirement from fire duty comes from the National Forest Foundation piece; the 1984 rental start and the builder's name (Stef Ludvikson, for both the 1928 cabin and the 1934 tower) come only from the Western News article — NHLR and firelookout.com do not name a builder, so that attribution rests on a single source. Two small, unresolved conflicts flagged above: the cabin's build year (1928 vs 1929) and the summit elevation (three different figures across sources). A third, odder wrinkle: the National Forest Foundation piece implies the log cabin standing near the tower today was moved to the site in the 1950s to replace a deteriorated building, which sits awkwardly against the 1928/1929 'first structure, still there' framing from NHLR and firelookout.com — the story notes this rather than resolving it. The Purcell Mountains location also comes only from the National Forest Foundation piece. No NRHP nomination form or newspaper archive hit was found in the search budget; a Chronicling America or Montana Memory Project search might turn up more on the 1934 or 1966 construction if someone wants to dig further.

No newspaper or NRHP nomination form located; the 1984 date is NRHP-eligibility, not a formal National Register listing, and the story is careful to say so. Two official-ish sources (Recreation.gov listing vs. the Forest Service's own Lolo NF page) disagree slightly on the lookout's water source: non-potable spring 3/4 mile downhill vs. a filterable spring 0.5 mile away. Location: the record's NHLR point and the FFLA 'Elk Patrol' point (48.46258, -114.89668) are about 1.56 km apart, and no source here explains why. Kind: the record says 'ground', but the 1940 structure is a 10 ft pole tower with an L-4 cab; the 1923 cab is described only as a frame cab with roof platform. Access: the two trail listings differ; one says closed, the other is silent on closure. No staffing or fire history found, so none is claimed. Photos: the NHLR photos are already on the record; firelookout.com credits photos to the Fire Lookout Museum, Gary Weber and Luke Channer, but no image URL was found, so none added.

Built year: the register's 1970 and the sources' 1935 cabin are both correct for different structures, so the story gives both. Staffing: 'staffed every summer' appears on the register and the tribal page, but neither page is dated, so the 2022 as_of was removed (it was the register's registration year). Height: the record's 4.3 m conflicts with the 20-ft tower the sources describe (proposed correction, not applied). Access: administered by the tribes on the reservation; no public visiting arrangement was found, and the story says to check with the tribe first. Elevation difference is under 10 ft. Nominator and lookout staff names are deliberately omitted. The 1979 and 1994 items come from a secondary history site quoting a newspaper and a newsletter; the originals were not checked.

Build year 1953 is well corroborated across NHLR, firelookout.com and 1952-1953 newspaper items quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. Staffing is only described as summer and is undated. The Moss Mountain Inn guide is a lodging site's hiking article and its road-access and gate details are undated. No fire history or rental listing found. Verify current access and staffing with the Flathead National Forest. Brief record fields (design L-4, 1953 build, 2011 registration) are supported, so no corrections proposed.

No source gives an end date for staffed fire-watch duty, or names any specific fire spotted from Garnet Mountain. The brief's record flags a build-year conflict across sources, but all three sources checked here agree on the same build sequence (1930 camp / 1950 cab / 1962 cab), so no conflict was found in what we read; it's possible the flagged conflict is against a source not checked in this pass (e.g. an NRHP nomination). Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft misstated Garnet Mountain as sitting 'in the Gallatin Range' -- source 2 lists the Gallatin Range only as a feature visible to the south, not the mountain's own range, so the story was corrected to list it alongside the other viewed features. Two footnote citations were also wrong: the 1950 secondhand-cab/Lincoln Mountain sentence had cited source 2 (Recreation.gov), which says nothing about that history, instead of source 3 (firelookout.com); and the 'one of the more popular lookouts' claim, which comes only from source 3's wording, had been attached to sources 1 and 2.

Brief's 'height_m: 1.8' field looks like an error or placeholder (1.8m is under 6 feet, implausible for any lookout tower; rec.gov says the current tower is 40 feet tall). Flagging as a possible data issue for the editor rather than a sourced correction, since no source gives a tower height in meters directly. Built-year conflict (1963 vs 1964 for the current tower) handled as the brief's note anticipated.

Two independent, detailed sources agree closely on the build history (1921 rag outfit -> 1939 L-4 on 20-ft pole tower -> 1964 R-6 flattop on 30-ft timber tower) and on staffing into the 1970s. Flagged a likely height_m error in the tower record (20 ft vs. the current 30-ft tower). Minor elevation discrepancy not flagged: NHLR gives 6,029 ft (1,838 m, matches record); firelookout.com gives 6,092 ft -- not material enough for a correction. Did not need to use the web-search budget; both cached pages were sufficient. Fact-check 2026-10-04: removed an uncited 'Clark Fork River country' detail from the opening sentence (not in either source) and rewrote two sentences that too closely copied source wording ('rag outfit' tent description; 'without permanent living quarters' line). Spot-checked the NHLR registry-number/date quote and both firelookout.com quotes (location and named personnel) directly against fetch_text.py output; all three matched the source exactly.

Construction, design and CCC attribution rest on the NRHP nomination (stated as belief). The brief lists NRHP 100002297 as a register; the nomination file calls the lookout eligible for listing. I did not confirm a listing date or final status, so the story says eligible. The last staffing year is not exact (firelookout.com says into the 1980s; NHLR calls it inactive in 1984). The rental is current per the Forest Service page (undated). Brief record fields (1939 build, L-4 design, 2003 registration) are supported, so no corrections proposed.

Elevation differs notably between NHLR (6,887 ft / 2,099 m, matching the brief's elevation_m field) and Recreation.gov (7,587 ft) -- flagged in the story rather than silently picking one, since neither page explains the gap and it's larger than a rounding difference. Build-year conflict between firelookout.com (1934/1954) and NHLR+Recreation.gov (1932/1962) also flagged; went with the two-source majority for the main narrative. No staffing-end date is corroborated outside firelookout.com, so that claim is attributed to it alone. No NRHP nomination PDF or newspaper source found in two web searches; confidence is medium given the unresolved elevation and date conflicts.

Construction history is well documented (NRHP nomination and NPS planning file). Current condition and access rest on 2012-era sources; no 2026 source was found. Elevation conflict: NHLR gives 6,810 ft (2,076 m), which matches the brief's 2075.7 m; firelookout.com gives 7244 ft. Not used in the story. The NPS planning file's date is not shown in the fetched text. The Wikipedia Built 1945 infobox matches the nomination. Pages read: 6 (NHLR, Wikipedia, firelookout, NRHP PDF, Whitefish Pilot, NPS planning PDF). Search: 1 query.

Build year is the main conflict: 1869 (firelookout.com), 1874 (Montana Free Press), 1876 (register and Visit Helena listing). The brief's record of 1876 is kept. Restoration cost and start month conflict as noted. The year 2025 for the restoration is inferred: the Free Press story is dated April 7, 2025 and says the work was expected to finish by the end of May, and KTVH does not print a year. Pages read: 6 (NHLR, Visit Helena listing, firelookout.com, Montana Free Press, mthistory.org, KTVH). Search: 1 query.

No fire at this site appears in the sources read. The brief's kind two_story is not verified: NHLR describes an L-4 cab on a one-story concrete base, and a search snippet quoting a firelookout.org directory (not read) called it a two-story cab. Left unchanged. Consider whether the 1954 event should be replaced rather than built. Staffing and current access are unconfirmed; no Forest Service page was read. One WebSearch was used.

Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story no longer says Indian Flats Cabin is rentable; its Recreation.gov page says it does not offer reservations there. Status is unsettled. The 2018 disposal notice says the lookout was excess; the recreation.gov listing (undated) says it is manned mid-June through September; the 2024 chapter report says it seems to be the primary lookout threatened. Not read, due to budget: a May 2021 Hogback Lookout Restoration NEPA document and a 2023 FFLA chapter report, both seen only in search snippets. The 2021 document may show whether the 2018 disposal went ahead or was replaced by restoration; it should be checked before publishing a status. Budget note: this tower used 3 WebSearch calls (one over the 2-call budget) and 6 page reads. Record's elevation 2380.2 m matches the NHLR figure. No corrections proposed.

Good agreement across NHLR, Wikipedia (citing the NRHP nomination), and Recreation.gov. No source gives an exact date for when staffing ended besides 'approximately 1946' or exactly when restoration occurred, only that it was 'abandoned for a number of years' before restoration.

Staffing conflicts: the register's October 2012 visit report says staffed sometimes and used in emergencies; the undated Chronicle feature says regularly manned; the smokejumper article (undated, refers to 2012 as past) says staffed in high fire danger. Story reports all three; facts.staffing uses the 2012 register statement. Height: 41 ft (register, firelookout.com) vs 40 ft (Chronicle, Montana Lookouts); height_m 12.5 is 41 ft converted. The register's description calls it Horse Mountain Lookout in one sentence, a name slip. Current access and climbability not verified on site. No photos added.

The brief's 'built: 1924' field is likely referring to the original pole-platform predecessor, not the structure now standing (built 1933); flagged as a correction. The current staffing claim comes only from firelookout.com, a hobbyist site with no visible date on that claim, so it is not strongly corroborated -- an NPS source confirming present-day staffing would strengthen this. Did not attempt to retrieve the NRHP nomination PDF itself (npgallery asset page returned only a metadata summary, not the full nomination text) or the NHLR newspaper-article PDF due to the per-tower read budget. Editorial pass 2026-10-04 fixed two footnote misattributions in the story: the 1924 pole-platform/log-cabin sentence was cited to Wikipedia ([^2]) but that detail is only in firelookout.com ([^3]); the 'chain of staffed fire lookouts' sentence was cited to NHLR ([^1]) but the quote is on Wikipedia ([^2]). The NRHP+NHLR registration sentence was missing a [^2] cite for the NRHP facts.

Two registrations share the name Jocko #2. This record (NHLR US 1543) is the standing 1969 CSKT R-6 timber tower. FFLOS US 2089 is a different 1934 Forest Service steel tower, removed, with footings only; keep them apart. Access level 'permission' in the record is not supported by any page read; it is left out of facts and should be treated as unverified. County (Missoula vs Lake) and elevation (7,636 vs 7,769 ft) conflict across sources. Staffing comes from an undated CSKT page. Leads not read: nwmt-ffla.org (Northwest Montana Lookout Association, lists historic, staffed and rental lookouts) and the CSKT preservation page. Page-read budget was used up, so no physical-state check was done.

Staffing: the register says semi-regularly staffed since 2001; firelookout.com says only that it was staffed in 2001. Access and rental not verified. Elevation: register 8,214 ft (2,504 m), firelookout.com 8284 ft; record 2503.6 m follows the register. The Powell County blog gives its newspaper quote as September 17, 1957 and then cites the same paper as September 17, 1954; the story says so. The Flathead NF Facebook lookout profile could not be read (page returned only its title), so it is not cited. Wikipedia says the 1957 lookout replaced a cabin of 1937, consistent with the register; it was used as a lead only.

The brief says the NHLR record shares a register number with another entry (US 1114, MT 62). Check for a duplicate record. Elevation conflicts (3,783 ft in NHLR vs 4943 ft on firelookout.com), and the record keeps the NHLR figure. Height correction: 15.2 m is 50 ft, the 1934 tower's height; the present 53-ft tower is about 16.2 m. The firelookout.com page is undated and says the tower is available for emergencies; the 2026 assessment says current access is closed for grizzly habitat. Do not encourage visiting. The 2026 condition assessment PDF linked from the NWMT page was not opened.

Status is undated: the decommissioning and window removal appear in two undated pages; only the 2017 collapse risk has a year. The trail sources disagree: Visit Montana gives Road 761 and 2.5 miles, easy; The Outbound gives Road 763 and about 3 miles, moderate. No staffing or fire record was found. The Forest Lookouts Montana page for Kenelty carries a 1956 newspaper item placing a man on the mountain without describing a job, and an item about a lookout on another mountain; neither is used. The record's 3.0 m height is close to the 10-foot (about 3.05 m) tower given by the source. A Forest Service Museum catalog record was mentioned in search but not read.

Thin sources. The 1937 build year comes from one Forest Lookouts page; the Fire Lookout Tower site says construction is unknown and presumes the purpose was wildlife observation, which the story reports only as that site's presumption. Public climbing and current condition are unconfirmed; no staffing, fire or closure record was found. Refuge visitor-center hours were not captured from the visit page, and a third-party listing's phone number was not used. The record's 30.5 m height matches the 100-foot figure, and 2,042 m matches the 6,700-foot elevation.

The 1977 build date is well supported and corrects the brief's 1969 build event. Staffing conflicts between NHLR (not regularly staffed) and the 2017 chapter report (DNRC part time); the as-of date is 2017. Current access is unconfirmed; no visiting or rental program found. height_m 6.1 converts the reported 20 feet of cab height, which is an inference from two sources. The 2016 Whitefish article calls Little Napa an L-4 design lookout in passing; design was not recorded because no source states it directly. One WebSearch was used. Five page reads.

Build date is genuinely unsettled across sources, including within Wikipedia's own article. No staffing history or fire history found beyond the disputed earlier-cabin-fire claim from firelookout.com.

NHLR, firelookout.com and Forest Lookouts agree on the 1969 cab, the 1974 move from Antrim Point and the staffing. Open conflicts: 1968 vs 1969 for the Antrim Point cab (firelookout.com Antrim page) and concrete vs cinder block base. height_m 3.0 is proposed for removal because it equals the base height. Access set to restricted as an inference from 'regularly staffed'; no source states visitor rules, so verify with the West Fork Ranger District. Staffing as_of is the read date because the NHLR text is undated. 'Still stands' is cited to the Antrim Point page (cite 4), because the Lookout Mountain pages say only that it is staffed. The NHLR rentals page read did not list this lookout. No fire history found in the sources read. No photos added: firelookout.com credits the Fire Lookout Museum and Gary Weber but gives no image URLs.

Record's 2023 event cites nwmt-ffla.org/2023/09/01/2023-projects/, whose cached text is an empty shell; the Lost Horse assessment is in the NMLA 2023 Year-End Report PDF (source 2), so that source URL should be updated. The access level 'restricted' is my reading of the flagged-route and no-road descriptions, not an official status; check with the Kootenai NF. No source gives the abandonment year or any staffing.

The brief flags a register-number conflict ('They share a register number'), presumably with another lookout in the dataset; none of the three sources read here gave any indication McCart's NHLR number (US 85) is wrong, so this could not be resolved from these pages and should be checked against whichever other record shares the number.

The brief flagged a register-number conflict ('They share a register number') but none of the three sources checked here show a shared/duplicate NHLR number; US 345 appears specific to McGuire on both NHLR and the firelookout.org list. That conflict may concern a source not checked in this pass. No source gives a specific fire credited to this lookout, or the exact date staffing began. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft's sentence on the 1923/1924 build-year split misattributed the dates, crediting Recreation.gov with the 1924 figure (it actually gives 1923, per source 2) and leaving firelookout.com unnamed as one of the two sources giving 1924; corrected. The physical-description sentence (pyramidal roof, cupola, interior ladder) cited only sources 1 and 3, but that detail comes from source 2's quote, so source 2 was added to the citation. firelookout.com (source 3) corroborates the 1928/1936/1957 construction sequence but was not directly footnoted in the story since Recreation.gov already covers it in more detail; kept as a cross-check source. Brief's source_pages label the Homestead page as a headquarters source; the headquarters page is montanalookouts.weebly.com/medicine-lake-nwr-headquarters.html. No staffing or fire use found; the tower is described as a wildlife observation tower. Build year is genuinely unresolved between NHLR (1930/1933) and firelookout.com (1940); the NRHP nomination's 'significant years' field (1939) was only partially legible in the crawl cache and did not include a clear text statement to resolve it, so I did not treat it as deciding the question. History from 1957 to 2018 is well sourced by the NRHP nomination. Present-day status and access rest on the nomination (form dated November 2, 2017), not a 2026 check; confirm with the Missoula Ranger District before publishing. Access level public is an inference from hikers visiting, not a posted status. height_m 16.2 is converted from 53 ft. firelookout.com's county and elevation are wrong or disputed. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-08: story reworded where it copied source wording, 'now serves' changed to the 2017 nomination's date, and evidence added for the 2006 shop move, the kit, the Missoula County claim and the vacancy.

Middle-tower date conflict (1950s vs 1968) not resolvable from available sources; flagged in story and resolved_conflicts. No NRHP nomination found for this tower. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the 'named for Col. David Minton' and 'first tower, 1932' sentences were mis-cited to source 1 (NHLR); that page does not contain either sentence verbatim (it instead says the original pole tower 'was replaced by an L-4 cab in 1932'). Brief's conflict note about differing build years is explained by NHLR's own description distinguishing the 1921 platform from the 1959 cab; no discrepancy found between the three sources checked.

NHLR and firelookout.com agree on the first 30-foot pole tower (about 1935), the L-4 cab, the unused years and no public access. They disagree on the replacement year (1945 vs 1941), the builder's name, and the location reference. The record's 1945 built date is the replacement tower; a correction is proposed. The 1921 and 1945 items are quoted on the Forest Lookouts page only; they are not confirmed as the same site as the 1935 tower, though the 1945 item names Montour Mountain. The 1921 item does not name the mountain (July 3, 1921, The Missoulian), so the story says so. height_m 9.1 is 30 ft converted. Status kept standing: NHLR calls the tower abandoned, not removed. Access set to private from NHLR. Search results also showed Archives West and Montana Historical Society material on the Blackfoot Forest Protective Association, but only snippets were seen, so they are not cited. No photos added; firelookout.com credits photos to the Fire Lookout Museum and Gary Weber with no image URLs.
Conflict between NHLR (active until 1999) and recreation.gov/firelookout.com (unused since the 1970s) noted in the story and in resolved_conflicts; genuinely unresolved from the sources checked here.

Thin record: three sources, one of them a single newspaper item quoted by Forest Lookouts (Choteau Acantha, May 31, 1934) that describes a plan, not a finished build. NHLR's description says little is known; firelookout.com gives only a short entry. Elevation conflict (5,239 vs 5,280 ft) noted. The record's access 'permission' has no source here; correction proposed to remove. record kind 'ground' not confirmed by any source read (sources say cupola-based / wooden cupola cabin), so it is left out of facts. The brief's coordinates (47.99295, -108.59646) match the NHLR; the west_us_lookouts coordinates in the conflict note were not checked. Not verified: current condition since firelookout.com's entry; whether any Fort Belknap access rules exist. No photos added (firelookout.com credits Luke Channer but gives no image URLs).

Current access and staffing are not verified. The staffing claim comes from an undated firelookout.com page. No rental listing was found for this lookout, and the story does not claim one. The Register's description says 7,796 ft while its elevation field says 7,700 ft (2,347 m); the record's 2347 m is kept. Recommend the Seeley Lake Ranger District confirm access and staffing.

Good staffing detail (Mathenys, last staffed 1971) and a notable 2017 Sprague Fire protection event, but sources don't describe the fire's actual approach/outcome for the structure beyond the wrap being installed.

Abandonment year conflicts (1973 vs 1978); both are stated in the story. Elevation differs across four sources; record kept. The record's 2016 assessed event is not supported by any source I read. Henry' 1973 text contains the typo 'n 1973' as printed.

Staffing is only described as summer staffing in undated sources. No 2026 status or access information was found in the sources read. No rental use was mentioned. Recommend the Kootenai National Forest confirm current status and access.

The brief's 1932 build and 1972 abandonment hold. The 1921 camp date reconciles the build-year conflict in the brief. Restoration date conflict: register and 2026 summary say restored in the 1980s; firelookout.com says restoration took place through 2000. Both are in the story. Elevation: register 7,606 ft (2,318 m, matches record) vs firelookout.com 7705 ft. The 2024 date for the window removal is inferred from 'started last year' in the 2025 newsletter. Record events 2016 (field assessment), 2018 (new shutters), 2022 (very good shape) and the 2024 pre-project assessment were not found in the pages I read and are left out of this research file; check them before publishing. Built-year discrepancy (1933 vs 1934) left unresolved per sources; worth a look at the NPGallery NRHP PDF (86000357) if a firmer date is wanted.

Current 2026 staffing is not verified. The newest staffing report read is the June 2018 Ledger article, and the Register and firelookout.com are undated. Access and visit rules are not stated. The record's coordinates match the Register (47.37222, -114.85889). Recommend the Lolo National Forest Plains/Thompson Falls Ranger District confirm current staffing and access. The distance and fate-of-1934-tower conflicts are reported in the story, not resolved.

NHLR and FirelookOut share nearly the same wording, so the 1923, 1925 and 1962 dates rest mainly on one text, with the 1962 date backed by the independent 2022 magazine article. No NRHP nomination or Forest Service document was found or read. The access level is unknown: staffed in summer and reached by trail, but no source says whether the cab is open to visitors. The brief's record checked out on coordinates, elevation (within the NHLR figure), and the 1962 build date; no corrections. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's window wording now reads fragile piece, to match the 2022 magazine quote; the summit wording now reads lookout site, because the sources say here; and the visitor-access sentence no longer carries a footnote, since no cited source addresses it.

The original site and the first build date are unknown in every source read. The record's access level 'permission' is not confirmed: the tribal page and NHLR say nothing about visitors, and a Facebook group post that mentions a tribal permit could not be opened, so it is not cited. Access is set to unknown. Height 16.2 m is the 53-foot figure converted, which matches the record.

The original lookout's date is not settled (1935, 1936 or 1937 across sources), so the story gives the range. The NRHP nomination is the strongest source for the current structure and the 2008 work. The NPS nomination PDF is OCR text, and the 'last of eleven' sentence is garbled, so the quote is a clean fragment. Staffing 'unstaffed' since 1972 is inferred from 'not used for fire detection much after 1972'. Current public access is unconfirmed. The visit detail rests on one SummitPost trip report. The 1931 and 1968 cabs are both real per the register and firelookout.com, so the record's build-year conflict is two cabs, not an error. Core build and registry facts are solid (NHLR). Very thin. The Register has no description beyond 'No information known at this time.' and gives only the 1930s as the build period, so no build year is recorded. Standing status rests on the FFLA Montana list and NHLR's description; the only account of the site today is one July 2026 trip report, which does not say whether the tower was climbed or what condition it is in. Early history is disputed. The Register and firelookout.com give a 1925 cupola; the newspaper items quoted on the Forest Lookouts page show Denver Laughlin as summer lookout from 1918 and say he had been there nearly 15 years by 1931. I did not check the newspapers themselves. The Register's first lookout, 'Richards', is not named in those items. No web search used for this tower.

Flagging a date conflict on the pre-1948 lookout (early 1920s vs. 1930-vintage) rather than picking one; worth a look if a primary FS record turns up.

The build year, L-5 design and 1996 register date agree across sources. Elevation and county disagree between the register and the two later sources; the record keeps the register values. No correction to the record: the OSM-based 1930 build year on the record is supported by the museum and marker. Three build dates for the tower do not agree: 1914 (Forest History Society), 1916 (register and firelookout.com) for the first cabin, and 1963 (register and firelookout.com) for the present tower; newspapers put the helicopter lift in October 1961 and report it on 3 January 1962. The record's height_m 12.2 is the 1931/1934 pole tower, not the current structure; correction proposed. Elevation (2,219 m, 7,281 ft) and coordinates match the NHLR page; no elevation key is in the research schema. Brief's R-6 design, 1964 replacement date and NHLR registration (July 14, 2000) are supported. Agency, height, registration and standing status agree across sources. Thin record: no construction year beyond the register's 1930s, no staffing history, no dated current-condition source, and no source for the record's permission access level.
