Park hours and whether the tower can be climbed are not stated in any source read. The registry's 'standing' is true only of the reconstruction; the original tower is gone.

Not a historic fire lookout. It is a park lookout tower in Cane Creek Mountains Natural Area that the park says is now open; the editor should decide whether it belongs in the fire-lookout set. height_m 24.4 converts the park's 80-foot climb; OSM's 25 m is close. The June 2025 date comes from the blog's web address, not a date shown on the page. Construction date and builder are unknown. Two searches and three page reads; the Facebook post returned no text.

The record's 1951 build year is the stone structure; the original steel lookout is 1938 per the Register, but a camping blog gives 1936 and 60 feet. Unresolved: that date gap. The blog's timeline (hurricane after a few years) gives no replacement date, so it cannot be checked against the Register's 1951 replacement. A Facebook post (not cited) gives 1949 and an 18 ft 6 in tower. Restoration date not found, so no event for it. Visitor hours not verified. 'Standing' refers to the stone structure, not the fire lookout. Wikipedia calls the summit tower abandoned, which does not match the Register's restored viewpoint; not used for that point.

Access is the main open question: the 2018 blog says fenced, and the undated trail guide says open, but its own May 2018 update says the fence was rebuilt and the tower closed until further notice. Verify with the tribe or the Fire Mountain Trail System managers before publishing. The 1957 build and BIA ownership match across the Register, the 2018 blog and the trail guide. The 1960s end of fire use rests on one blog that cites Peter Barr's book; not checked against the book. Restoration plan (2008) has no later record. Facebook posts that call the tower abandoned, and the Grokipedia page, are not cited. The Wikipedia 'Mount Noble' article is about an Antarctic peak and was not used. Read budget: 3 distinct pages and 2 searches. Height 60 ft converted to 18.3 m.

Beyond the NHLR register page, no newspaper or Forest Service archival material turned up for this specific tower in cached sources or three web searches; a 'Sterling Mountain' NRHP tower that surfaced in search results is a different structure in Orange County, New York, and was excluded. Wikipedia calling the tower 'abandoned' sits a little oddly next to NHLR's description of an open trap door and NPS radio-repeater use -- worth a direct check of current NPS trail/tower status pages. Current staffing and public-access level are inferred, not confirmed by an authoritative current source.

Story sources are 2019 and 2023 items; no 2024-2026 status found, so the access note should be rechecked with the Tusquitee Ranger District before anyone visits. The brief's agency field comes from the Register's administrator line and differs from the Forest Service sources. Staffing and current-use claims conflict across sources; the story says so. Facebook posts that appeared in search results were not used because they were not fetched.

The 18 m height in the brief matches the 1934-36 state report's 59 ft 3 in steel tower, not the NHLR's 50 ft Aermotor (15.2 m), so height_m is left out of facts. The record's 1936 build year is from NHLR and the Journal-Patriot; the 1934 report is quoted second-hand by Forest Lookouts and was not checked against the original. The Journal-Patriot article is partly paywalled, but the quoted lines were readable and the article's own date is not shown. The Wilkes Record column is dated December 10, 2023. A TV item quoting a ranger on a 1936 CCC build was not fetched and is not cited. NHLR's 'restricted for electronics use' is quoted as written; no source explains what it means. Access is set to restricted because the tower is described as unsafe to climb; no official closure notice was found. Staffing is recorded as unstaffed on the strength of the undated Journal-Patriot report.

Build year (1932), location and the 2018 restoration agree across sources. Unverified leads not used: a search summary says public access ended in 2017, and another says a CCC camp manned the tower from 1933; neither appeared in a page I opened. Elevation: the register and Smoky Mountain News give 3,670 ft (1,119 m, matching the brief's 1118.6 m); Romantic Asheville gives 3,643 ft. No post-2018 condition report was found; the travel guide calls the tower in excellent condition but is undated, so verify the current state before relying on access.

No source after 2016 gives the tower's condition or access; the Wikipedia access line is undated. The 2015 report says rehabilitated while the 2016 goals still plan a restoration announcement, so the story says the record is unclear. Staffing history (NPS staffing until the late 1960s, cabin removed 1987) appeared only in search snippets, so it is left out. The record's height_m stays null: the register's 60 ft is the tower height, and the cab-floor height is not sourced. Quotes from the 2013 article come from an archived copy with no named publisher.

Four pages were read: the tnlandforms.us North Carolina tower list (map revised June 2021), the OpenStreetMap way, and the NHLR and FFLOS North Carolina listings. Two searches gave no history for this tower. The name link between Tirzah (tnlandforms list) and Glenns Mountain Fire Tower (OpenStreetMap) comes from the brief's records; neither page names the other, so please confirm it before publishing. The OSM page was not checked for coordinates. The brief's status 'standing' rests only on the OSM map entry. Design, height, build date, staffing, agency and access are unknown and omitted. The NHLR page shows 31 lookouts and no Tirzah, which supports 'not registered' by inspection of the full list. A Mapcarta search snippet placed the tower in 'Mount Tirzah Township'; it was not read, so it is not used. Read budget ran over: about nine fetch_text calls, including one failed NHLR request, and the early reads were partly repeated. Fact check 2026-10-09: the OSM page names only Glenns Mountain Fire Tower and the tnlandforms list does not mention Glenns, so the name link is still the brief's own and no source confirms it. The NHLR North Carolina page was read in full: 31 names, no Tirzah. The FFLOS page names Big Stamp Lookout Site and Frye Knob. The story now says 'lookout register' (both registers are national) and drops 'north-central', which no source states.

The Register page has no visit reports. Current condition rests on a 2016 photo caption, and the staffing end date (late 1990s) comes only from that caption. Access is private land per the Register. Search results from Facebook and a Walker Top group were not used because they were not fetched.

The NRHP nomination PDF (npgallery GetAsset for NRIS 00000164) returned no readable text, so the 1999 Van Dolsen nomination was not read; it would settle the height and staffing dates. A Facebook post from Old Homes of North Carolina reports a 1970 sale by the Haithcock heirs to the state and a spring 1993 end of staffing, but it could not be fetched, so it is not used. No source found on current access or climbing. The 1932 state report is known only through the Eastern US Lookouts quotation.

Current condition is unknown beyond the 2019 Register nomination photos and an undated trail-lookout status line. No closure notice was found. The brief's 1933 build year drops the Register's 1933-1942 range. The access level 'restricted' is our reading of the removed steps, not a posted rule.

The record's 7.6 m height was the earlier 25-foot wooden tower; corrected to 53 ft (16.2 m). The 1935 versus 1937 build date is unresolved; no NRHP nomination or Forest Service history was read. Eastern US Lookouts quotes a 1936 newspaper plan for a 43-foot stone tower, but the built height was 53 feet. The NHLR and Eastern US Lookouts spell the memorial name Bryne; the Forest Service and Eastern's 1939 quote use Byrne. Current climbing rules and hours were not found in any source. The 2016 fire is dated November 23, 2016 by Eastern US Lookouts only.

Built year is disputed: the register says 1936 and Willhite cites a 1934 USGS benchmark note, so both are kept as events. Burn cause differs: register says vandals, Willhite says arson. Material differs: register says metal, Wikipedia says wooden. Deck date: register says 1993, Willhite says early 1990s. The 2016 fire line rests on Wikipedia alone; a Forest Service or news source would strengthen it. Access and climbability come from undated sources. The record's height_m 9.0 (OSM) is close to the register's 30 ft, so it is left as is. The 1948 Shaffer detail is from Willhite only. The story no longer says the observation deck exists today: the only source is undated, so it is attributed to Willhite.

Staffing and notable fires are not in any readable source. A 2002 Wilmington Star-News obituary (seen only as a search snippet; fetch returned HTTP 403) says Willow Atkinson Baker began as Wilmar Fire Tower operator in about 1958. Not used because it could not be read. 2024 social posts call the tower abandoned; not used as sources. Confirm the 2018 auction and current owner with the NC Forest Service or the county before publishing. The NHLR page is the only source for the post-1936 history.

Only the NHLR page is an official record. Build year and the 1969 staffing end come from two hiking-guide sites, not from Forest Service or archive records. A Transylvania Times destination-hike article (1934 build, USFS and CCC) returned HTTP 429 twice, so it is not used. Another guide snippet (theoutdoorsapp) mentions the tower was 'originally in 1934' and 'reconstru...' (cut off). If the tower was rebuilt, the built and restored events need correcting, so check the Forest Service or NRHP records before publishing. The record has no height; the NHLR gives only the cab and base dimensions, so height_m was left out. Access is marked public on the basis of trail access on national forest land; confirm current climbing rules with the Highlands Ranger District.

Two independent sources agree on 1936 and 100 feet. The 2005 PDF text runs in columns, so the quotes are single lines. The standing status comes from the FFLA list, which is undated. No staffing record was found, and no source says whether visitors may climb the tower. The FWS refuge page (fws.gov/refuge/lostwood) was checked by keyword and mentions no tower. The brief had no agency; USFWS was taken from the 2005 brochure. No NHLR or FFLOS detail record turned up in search.

Build year and builder not found in any source reached (WebSearch and the Wikipedia refuge page had no tower entry). Relocation (1992), cost and registration are well sourced. Access is unconfirmed: the museum's visitor page does not mention the tower, so no access key was set. Height 33.5 m is our conversion of the register's 110 ft. Do not confuse with the separate Northern Lights Tower, an 88.5-ft steel sculpture in Rugby that the museum page also describes. LOC HAER photos returned 403, so no new photo was recorded.

Identity is the weak link. The West Lookouts list files the 100-foot tower under 'J. CLARK SAYLER WILDLIFE REFUGE (UPPER SOURIS)' with no HQ label. The HQ match rests on the Forest Fire Lookout Association row 'Upper Souris NWR – HQ' at 48.46032, -101.57283 plus the Upper Souris label. Treat as probable, not confirmed. The same list moved a different J. Clark Salyer HQ tower to Rugby in 1992; that is not this tower. Lead, not cited: HAER survey photos on loc.gov (hhh.nd0028, hhh.nd0033) describe a lookout tower at the refuge headquarters, but loc.gov returned 403 to fetch_text. Not found in any page read: reason for construction, staffing, notable fires, current public access, rentals. The FWS visit-location page in the cache has no directions. Brief record had no height; 30.5 m is 100 ft converted. Verification 2026-10-09: the story no longer says the tower was erected 'at the site' or that it 'stands at its headquarters'; the HQ link is stated as unconfirmed. 'And rest' was dropped from the founding sentence (the Wikipedia text says breeding ground only).

Build date is the open question. 1935 (register and West Lookouts, which may share a source) conflicts with the USFWS early-1940s CCC statement quoted on the register and with the 1937 WPA newspaper item quoted on the south page. Needs a primary source (refuge history, USFWS or Nebraska State Historical Society) before the built event is firmed up. Height 18.3 m is our conversion of 60 ft. Nominator is listed as 'Admin' on the register page. A Living New Deal search snippet reportedly says the WPA built 'the fire tower' at the headquarters site; not used because that page returned 403. Access and visit rules not confirmed; the FWS visit page was not read. Read budget exceeded: several reads returned 403 or the wrong page.

Build date unresolved (see resolved_conflicts). The 100-foot figure comes from the 1937 newspaper item and does not name which refuge tower it describes, so no height_m was set; the north page gives 60 ft for its own tower. Primary source to try: the FWS press release 'U.S. Improves Duck Refuge in Nebraska (Crescent Lake Refuge)', June 12, 1937 (fws.gov archive; PDF is 19370612.PDF on the media page, not reached: a guessed URL returned 404). Access not established; the FWS visit page does not mention the towers. Read budget used: 6 page reads and 2 WebSearch calls. Register nominator is 'Admin'.

Brief said status standing; kept, with a status note for the cab loss. The 1944 date comes from NHLR only. A Forest Fire Lookout Association post seen in search (not fetched, so not cited) gives 1973 for the current third tower; check before changing the 1944 date. Elevation: NHLR 2,907 ft (886 m); Forest Service page shows 2,922 with no unit. Height 50 ft is from one news report. No staffing source found, so staffing is omitted. Photos on the NHLR page have no captured URLs; none added.

Build year (1935), CCC origin and registration rest on the NHLR entry; the same text appears on westlookouts.weebly.com, which is not cited separately. The only lookout-era record found is one August 1937 CCC work report, so staffing, end of fire watch, and any notable fire remain unknown. Nothing found says whether the cab survives in its original form. The brief's access 'unknown' is now public via the trail to the observation deck. height_m is converted from 100 ft. wheninyourstate.com returned HTTP 403 and was not used. No NPS or Nebraska Game and Parks history was checked.

The NHLR page narrates refuge-wide CCC/WPA history (canals, fencing) and separately states the tower itself was CCC-built, but gives no specific construction year for the tower. No source here covers staffing history, climbability, or visitor access, so those were left unknown rather than guessed.

The sources say the Abenaki Tower was never a fire tower, but the Forest Fire Lookout Association list classes it as an observation tower ('Obs Tower'). The editor should decide whether a fire-lookout directory should carry it; the brief's kind 'tower' does not claim fire use. The marker names the builder only as 'residents of Melvin Village'. The Laker article (2018) was read in full on the 2026-10-09 check. It names Tuftonboro resident Lewis McIntire as the winning $400 bidder to construct the tower, and describes a taller rebuild in 1977-78 (Kirk Titus hired to rebuild, Bill Cornell designed it, re-dedicated 22 July 1978). The 1977-78 rebuild is now a 'rebuilt' event and the story says so. The story keeps the marker's builder wording and does not name McIntire; the editor may decide whether the builder line needs the Laker's account. The marker page (HMDB) was read in full: its trailhead location, its 'historical and continuing contributions' wording and its Abenaki Tower Trail Association excerpt are confirmed. The association's own site was not read; it is the likeliest source for upkeep and current climbing rules. Other search snippets say the tower was 'originally constructed in 1924 by local volunteers' and describe it as stone and wood; they were not read, so they are not used. The FFLA row has no NHLR or FFLOS number. Its coordinates match the brief (43.67226, -71.29064). The climbable flag rests on the 2018 visit. About seven page reads were used for this tower, which is over the budget.

The 2022 chapter report and the FFLA New Hampshire list are the only sources read. Both date from 2022 or are undated, so the current condition and access are unknown; the story says so. The brief's events were garbled: '2022 built' is corrected to a relocation and erection, and 'None relocated' contradicted 'Moved from Alabama'. The FFLA list says 'Relocated from AL'; the 2022 report says the seller has not said where the tower came from, so the Alabama origin stays attributed to the list. Two searches found no other source naming the earlier site. A Davana sale-list PDF (DAVANA-LLC-0725.pdf) was read in part for context; the matched lines do not mention Hooksett or Bass Pro. The coordinates match the brief (43.04077, -71.47663). About six page reads and two searches were used for this tower. Fact check 2026-10-09: the story said the 2022 report 'says something different'; it only fails to confirm the Alabama origin, so the wording now says that. The story also said all sources date from 2022; the FFLA New Hampshire list has no date, so the story now says the report dates from 2022 and the list is undated. Both pages were read in full and the quotes were confirmed.

Brief's height_m 121.9 (about 400 ft) is not supported; NHLR's 34 ft tower plus 1979 10 ft addition gives 13.4 m, and that is proposed as the correction. Build date: 1914-15 (Historic Structures), 1915 (NHLR), 1913 (Trailspotting), left as a stated conflict. Agency: NHLR names the NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development; a search snippet pointed to a dncr.nh.gov news release, which returned 403 when fetched, so the newer agency name is unverified and not cited. Final 2023 costs and the actual 2024 reopening are not confirmed beyond the newsletter's expectation and Trailspotting's 2025 'refurbished in 2023' statement. Staffing: NHLR's 2016 visit report says 'Sometimes' staffed, during fire season; no current staffing source found. No specific fires were named in sources read. Left out on purpose: a 1952 death at the lookout cabin in the Forest Lookouts item and a 1957 newspaper mention of a named lookout, since they concern private individuals and are not needed for the tower's history. The Historic Structures page is a third-party history site; its dates are cited as its own claims. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with public trail access and seasonal road-gate hours from Trailspotting; climbing the cab is not stated in any source. Budget note: the Historic Structures page was grepped several times from cache; it counts as one page.

Brief's 2002 registration and 2008 cab replacement check out (NHLR; FFLA 2008 chapter report says a new cab was installed). Brief's record has no built year or height; built 1915 is supported by NHLR, Historic Structures and the 1915-1916 state report quoted on Forest Lookouts. Height conflict: 32 ft (NHLR, Trailspotting) versus roughly 40 ft if the 1970-1980 cab addition is counted (Historic Structures); no height_m set. First-use year 1912 or 1913 is unresolved. The NHLR 2016 visit report and the Trailspotting 2025 hours are the only current-condition sources; the NH state staffing claim is from the 2016 visit. The 1948 hay-fire item is from Forest Lookouts and spells the town Stratford; it is cited as a fire the lookout reported, names of private officials omitted. Town spelling: Farmington (Historic Structures, Trailspotting) with Strafford County (NHLR). Wikipedia was read as a lead; its town and county lines agree but it is not cited. Page budget: six distinct pages read, one WebSearch.

Record elevation_m 848.3 does not match the 3,121-foot summit in the 1954 press reprints (about 951 m). elevation is not a facts key, so it was not changed; please check it. climbable=true is inferred from the register's stairs and the 2024 visitor reports, not from a published visit rule. No rental information was found. The state's closure notice gives no year, so the access note does not name one. No current 2026 status check was done.

Only secondhand sources back the history: an undated NH Family Hikes roadside guide with no citations, and a 2014 hike report. No NHLR entry, FFLA chapter report, state record or newspaper item was found, and the Forest Lookouts Carter page has only a title card. The 1897 date and the Carter family's role should be treated as tentative. Do not confuse with Carter Dome (us-nh-carter-dome, a gone tower at 44.26715, -71.17922), which is a different site. Access: the NH Family Hikes guide says the tower is private property, so the record should not invite visitors to the door. Leads: Jefferson town or historical society files, and Carter family or railroad history, for the owner and build date.

Height after the wooden cab conflicts (41 ft vs about 51 ft implied by the Register). Open days differ by year: the 2019 newspaper gives October 13 and 14; the 2021 blog says one weekend a year. henniker.org returned 403 to fetch, so current open dates are not verified. The 1997 Register date and the 1997 rescue are both sourced. No specific fires were found. No photos added.

The main history comes from Historic Structures, which reproduces a detailed description of the tower and its history. It is a secondary source and its own citations are not visible to us, so treat its dates as strong but not verified against the state record. The Forest Lookouts page has only three dated lines. The 2009 record event should be 'modified' (cab), not 'replaced' (tower); see corrections. Height is unresolved (24 ft vs 34 ft) and is left out of facts. Access: the tower is inside a private preserve and the sources say it is closed to the public, so the record should not invite climbing. Leads: the NH Fire Tower Quest Program PDF from NH Forests & Lands, cited by the Corbin Park Wikipedia article (not fetched; the state site returned 403 for the related history PDF); and the Blue Mountain Forest Association for lease and access terms.

Cab fate conflicts: NHLR says the cab was later removed and Trail Finder says it was removed once out of use, while FFLA says the state burned it around 1985. Stairs: FFLA says burned, Trail Finder says removed to discourage climbing. The story reports both. NH Family Hikes lists a 'North Deer Mountain' in Pittsburg whose stairs were removed; it may be this tower, but I did not use it because the name match is not certain. onlyinyourstate.com returned HTTP 403 and was not used. The rehabilitation status is only as of the 2023 FFLA report; no later news was found. The access level 'restricted' is my reading: the wooden steps were removed to discourage climbing (trail guide), and no source says the tower is formally closed to climbing, so the story no longer says it is. The steps are cited to FFLA and the trail guide, since NHLR does not mention them. No photos added.

Coordinates differ between NHLR (42.81339, -71.65592) and firelookout.org (42.80479, -71.63033), about 2 km apart; not changed. The 2016 renovation completion is not confirmed by any source read. Access: the cabin is closed per a 2021 hiking blog; the story now says visitors can climb to the level below the cabin, and does not encourage climbing. The NH state fire-tower page returned HTTP 403, so state access and staffing rules are from news and blog sources. Staffing as_of is the 2016 visit date. The 2021 height and access notes rest on one hiking blog.

The 1934 date rests on NH Family Hikes alone (AllTrails repeats it, unread). NHDFL pages and PDF returned 403 to fetch_text and WebFetch, and Living New Deal returned 403, so the state record is unchecked. The record's kind 'platform' conflicts with FFLA's 'Open Tower'. FFLA files the site under non-lookout structures. Current stair condition and closure status are not verified.

The record's kind 'tower' is kept, but the sources describe a public park observatory. FFLA lists it as 'Obs Tower', and NH Family Hikes says whether it was ever a fire tower is a matter of debate, so the editor should decide whether it belongs in the fire-lookout set. The 1880 to 1913 history rests on Wikipedia and the Dover page, which agree on the main events. The 1993 date comes only from Wikipedia. Leads: the NRHP nomination for Garrison Hill Park and Tower (NRHP No. 87001413), which Wikipedia cites and which would confirm the 1880s ownership and the 1990 and 1993 dates; and any City of Dover record of fire-tower use, if one exists.

Elevation is unresolved: the Register lists 525 ft (160 m) for the site, while the Weirs Times describes a 1,300-foot summit. The record's 160 m is left unchanged for the editor to check. Register coordinates (43.86, -71.26) differ from firelookout.org (43.87691, -71.29874) by about 3 km; not changed. The Forest Lookouts page for Great Hill has only a header and no body text, so it is not cited. Living New Deal and franklinsites were not read (Living New Deal returned HTTP 403). Access is public per the town's reopening notice; the story does not encourage climbing.

Height: the record's 14.3 m is the original 47-ft tower; the register's 39 ft (11.9 m) is proposed. The 1958 survey's 35 ft overall is unresolved. Elevation: the register's 855 ft conflicts with the 1,884-ft (2025 guide) and 1,907-ft (1966 item) summit figures; the proposed 574.3 m needs a human check. Status: the register (undated) says part-time; the 2025 guide says no longer active. Access: public trails and a locked cab per the 2025 guide; not checked with NH DRED. Staffing as of 2026 unknown. Not verified: any changes after 2025. No photos added.

Current status and access are unverified after 2010. The NHLR rental link points at nhdfl.org, which did not resolve, and the NH state reservations page returned 403, so rental terms are unconfirmed. Sources 2 and 3 are secondary (a hobbyist site quoting newspapers; a hiking article with no date visible in the cache). The 1937 closure and 2009 vandalism are known only from the Forest Lookouts page. Brief record's access 'unknown' can be set to public for the trail; the cab's visitor status stays open.

The tower's own NHLR page is rich (built year, design, WWII use, administering/cooperating agencies, nomination, and a 2019 field inspection with staffing/condition detail), but outside corroboration is thinner than the 'well-documented' label implied: Wikipedia and the state park site confirm 1932 and public access but add little else, and a promising newspaper piece (Conway Daily Sun, 'Milan Hill's fire tower is 1 of 15 still in use') returned HTTP 429 on every fetch attempt and was never read -- worth another try, it likely has more on current staffing and may confirm or refute a claim (surfaced only in AI-synthesized web-search summaries, not in any page actually read) that the 1932 tower replaced an earlier one on nearby Jodrie Hill. I left that claim out of the story entirely since I couldn't verify it against a primary source. On location: the record's existing lat/lon (from ffla) is corroborated by OpenStreetMap's independently mapped tower node, while the NHLR page's own stated coordinates sit about 1.65 km (roughly a mile) away -- this likely resolves the 'conflicts' entry already in the tower record in ffla's favor, though I'm not proposing a formal correction since the record's location field already uses the better-supported value. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04): the CCC-camp sentence was footnoted to the state park page, which does not mention the CCC at all; moved that citation to Wikipedia, which does state it. Also corrected the story's claim that the NHLR/FFLA coordinates differ by 'a mile and a half' -- the actual gap (1,653 m) is about one mile, not 1.5. Used 2 of 3 allotted WebSearch calls (research); fact-check pass used WebFetch only, no WebSearch.

The 1910 build and Timberland Owners funding come from the NH Family Hikes history page, a secondary source. The NHDFL state PDF returned 403 to both fetch tools. The 1940-1981 steel tower dates and the platform age come only from VFTT forum posts and are flagged unverified in the story. The cab removal date is unknown. The record's kind and status_note are correct; agency is null in the record. Staffing is inferred from 'not in active service' in White Mountain History, which is undated.

Record gaps: no height and no access rule found. Access was left out because no source read gives a visit or climbing rule, so the story asks visitors to check with the state. The FFLA report is titled 'FFLA New Hampshire Chapter Report for 2019' in its text, so the 2019 year is confirmed. The record's 'state replaced the cab' is not in the report; see corrections. The 81.7 m height in the record looks like an error and should be checked before publishing. The fire record is for the mountain station and watchman, not necessarily this structure. Search results mentioned a 27-foot 1924 steel tower and a 1953-54 larger cab; I could not read those pages in the session, so they are not used. One search snippet also said a 2019 date was not found; the FFLA 2019 report does mention cab work, so that snippet was wrong.

Core history (1912 estate tower, 1941 transfer to the state, enclosed cab, 1992 registration) is consistent across the Register, the historic-structures summary and the 2026 state sheet. Open points: whether the cab came in 1941 or after; current height (37 ft in one summary; a Weeks State Park Association search snippet says 56 ft, not fetched so not used); staffing is not stated. The historic-structures page gives 420 acres for the estate in one place and donated 431 acres in another; the story avoids acreage. The NH Division of Forests and Lands history PDF returned HTTP 403, so it was not used.

Most history comes from the Register and a 1929/1947 newspaper excerpt quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the 1947 article is not checked against the original paper. The 2019 chapter report does not name the tower's operator and its staffing line is for the state's towers in general, not Oak Hill, so staffing is left as historical only. Its staffing line also rests on one member's account, as the report says. The 19.8 m height is from OpenStreetMap, not from the Register. The blog spells the road Sharker in its URL and Shaker in its text; the story uses Shaker. Climbing is described in one hiking blog only; no official rule was found, so the story does not say the tower is open to climb. Lead for later: any Concord or Loudon city or town record that confirms the tower's ownership and public access.

The brief's built year 2004 comes from the NHLR Built field, which dates the replacement cab; the tower is 1939 per NHLR's own description and Historic Structures (see corrections). Height: 41 ft (NHLR, Historic Structures) vs 27 ft (NH State Parks history, undated). The park history also says the 1939 cabin no longer exists; that is not a conflict with the 2004 replacement cab, but the document is undated and gives 27 feet, so I treated it as the weaker source. The story no longer says the watchman was on duty when lightning struck in 1960: Historic Structures names the watchman of that time (on the job since 1941) but does not place him at the cab then. The 1960 cab: NHLR says burned and repaired, Historic Structures says destroyed and rebuilt that season; the story reports both. Staffing as_of is 'undated' because the NHLR page has no date. NHLR says staffed on class 3 days and above; Wikipedia says staffed seasonally. Historic Structures states the tower is one of 15 active NH fire towers; not used. No photos added; no on-site check.

The Register and the 1914 and 1930 items are consistent on the first steel tower, the 1971 raise and the 1976 cab. Sources do not agree on the site elevation: the Register says 549 feet, but the park sheet puts the tower on the 908-foot summit of South Mountain. The 1930 house item is a plan from a newspaper, not a confirmed use. The 1938 and 1920 items are from a Portsmouth Herald excerpt quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and not checked against the original paper. The 2016 chapter report's statewide staffing line is not specific to this tower and is not used. The OpenStreetMap way lists the operator as NH Division of Forests and Lands; the Register names NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development, so the story uses the Register. Climbing is supported only by two personal blogs and a park mention of the view; the story says to check with the park. Leads: park or NH Division of Forests and Lands notice about tower access; a 1914 Biennial Report copy for the original build detail. The 1930 notice also says the tree line was replaced by ground wire; the story does not say the Goodrich house was wired.

Current staffing is unconfirmed. The 2025 chapter report says Kearsarge was staffed, but Wikipedia says that name also belongs to a Merrimack County mountain, so the report cannot be tied to this tower. The NHLR entry gives no visit reports. The 28-foot height is read as the tower's height from the register's '28' steel tower' line. Start date disagrees across sources: Forest Lookouts gives a 1910 lookout station; the Weirs Times gives a 30-foot wood tower built 1911 and a 2,702 ft summit. Both are kept and not reconciled. Builder is disputed: the register credits the NH Forestry Commission, Willhite credits the CCC with Forest Service funds. Height: the record's 24.0 m matches no source; the register's 53-ft steel tower (16.2 m) is proposed, though it is not stated whether 53 ft includes the cab. Not verified: current climbing rules, hours, or whether the observation deck is open in winter. No photos added.

Elevation conflict: the register's 388 ft (118 m) matches the brief's 118.3 m; the crest figures are 605 ft (Derry News) and 604 ft (Derry survey). The story reports the Derry News figure and the register's figure. Agency: the department name the brief used is on the register, so it was not an error; the story names only the Division of Forests & Lands. Historic Structures gives both a leased 1-acre tract and a 2-acre purchase for the Mears land; the story uses the 2-acre figure from the quote. No photos recorded.

Thin record: two short sources. No build date, builder, owner or access rules found. Editor may want a reference check (Baird and Haartz field guide, Coos County registry) before publishing.

Current public access, climbability, and staffing status (volunteer vs. paid, active vs. seasonal) were not confirmed in this pass; the NJ DEP detection-program page would not render via the text fetcher (JS-only or blocked). NJ DEP fire-tower pages (dep.nj.gov/parksandforests/wildfire/fire-towers/ and nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/fire/program/detection.html) returned no text from the cache, so they are not cited. Status is unverified. The brief says standing, but I found no source that says the cab survives today, so no status key is written. Page reads went over the budget of six (the Batsto Facebook post came back empty and the NJ forum thread was an extra read). No photos added.

Pre-1934 tower chronology is genuinely muddled across sources (1880s platform / 1909 iron tower / 1916 frame tower claims); worth noting as unresolved rather than picking a version. Exact April 1932 fire date not pinned down beyond 'last Friday' before an April 15, 1932 article.

Access level 'restricted' is an inference from active agency service; no source states a public visiting rule. No current staffing data was found, so no staffing fact is recorded. Good corroboration across a historical register, a period newspaper quote (Courier-Post, 1940), the Wikipedia tower-list table, and a 2024 news feature confirming the tower is still actively staffed; all of those checked out against their cited sources. One claim did not hold up on cross-check: NHLR's Blue Anchor page says the original Aermotor tower was relocated to Stokes State Forest in 1932 to become 'the Culver tower,' but NHLR's own page for that lookout (Culvers Lookout, US44/NJ1) dates its present 47-ft Aermotor tower to 1933 and never mentions Blue Anchor — so the 'same tower, still standing at Stokes' claim in the earlier draft was an overclaim, now softened and the discrepancy disclosed in the story. Also removed an invented 'winter of 1920-21' detail not supported by the cited annual-report quote. No source found on public climbing access, so access.level was left unchanged rather than guessed.

Staffing as_of is the April 2023 visit report; no newer staffing data found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from active status and the locked cab. History from 1922 to 1997 is well sourced (NHLR plus 1922-1924 press and state reports). Current status rests on NHLR visit reports from 2018 and a 2022 repainting comment, not a 2026 check. Staffing as_of is the December 2004 visit report; no newer staffing or access data found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from the fence and locked gate. No visiting directions were confirmed; the earlier 'directions are signed from the road' note was not supported by the register and was removed (the register's access checklist has an unanswered 'directions signed' item).

Dates conflict: first use 1908 (Wikipedia, NHLR) vs first state tower 1918 with April 1919 start-up (Willhite); present tower 1933 (NHLR) vs CCC tower 1934 (Willhite). Not settled. Only the NHLR gives the 1944 build year. Brief record checked: the 1994 NHLR registration is correct. No corrections needed. Access was 'unknown' and is now 'closed', per the NHLR 2020 visit report. Only two sources (NHLR and Wikipedia), and they agree. A firelookout.org listing (Active, 1937) seen in a search snippet could not be fetched (404) and is not cited. The 1922 opening and the registry's 1922 build year agree on the year; the month is unclear. The 1950 build year and the register details rest on the NHLR page alone; no NJFFS, newspaper or state document was found for them. The 1916-1919 history comes from 1916-1919 newspaper and state report clippings reprinted on the Forest Lookouts page. The 1924 state tower and the 1946 addition come from the NHLR page only. The two Former Fire Lookout Sites records (Windbeam and Pierson Ridge) describe the same tower differently: Windbeam says it went to Pierson Ridge circa 1971 and to Ramapo in 1983; Pierson Ridge says it went to Ringwood State Park in 1971, was later destroyed by vandals, and was rebuilt at Ramapo from 1983. Fetching the NJ DEP fire-towers page returned no text. The Windbeam page's 1923 newspaper quote (easternuslookouts.weebly.com) was not used.

Identified from the Morey's Piers and Coasterpedia pages, plus the OSM way. Dedication year 2026 is supported by the Pine Barrens article's April 9, 2026 dateline and its 250th-anniversary-this-year wording; the nj.com article returned HTTP 403. Identity is settled: the Devil Mountain site entry says the tower became Atole, and the register describes the same Forest Service design. (5) Access: no public rules found; restricted is an inference from tribal land and BIA service. No notable fires found. The record's material 'steel' is supported by the register's steel tower.

Core facts (build, design, elevation, 2016 use, 2022 registration) rest on the NHLR page and are corroborated for the CCC build by the NPS page. Not verified: whether the cab is open to visitors or rented, current staffing, and any fire history; the story says so. This dating is from general knowledge, not from the sources here. The NPS CCC page contains no mention of the lookout (checked by grep). The 1940-41 correction is left for human review; events.year stays an integer, matching the other records.

Built 1959 date agrees across NHLR, the 2020 report and Zinn; the earlier history rests on Zinn's chapter, which dates its sources. Conflict: NHLR's 1930s first-lookout claim does not match Zinn. The 1988 thematic nomination and any NRHP nomination on npgallery were not read.

Source [2] (westlookouts.weebly.com) is an amateur compilation site, apparently drawn from old newspaper clippings; its specific names (Buck Wheeler, Jim Cain, A.K. Bourne, Mrs. T.C. Clifton) and fire dates (1936, 1941) could not be cross-checked against a primary source and should be verified against Nevada newspaper archives if this page gets more scrutiny. The build year (1931 start vs. NHLR's 1932 completion) is not a real conflict - both describe the same winter 1931-32 construction. On fact-checking, the 1964/1970 staffing detail was also not a real cross-source conflict: 'closed for the season' in 1964 (source 2) describes a routine seasonal closure, not an end date, and source 3 (Tahoe Daily Tribune) independently corroborates staffing continuing into the 1970s - the story previously framed this as 'sources disagree,' which overstated it, and has been corrected. Also corrected on fact-check: the NRHP-eligibility-in-1997 claim was mis-cited to sources 1/3, which don't contain it; it is only in source 4 (South Tahoe Now), and has been re-cited there. The source 3 article (Tahoe Daily Tribune) is itself dated December 19, 2001, not current - it names a 'National Trust for Historic Preservation' registry listing, a different, private-nonprofit designation from NRHP eligibility; the story does not currently mention that National Trust listing. 'Last Forest Service lookout built in the state' was also corrected to 'remaining in the state,' since NHLR's source text says 'the last U.S. Forest Service lookout in Nevada' (i.e., the only one left), not that it was the last one constructed. The 2013 relocation-to-White-Hill proposal's outcome is unknown; could not find any later source confirming or denying the move happened, so current physical location/status is uncertain despite the tower record's 'standing' status. A 2001 Las Vegas Sun piece and a 2013 Carson Now piece look relevant but returned paywall/403 errors and were not used.

Open items for a human: (1) the observer's cabin date is disputed. The 1941-model cabin is said to date from 1950, but the 1964 survey description quoted by the Eastern site says there was no cabin at the top and that one was added later; the story reports both and does not pick a side. (2) Record coordinates (FFLA 42.04976, -78.01363) and NHLR (42.054757, -78.014137) are 557 m apart, as the record's own conflict note says; no source here settles which point is the tower. (3) The 80 ft figure is overall height; the sources do not give height to the cab floor, so height_m is left unset. (4) The record's agency 'Private Owner' matches NHLR; the Conservation Department built the tower but is not the current administrator. (5) The current landowner is a private individual and is deliberately not named. (6) Visit or access after 2002 is not documented; access is recorded as private/closed on the strength of NHLR and NYSFFLA.

Unresolved: cost ($300 in the register vs $530 in the group chronology) and height (35 ft vs 40 ft in Wikipedia) disagree; the story reports both and the record keeps the register cost in the event note. The register's elevation (2,500 ft, 762 m) is for the lookout site; mountain heights in other sources differ, but those came from search snippets that were not read, so they are not used. The 2018 visit notes glass not intact; the current condition of the cab and any climbing rules are unverified. Andy Arthur's trail map page returned 403; the Daily Gazette centennial article and the 2003 Azure Mountain News PDF were not read. Brief record's events listed only the 2003 registration; the 1914, 1918, 1978, 2001 and 2002 events were added from sources 1 and 2. A July 5, 2007 register visit report says the tower is currently open for general public use; that is too old to treat as current, so the story does not rely on it.

Built dates agree across the three sources (1887 club tower, 1905 wooden replacement, 1919 first steel tower, 1930 present tower) once the NHLR, state guide and Wikipedia are read together. Wikipedia's section heading dates the club's establishment 1885-1909 but its text says 1887; the story uses 1887. Height differs (47 vs 47 1/2 ft). The reopening year is not stated in the Wikipedia text read, so no restoration year is recorded. The access and staffing evidence is from a 2017 NHLR visit report, so current status should be checked. The state guide is a multi-column PDF; its quotes were taken from single lines. Wikipedia's coordinates (42.06972, -74.57444) differ from the record's (42.045395, -74.594604), which matches NHLR; left unchanged. A later NHLR visit report says the tower is open Friday to Sunday, but it is undated in the text read, so it was not used.

The tower's history is well documented in the NHLR detail page, which the record cites. The planned NHLR history PDF (2966), chapter PDFs (2962, 2963) and beebehill.info all failed (404 or DNS), so their content is not used. Relocation year conflicts: NHLR gives November 1963 for the move to Beebe Hill and Wikipedia gives 1964; a web search summary also mentioned a 1932 versus 1933 Washburn re-erection and a 1988 end-of-season closure with a 1989 official closure, but those came from search snippets and were not read on a fetched page, so they are not in the story. Current status is the main open question: Wikipedia (late 2024, unsafe) versus NYSDEC page (open to the public) and NHLR (restored 2025). Verify on site or with NYSDEC before any climb. Access level is public for hiking the forest; climbability of the tower itself is not established and is left unset. The NHLR notes the tower was Aermotor LS-40 60-foot as first erected, not necessarily its current height.

Build history is consistent across sources only at the level of a 1912 station with a wooden tower and a 1917 steel tower. NHLR lists 1917 as the build year, which the brief also uses; Wikipedia and the Explorer say 1917 replaced a 1912 wooden tower. Closure date conflicts: NHLR says closed 1988; Wikipedia says out of service 1988 and officially closed early 1989; Stream & Steeple agrees with Wikipedia. Ownership conflicts: NHLR says administered by NYSDEC and the Explorer places it in the Hammond Pond Wild Forest, but Stream & Steeple says private land. Trail length conflicts (0.3 vs 0.4 mile). Access is set to public for the site only; no source confirms that climbing the tower is permitted, and the story advises treating it as closed. Stream & Steeple lists Belfry in an ADK Fire Tower Challenge that requires climbing fire tower summits; that is not a state opening. Staffing history rests on the Explorer's 'until 1988' and the 2017 visit report; the Podskoch book and the Landmarks of Moriah post were not reachable. andyarthur.org pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The height is converted from 47 feet. Verification pass 2026-10-08: the story's 'site is open to the public' wording was changed to the tower being accessible, as Stream & Steeple states; the 'no source says climbers' sentence was corrected for the challenge text; 'cab glass broken' was changed to 'not intact' to match the form.

Three independent sources agree on the 1934 CCC build, the 1988 end of fire watch, the early-1989 closure and the September 13, 2021 reopening. The NHLR page gives no build year, so 1934 comes from the DEC release and Wikipedia. The 1935 first-staffing date rests on Wikipedia alone. The DEC release says the tower was open for recreation after the upgrades; access is recorded as public, climbable true, on that basis. Current staffing is not documented after the 2017 NHLR visit (not staffed). An andyarthur.org page gives an early-fall 1934 construction date, but it could not be fetched, so it is not used. The DEC release's sentence on a Forest Service chapter agreement was cut off in the cache and is not used. Height is 59 ft 3 in per Wikipedia (18.06 m). The NHLR visit report predates the 2021 work, so its condition findings are historical. Verification pass 2026-10-08: the story's visitor-rules sentence had no support in the DEC release and was replaced with the DEC's sunrise-to-sunset hours; the 1,960 ft figure is from the NHLR and DEC, and Wikipedia's 1,962 ft is named in the story; 'no one had a key' was corrected to the report's 'we had no key'.

The brief dated the build to 1918. Sources show a wooden lookout in 1911 that the 1918 steel tower replaced, so both are listed. Three different closure years (1988, 1989, 1990) are reported as found; a DEC or NYS Archives record would settle them. NHLR says the tower is closed and fenced; do not encourage climbing. The NYS Archives has 1918 photos of fire observer William C. Noble at Black Mountain (digitalcollections.archives.nysed.gov), seen only in search results and not used. The andyarthur.org pages returned 403 and were not read. No NRHP listing was found. Revised on fact-check 2026-10-08: the 80-ft total is now reported with the caveat that 35 ft plus 39 ft is 74 ft, and the story does not resolve it; 'still stands' is now footnoted to the present-tense Wikipedia text; sentences reworded where they copied source wording.

Brief status_note says the cab is gone (FFLA). Not verified: the NHLR 2007 visit report says there is no roof and does not mention the cab, and the FFLA asterisk footnote was not read, so the cab claim is left out of the story. Brief access 'unknown' is answered by the 2007 NHLR visit report (entry by permission; not open to the public); that report is nearly 20 years old. Wikipedia's Black Rock Forest article also mentions an observation tower on the 1,402-foot Black Rock peak; it is not established that this is the NHLR tower (398 ft elevation), so it is not used. Searches found no construction or Stillman-era records for this tower.

Dates are solid: the 1911 wooden tower and 1917 steel tower (NHLR, brochure, Wikipedia), 1990 closure, 1994 rehabilitation, 1995 NHLR registration, and 2001 NRHP listing. Current status rests on an undated Fire Tower Challenge brochure and a commercial listing, so re-check opening status and the summer steward programme before relying on it. The brochure layout mixes several towers, so only its single-line statements are quoted. The NHLR 2018 visit report notes plans to repaint and redeck in 2018; the outcome was not found. The NRHP nomination PDF is not digitized (NPGallery says so), so no nomination text was used. The Blue Mountain Fire Observation Station Wikipedia entry gives a 1975 observer cabin and 1960s radar remains; not used. No photos were added.

Brief claims not found in any page read, so left out: the Davanna LLC inventory on 25 Aug 2020; the 2023 Delaware County permit-holder role; the Excelsior Towers re-erection and 17 Oct 2024 visibility date; the 4 January 2025 opening day. The only county reference found is Delaware County Board of Supervisors chair Tina Molé in the Friends' home page video caption. Sources are interested parties: the NHLR nominator, Laurie Rankin, is a Friends board member per the Friends' history page, so 'the Friends say' is their own account. facts.agency stays 'Clark Family' because NHLR lists that; the Friends' site says NYC DEP owns the summit and the Friends maintain the tower, so the agency field may need a better answer. The May 2 opening year (2025) is inferred from a Friends' home page post that says 'last year' in a note about John Bramley's death; the page does not give the year outright. Not verified: whether the tower can be climbed outside steward days. No photos added.

Core facts (1933 build, private owner Cedar Heights Timber LLC, September 2, 2023 opening, trail details) are confirmed by two or three sources each. Not confirmed: the brief's 2022 restoration details (stairs, roof, painting by August 2022), which the town notice does not support; a correction is proposed above. The brief's Sept 15, 2023 ribbon cutting appears in the town notice as scheduled, not as held, so it is not in the story. The brief's height was absent; 60 ft converted to 18.3 m. Whether climbing the cab is permitted is not stated in any source. The NHLR page is stale on the reopening date. A HistoriCorps caption that appeared only as a search snippet (not opened, not cited) gives a 1939 build date, which conflicts with the 1933 date in the register and the newsletter; the editor may want to check it. The Adirondack Almanack and Wikipedia results were seen only as search snippets and are not cited.

Height 15 m comes from Wikipedia, which cites the NYSFFLA searchable list (not read); verify against that list before publishing. The 2020 newsletter is the source for 'off limits'; current access in 2026 is not verified. The Adirondack Explorer article is undated in the copy we read; it refers to 2022 legislation, so it was probably written in 2022 or later, and no later status report was found. The Adirondack Council release (search snippet only) argues a tower can be built without an amendment; not used.

Height is given as 60 feet in both sources; 18.3 m is converted from feet. The 'closed to the public' status comes from the undated NYSFFLA list entry; no source gives a date, so the current condition is not confirmed on site. Wikipedia's private-property statement is a secondary claim; its own references (Laskey 2003; Starr roster) were not read. The 1953 Ferris notice is a Chronicle-Express item as quoted on Forest Lookouts and is not checked against the original. The Forest Lookouts page spells the county 'Duchess' in one place; the record and other sources use Dutchess, so no correction is proposed. Staffing after 1960 is not documented in the sources read.

Build year: NHLR says 1950; the October 1950 Post-Star report says the tower had just shipped and was in temporary storage; the April 1951 Times Record says it was being built. The story reports this rather than choosing; the NHLR 1950 date is kept in events. Height: 80 ft (NHLR and 1950 report) vs 81 ft (1951 paper). The record's height_m 24.4 matches 80 ft and is left unchanged; the sources do not say whether the height is to the cab floor. Status label: the FFLA New York list shows this site with status 'Private' rather than 'Standing'; NHLR describes it as still standing and in NYSDEC use, so the record's 'standing' is kept, but a human should check the FFLA label. Observer names come from a state roster and a 1951 paper; no residences are given. The private property where the tower was stored in 1950 is not named. Radio users: the roster says 'several agencies'; the story uses NHLR for today's NYSDEC use. No corrections proposed.

The brief's Starr PDF link (nhlr.org/nhlr.org/media/...) returns 404; the working URL is nhlr.org/media/2967/... and is used here. The brief's 2008 relocation is contradicted by the Starr article and the Saratogian and is corrected to 2010. A web search snippet for Wikipedia's Cornell Hill page says summer 2008; that page was not read and is not cited. The ownership question (Mackay purchase in 1976 versus a nominal-fee sale after decommissioning) is unresolved and should be checked before publication. The current Town of Wilton rules page was not read, so today's guided-visit rule is unknown. The local record ../us-ny-cornell-hill/ was not read. The Starr article is a two-column PDF, so some quotes are split on single column lines; those were chosen to stay inside one column.

Brief's NRHP 11000253 confirmed by Wikipedia (No. 11000253). The register's 'owned by the State Police' note is undated and superseded by the 2012 handover reported in the Almanack. Permission to climb is not stated outright; climbable true is inferred from the 2025 repair of all 80 steps and the hiking-destination description, so confirm with Grafton Lakes State Park. The register's 2016 and 2017 visit reports are old and not used for current condition. The register's 2018 playscape tower and the Helen Ellett observer anecdotes are not used. The NRHP nomination PDF was not read.

Staffing, closure and 1940 build are consistent across NHLR, nysffla and Wikipedia. Elevation differs slightly (NHLR 2,108 ft; Wikipedia 2,106 ft); the record's 642.5 m is kept and not put in facts. The NHLR photo credit (Laurie Rankin, 2012) has no image URL, so no photo added. Not verified: the current owner or use of the radio equipment, and whether any recent visit or closure record exists. Access is inferred from the NHLR closure note; no visit report found.

andyarthur.org returned HTTP 403 in the cache and was not used. The NYSDEC fire-towers page was not read. The Oct. 14, 2025 ribbon cutting is only reported as scheduled; no post-event source was read, so the reopening is not confirmed. Climbing permission is not stated outright, so the visit fields stay with trail details only. Brief's record height of 20.0 m appears to be an error (60 ft = 18.3 m). The 1932 Huntington donation to SUNY appeared only in a search snippet and is not used.

Solid on the 1909 wooden tower, 1918 steel tower, 1919 blowdown and 1920 rebuild (Register, a state report quoted on Forest Lookouts, and the 2020 NYSFFLA newsletter agree). Closure year is disputed: Register says 1988, Wikipedia says lookout work ended after the 1988 season and official closure was early 1989. The record's note that the tower carried State Police radio equipment for years is not supported by any source read: the Warren County document shows the summit as a county transmitter/receiver site but does not say State Police use the Gore site. The record's note that hikers still visit the site is also unsupported; the Register says the tower is closed to visitors, so the story does not say hikers visit. Wikipedia says the 1918 replacement was made by the Civilian Conservation Corps, which was not founded until 1933, so that claim is not used. The record's height_m 5.5 is the 1909 wooden tower (see corrections). The FLO New York list places the tower at -74.04878, about 3.6 km west of the Register and record coordinates (-74.00397), which match the Register's coordinates; the record coordinates were left as they are. No photos added: the Register's June 26, 2020 photo is credited to Laurie Rankin but its licence is not stated.

Build year: the brief had none. The 1930 date rests on the Middletown Times Herald (Aug 1930) and the 1930 state annual report, both quoted on the Pocatello Mountain page of Forest Lookouts, plus the NHLR's statement that the tower was first erected on Pocotello Mountain. A Facebook group post dated the Pocatello tower 1930 but the page could not be read, so it is not cited. Access 'unknown' in the brief is replaced by 'restricted' from Bob Spear's undated Register history notes (gate and private-land remarks), which may be out of date. The brief's elevation (396.2 m) and OSM node were not read and are not used. Current climbability and the tower's present condition are not established by any source read. The April 2021 newsletter's 'Roosa Gap' paragraph about reopening refers to a different tower and is not applied to Graham.

The build date conflicts: register and Starr say construction ran late 1916 to early 1917 (story uses this), while Wikipedia gives 1917 and reports a plaque saying the original wood tower dates to 1916 and the current steel tower to 1920. The plaque was not read directly, only through Wikipedia. Access and staffing rest on 2017 visit reports and a 2017 Explorer article; no 2026 source was found, so current access and whether a steward is present now need confirming before any visit guidance. height_m 12.2 is converted from the register's 40 ft. Not used: andyarthur.org (both pages returned 403); hadleymtfiretower.org (the committee's site returned no text through fetch_text, so its history was not verified; a search snippet mentioned 1903 to 1915 fires and an Ohmer origin, which are unverified and left out); Facebook and Grokipedia search snippets. Photos: the register lists photo captions only, with no image URLs in the cache, so none recorded. Budget: 1 WebSearch, 6 successful page reads, 2 failed andyarthur reads. Brief record checked: elevation_m 816.9 matches the register's 817 m; no corrections proposed.

Brief's access field was 'unknown'; sources support public/volunteer-staffed access, consider updating. Height given in brief record omitted; 60 feet converted to 18.3m here from NHLR description, not from the brief's own height_m field (brief had none).

Brief build year 1919 confirmed. The start of fire watch is 1909 (NHLR) or 1910 (Friends via Explorer). Staffing records conflict across NHLR visits. The 2010 reclassification comes from Adirondack Life. A Daily Gazette piece gives 2014 for a St. Regis Mountain parcel, not Hurricane, so it is not used here. Pure Adirondacks is a hiking blog for the 2015 reopening; current access was not verified. The last NHLR visit is March 2018, so the roof and condition may have changed. The NRHP nomination (npgallery d62496c9) was not read. Revised on fact-check 2026-10-08: 'Today' now reports the 2018 visit findings; the well-signed trails claim is footnoted; the 1979 closure is attributed to the Friends group; the removal of the Primitive-land tower is no longer presented as caused by its land classification.

Brief's April 2017 closure and 2022 closure are not supported: earliest closure found is the NHLR visit of January 21, 2018; fenced off by November 2021 per Hike the Hudson Valley. Brief's 'finished 3 June' (2018) and the May 21, 2021 paint-over were not found in sources read and are omitted. A Facebook and a Reddit search snippet mention a later volunteer effort to reopen the tower, but those pages were not read, so nothing from them is used. 'Today' status rests on the 2023 chapter report and a 2021 note; a fresh check is advisable. The 1932 newspaper item is seen only as quoted on Forest Lookouts. The brief's 'Gate Hill' name for the tower is not in any source read beyond that 1932 item. Photos not added.

The brief had no build year; 1925 is added with the 1926 operating-year conflict noted. Access is marked restricted because a 2018 landowner closure is reported in the Explorer, but the Explorer piece is undated in the cache and no source says whether climbing the tower is permitted. The Explorer author climbed the tower; do not encourage climbing. The full NRHP nomination was not retrieved; the NPGallery listing had only metadata. The only NHLR visit is January 2018, so current condition is unknown. The NHLR page and the Wikipedia page are the sources for the staffing and build facts. Revised on fact-check 2026-10-08: 'covered in graffiti' now follows the Explorer's 'canvas for graffiti'; the 2021 DEC role in the roof and porch work is stated; the Explorer author still reached the tower after the 2018 closure report, which the story notes; the climbing sentence now cites all three sources it refers to.

Removal date conflicts (1977 vs 1980s) and the mountain's direction from Long Lake conflict; see resolved_conflicts. The 1911 wooden tower and 1918 date rest mainly on Wikipedia, which cites a New York fire-lookout list that was not read. The Explorer profile is long; only the opening and the early history passage were read. The 1990s rebuild and the 2022 registration rest on the NHLR entry alone. Museum hours come from the museum homepage and may change seasonally. Brief record corrected: the museum tower is a rebuild from Kempshall and West parts, so the name is corrected. No photos added. Not verified: whether climbing is allowed on every open day. Check 2026-10-09: all 22 quotes were found on the first run; four footnoted claims were corrected (beside to near the hamlet, summit to mountain for the 1911 tower, Wikipedia 'says only' overstatement, and the missing footnote for the single exhibit tower) and the undated 'Today' hours claim now attributes the hours to the museum homepage.

The identity of the Oak Orchard tower is not confirmed. The FFLA lists a platform tower relocated from Kings Park, and Wikipedia mentions an observation tower on Albion Road without linking it to Kings Park. A Facebook post by the FFLA New York chapter reportedly says the lower 47 feet were re-erected at Oak Orchard; the page did not open beyond its title, so the story does not use it. Standing rests on the FFLA list alone. The register's 1948 build date and the 1947 staffing date disagree, and the sources disagree about who controlled the tower after 1959. Searches: 1 WebSearch plus a cache search; about 5 distinct pages read.

Dates conflict: NHLR 1934 at Gilbert Lake, Wikipedia 1932, and the NHLR Built field 1948. Current status rests on the April 2017 NHLR visit and an undated Gilboa article; no source after 2017 was read. The Gilboa 'tallest tower' claim is unverified. A Daily Star article that might add closure detail returned HTTP 429 and was not read. The page-read budget was exceeded by one (a second Wikipedia fetch).

The 1917 erection is consistent across NHLR, Wikipedia and NPGallery metadata. The 1927 hurricane rebuild appears only in NHLR. The NRHP nomination PDF is marked not yet digitized, so Wikipedia's 1912 wooden predecessor could not be checked at source. Current condition rests on the 2018 NHLR visit and an undated DEC page; no visit after 2018 was found.

The build year (1917) and the 1988 end of service agree across the NHLR, Wikipedia and the Almanack; the 1910 station predates the tower and is noted. The record already has 1917 built and 2017 registration, both correct; no correction needed. Staffing and access come from an undated NHLR entry and a 2022 Almanack article, so a current check with NYSDEC or the Town of Saranac is advised before any visit. The NHLR says the 2005 repairs were by NYSDEC with the Student Conservation Corps. No new photos were added.

Build and re-erection dates agree across four sources. Unresolved: end of fire watch (1970 vs early 1970s), model (LL25 vs LS25), county (Essex in NHLR, Hamilton via the chamber's link), and site name. Current access rests on a tourism page, not a village notice; confirm hours before publishing. The brief's relocation entry was garbled and is corrected.

Build year, design and private status rest on Wikipedia, which cites the NYSFFLA searchable list; we could not open that list. The Adirondack Forum post is a visitor's remark, cited only as unverified. No staffing record, fire record, recent photo or condition report found. No corrections proposed; the record name is kept, though Wikipedia uses Meenahga.

Only one source describes this tower: a row in the FFLA index (name, county, coordinates, type, status). Searches for its history returned only the Herkimer Moose River Mountain tower, which is a separate, removed site. Two Facebook group posts titled 'Moose River fire tower story' appear to mention a tower near Half Moon Lake in Watson, Lewis County, but the pages could not be read beyond their titles, so they are not used. Rock Mountain (Lewis Co.) in the index is at 43.81416 -75.23833, a different site. A local source (Lewis County historian or NYS DEC) is needed before a fuller history is published. The record's kind 'tower' is consistent with the index's windmill tower type; no correction proposed.

Correction proposed, not applied: county Suffolk should read Kings (Brooklyn). Height is unresolved: the 1910 lookout was a 20-foot tower and the 1916 erection was a 40-foot Aermotor LS-25, and the source does not say whether the second replaced the first. The sibling record us-ny-moosehead-mountain has height_m 6.1 (20 feet) and may describe only the 1910 tower; left unchanged. The record's 'rebuilt' 2016 event is kept in the record but the sources say refurbished and re-erected. Access and climbability rest on a May 2021 visitor blog; nothing later was found, and the Todd Group page is a contractor's marketing page. Historical facts come from the Forest Lookouts compilation of newspaper items, not the originals. Used 1 WebSearch and 4 page reads plus one cached local page.

The brief's 1912 'built' event refers to the first wooden tower; the present steel tower dates from 1917. The height conflict (47 ft in NHLR and ADK vs 56 ft in Wikipedia) is unresolved. Current public access is not confirmed: NYSDEC calls the land private and the tower restored, the register says OSI administers it, and ADK describes closure before its volunteer restoration. The access level is set to restricted for that reason and should be re-checked with OSI or NYSDEC. The 2010 'closed' event year is the year of ADK's account, not the closure date. The LA Times 2004 article on the wilderness debate and an andyarthur.org page were not readable (403), so they are not cited. The staffed_last year is not an event because the register says only 'the mid 1970s'. Wikipedia's retrieval date is October 29, 2025 per its reference list, not the accessed date.

Height conflict (35 ft vs 40 ft) is unresolved; the NRHP nomination PDF (Haynes and Garofalini, 2000) is not digitized on NPGallery, so it could not settle it. Adirondack Explorer carries an old COVID-19 editor's note saying the towers are closed; not used, so current access rests on the NHLR and Explorer text. NHLR gives the lookout elevation as 2,519 ft; Explorer gives the peak as 2,539 ft (not in facts). No notable fires are named in any source read. Friends of Mount Arab's history page returned 404 in the cache.

The 1931 build date is consistent across four sources. The retirement date conflicts: NHLR says 1987, Historic Structures says permanently decommissioned around 1975 after a brief return to service; the NHLR's 50-year claim and the restoration group's five decades match neither the 1932-1972 observation dates. The record's access 'unknown' is replaced with public on hiking-destination evidence, but the Scenic Hudson page is undated and current access was not checked against a live source. The 2009 NRHP date comes from Wikipedia, which cites the NPS weekly list. The 'restoration now completed' wording is from Historic Structures and is undated. The record's 2005 NHLR registration and the 18.3 m height are correct. No new photos were added.

The us-ny-mount-morris record merges two towers. The Manhattan Mount Morris watchtower in Harlem (Marcus Garvey Park) has its own record, us-ny-harlem-fire-watchtower. The 2019 restored event and the 'Mount Morris Fire Watchtower, Harlem' other name belong to that tower. The nysffla_projects row for the Harlem tower carries the Franklin County coordinates (44.15976, -74.47517) because it was matched to this record by name; fix the matching as well as this record. The 22-foot (6.7 m) height and 1919 completion are consistent across Wikipedia and Forest Lookouts. Ownership and current condition remain unresolved: a state or town records check, or a recent site report, would settle them. Access is recorded as closed, so do not encourage a climb. No new photos were added.

The 1940 build, 1988 end of service and 1989 closure agree across sources. The record's 'ownership: state' conflicts with the NHLR's statement that the Town of Kent owns the tower, so a correction is proposed. The record's 408.4 m elevation is not supported by the sources read; the 388 m mountain figure is proposed. Staffing and the 'open to the public' status come from undated sources and should be checked before a visit. The Town of Kent guide's 'recently restored' wording is undated. The 2009 NYSAC award and the Kent Wikipedia article's 'tallest remaining fire tower' claim were seen only in search snippets and are not used. No new photos were added.

Current condition and public access are unconfirmed. Wikipedia is the main source and cites no update after its restoration call. The marker page is about the Summit tower restoration; only its 1928 caption is cited. An online hiker post (Hike WNY group) says the stairs were removed and the tower is closed off, but we could not read it, so it is not used. Wikipedia gives 2,142 ft in the infobox and 2,144 ft in the text; elevation is not used. Wikipedia spells the park name Alleghany once; the park itself uses Allegany.

Fact-check 2026-10-09: the towers6 entry for New Boston names no fires and no named observers, which is the basis for the story's statement that none were found. Build year conflict, unresolved: the NYSFFLA list gives 1950 for an 80-foot Aermotor LS40 at New Boston. A Waymarking listing that appeared only in search results says 1914 on Tug Hill; the page body could not be read, so it is not used. Reopening conflict, unresolved: the 2004 annual report says the tower was open after a 2004 grand opening, while the NYSFFLA list says it was restored and reopened in 2016; no source explains the gap. A 2016 Spectrum News item seen only as a search snippet calls the zoo tower the old Lowville tower; DEC and the chapter both say New Boston, so that snippet is treated as a mislabel and was not used.
