The record's county (Sumter) is the current location; the register gives the original site as Marlboro County, so the record is not wrong but both counties are relevant. Sale date is 'late 1990s' (register) and 199?? (Forest Lookouts), so no event year was assigned for the move. Condition after the 2013 registration is unknown. The owner is a private individual; the story does not name them. Height 100 ft (30.5 m) is the tower height; the register's 248 ft (76 m) is ground elevation.

Design, original owner and 1938 build are well supported. The McIntosh purchase year conflicts across sources (late 1990s vs 199?? vs early 2000s) and is left open. The Register's 100 ft height versus the magazine's unassigned 110 ft towers is also unresolved. No staffing names, notable fires, or public-access statement were found. The magazine copy we read is dated June 2018. The 2013 registration date is from the Register.

The NHLR detail page is the main source. The FWS visitor guide gives island access and describes a 16-foot observation tower near the public dock, far shorter than the 110-foot lookout. Wikipedia is used only for the boat-access and ferry claims, which are not checked against the ferry operator. The Forest Lookouts page has only a header and no narrative. No staffing or fire history was found. No source says whether the public may climb the tower, so no access level is recorded. The NHLR's construction-by-Bureau-of-Biological-Survey claim versus the 1936 transfer is unresolved and needs a 1930s refuge history. The NHLR photo credit (Sarah Dawsey) has no image URL in the cache, so no photo is recorded.

Build date, CCC erection and the 100-to-40 ft reconstruction come from the Register and Forest Lookouts. The McIntosh purchase year conflicts (late 1990s vs 199?? vs early 2000s). A trail-guide search result (thedirtymule.com, Sumter National Forest Cassatt Fire Tower Ridge Circuit) returned 403 to fetch_text. A WebFetch summary, not a verbatim quote, says the page places the tower's old foundation in Sumter National Forest near Camden and that the tower's own build and move dates are not given. That is unverified and not used in the story; it needs a human check, since the original site may still hold a foundation. No staffing names or notable fires found.

Build date, height and the 1995 move are supported by both the Register and Forest Lookouts. The current location rests on the Register's 'yet to be moved' statement and a June 2018 magazine feature that describes a visit about fifteen years earlier, so treat it as inferred. No staffing names or notable fires were found. The Register's coordinates place the record in Richland County, and the current site may differ from the coordinates in the brief. The magazine's '2003' auction note is general and not used.

Build date is circa 1933 per the register and 1933 per the Facebook post, so it is treated as solid. Staffing, notable fires and any recent condition report were not found; the Forest Lookouts page has only the 2005 sale. The register's 'Bamburg' is read as a typo for Bamberg. The Facebook post comes from the Butterfield Plantation page, so its statements are the owner's account. The status 'standing' in the record is consistent with the post's account of the tower being erected at Butterfield, so it is not changed. Used 1 WebSearch and about 5 page reads.

Status is the main open question. NHLR registered Elko in 2026 with a photo and no description of present condition. The Eastern U.S. Lookouts list marks it Removed with no date. No build date was found. The SCFC closure date applies to the whole tower system, not to Elko specifically. This is not the Barnwell lookout (us-sc-barnwell), which is a different tower. The standing-to-removed correction is dropped: the register does not say whether anything stands, so the status stays open.

Only the register, the SCFC history page and Wikipedia were readable. WLTX and Post and Courier articles on the tower returned 403 and 429 and were not used; they would likely add access and staffing detail. Access and staffing are left out because no readable source states them. The Wikipedia article cites the register, so its 1936 date is not independent. A search snippet from an SCFC 'important fires' page mentions a different 'Gaston Fire' (a wildfire elsewhere, not linked to this tower); the page was not read and it should not be tied to the tower without a source.

NHLR gives only the 1930s for construction, so no built event is recorded. Staffing status none rests on the Forest Service statement that the tower is no longer in use and on NHLR standby status; the as_of date is the research date, and the staffing end (1993) is the last documented date. The county conflict is unresolved. No climbing information was found in the sources read, so visit.climbable is omitted. Hillmap and the OpenStreetMap node were checked but add no history. No new photos.

One substantive source (NHLR). The Forest Lookouts page has only a header (Charleston County; spelled 'Cape Romaine Wildlife Refuge' there, 'Cape Romain' in NHLR; the story uses NHLR's spelling). The record's status 'standing' is contradicted by NHLR (abandoned, legs collapsed June 2014), so a correction is proposed for human review. Height 60 ft converted to 18.3 m (structure height, not cab). No source gives access, staffing, or condition since 2014, so no access or visit facts are recorded. One web search for removal or collapse news found nothing relevant. The record's June 2014 downed-tower photo was not re-read. No new photos added.

Build year (1938, CCC and WPA) and registration date (July 27, 2006) are from the NHLR entry alone. The brief's status 'standing' is not confirmed by any source read; the NHLR entry does not state current condition, so facts.status is omitted. No staffing or fire history was found, so no staffing facts or fire events are recorded. Tower-specific access and climbing rules were not found; the access level 'public' reflects the open university forest with trail rules, not a statement about the tower. The Clemson World items concern the Lake Issaqueena recreation area, not the tower, and are used as context only. The 'other' event for 1934 is the WPA land program, not a tower event. The brief's coordinates match the NHLR coordinates. No new photos.

Thin record. One substantive source (NHLR). The Forest Lookouts Leeds page has only a header (Chester County, Sumter National Forest, satellite view). Two web searches for current status or staffing found nothing. The record's status 'standing' is not supported by any source read, so facts omit status; a human should check whether the tower still stands, perhaps through the Forest Service Enoree Ranger District. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m (structure height). Elevation in the record (200.3 m) matches NHLR. Story uses 'about 1936' for the build year. No photos added; the record already holds the NHLR image (us959_leeds.jpg).

Only the register and the SCFC history page were usable; no build year, operator or fire history for this tower turned up in two searches. The register's 'one of the original ~140' figure is not the same as a later SCFC social post that says 'more than 130'; that post was not fetched and is not cited. The register calls the tower in poor condition as of 2013; no newer condition report was found. Height 80 ft converted to 24.4 m, matching the record.

Thin record. Only the register page supports any tower-specific fact: location, elevation, registration, nominator and administrator. No build date, design, staffing, fire history or condition was found in the sources read. The register names the Forestry Commission as administrator, yet the Commission closed its fire tower system in 1993; the sources do not explain the link, so the story says so. The record's 'standing' is not confirmed by any source read, so facts.status is 'unknown' and no correction is proposed. The Forest Lookouts page for this tower returned a 404. Searches used: 3 WebSearch calls for this tower, one over the 2-call budget, because the first results did not identify a build date. About 4 page reads. Verification pass: the SCFC history page was searched for Lesslie, York, Ballenger and the tower name and has no mention of this tower; the story now says so, and no longer says the landowner is the contact (the register names only the administrator).

Two accounts disagree on Joe Price's years at the tower: 30 (May 1972 item, which also gives Trula 25) versus 35 (1992 obituary). Neither gives a start date; the story says so. The 1972 and obituary texts are as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not read from The Index-Journal itself. An Augusta Chronicle 2007 article (CCC-built towers in Sumter National Forest) returned HTTP 403 and is not used. HikingWNC is a hiking guide, cited for access only; its upper-deck line may be dated. The September 2020 NHLR visit report is the only current-condition evidence; a later visit could change the status. Access level 'restricted' is a judgement from the fence and posted signs; a human could set it to 'closed'. Staffing 'not staffed' comes from the NHLR visit form. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m (structure height). No new photos added (record already holds the 2020 NHLR image).

Thin sourcing: only the register and the SCFC history page were readable. Two dates conflict and are unresolved: the register puts the 1990 private sale 'after the abandonment' of the state system, but SCFC says it closed the system on 1 October 1993. Unread sources: a Facebook group post by Ted Brown says the tower was built in 1938/1939 (fetch returned title only, so not used); a Waymarking page calls it the summit of the county's highest point (fetch returned title only, not used). Do not confuse this with the Little Mountain in Newberry County, which has a Wikipedia article. Height 75 ft converted to 22.9 m from the register.

Brief lacked design and height; added from NHLR (54 ft = 16.5 m). Brief elevation 645.3 m matches NHLR 645 m. OpenStreetMap node 357111624 tags ele=658, not used. Build date is unresolved: NHLR says around 1935, but a February 1941 newspaper item, as reprinted by Forest Lookouts, announces plans for a tower on Long Nose mountain west of Walhalla. The story gives both; this may be a replacement or a different site. Current use is undated (NHLR). No source read documents public access or current condition. Search results for Long Mountain (a Facebook reel and a blog) were not read as page text and are not used. No photos. Confidence is low because the only substantive source is the register.

Register and one 2020 blog visit are the only sources read. Height converted from the register's 54 ft. Register says the Forest Service used the tower until the 1980s; no exact year, so no staffing event was recorded. Access and climbing status are unconfirmed; no Forest Service page was checked for closure notices. The brief's standing status rests on the 2020 blog and the register. The OpenStreetMap node (height 16.5) agrees but is not cited. Story does not encourage climbing.

Builder and date disagree: the Register gives 1940 and the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service; the Town's RFQ gives the 1930s and the U.S. Biological Survey. Both are cited, not resolved. Staffing end date is unknown ('until recent years'). Access is unknown: no source read says whether the public may visit or climb. Record coordinates match the Register's; elevation 7.6 m matches 25 ft. Unfetched search snippets (a Village Museum Facebook post, a Town picture PDF with no text layer) suggest c. 1935 and Forestry Commission use into the early 1980s; not used in the story. Worth a human look: the FFLA report's '$14,000 matching' phrase is broken across lines and was not used.

Ownership is described as the garden (NHLR says Moore Farms Botanical Garden, LLC). The NHLR describes the purchase as coming from the state forestry commission, while the garden and Wikipedia describe an auction in Olanta; these are compatible and the story reports both. Visit rules come from Wikipedia and the garden's booking prompt; no source says the tower can be climbed, so none is claimed. No photo credits were recorded because no image URLs were captured.

Built date, design and Forest Service use are well supported by the Register and 1935-36 newspapers as quoted on the Forest Lookouts site. Open points: (1) the Forest Lookouts site gives the tower's location about 2 km from the Register's coordinates (34.10012, -82.35429 vs 34.08306, -82.36278); the record keeps the Register point, which was not checked on a map. (2) Elevation differs: the Register gives 824 ft, the marker gives 832 ft for the mountain, and the Forest Service page says an 800-foot mound. (3) The Forest Service trail page's Hurricane Helene closure note sits under a 'Current Conditions' heading, and the page's last-updated date is April 22, 2026; access today should be confirmed before any visit. (4) The access level 'closed' is inferred from the 2020 visit notes, not from a current agency notice. Visit report and fence observations are from one 2020 volunteer visit.

Brief said built 1936; NHLR gives circa 1936-1938, so the event year is the low end of that range. 'Possibly a Bethlehem Steel model' is NHLR's own hedge. The 1993 abandonment is one NHLR statement, backed by the statewide SCFC closure date; the staffing 'unstaffed as of 1993' is inferred from those two, not from a staffing record. No access or visit data was found, so the access and visit keys are omitted. The eastern lookouts page and the hillmap and OpenStreetMap pages add only name, county and agency, so they are not cited. Used 3 web searches, one over the 2-search budget. No fire history, newspaper coverage or NRHP listing was found.

The sale is undated in the sources: 'late 1990s' per the register and '199??' per Forest Lookouts. It is left out of events until a year can be sourced. The record's agency field holds the owner's name, so a correction is proposed for a human to apply. The 40-foot height is the current structure; the register does not give the year of the reconstruction. No staffing names or fires beyond the 1936 towerman notice were found. Used 1 WebSearch and about 4 page reads.

Thin record: one register page with a 2020 visit report, one Forest Service history page that does not name this tower, and one hiking guide for access. No staffing, fire or repair sources were found, and the story says so. The record's material 'steel' is not stated in the sources read (the register gives an Aermotor LS-40 with a metal cab), so it is not repeated in facts. The 100-foot figure is the register's tower height and is taken as height_m 30.5. The access level 'closed' rests on the 2020 visit and the hiking guide; the current agency status is unknown. The Forest Lookouts page for Tip Top was checked and adds only the county and forest names.

Only one page is about this tower: the NHLR detail page, read in full. Everything tower-specific rests on it. Wikipedia's Ulmer town article has no tower mention. Read for context: the SCFC pictures page and history page, and the NHLR Leesville entry. Not read: the anyplaceamerica topo page and the rootsandrecall Ulmer page. Three search calls ran (one general query, two Ulmer-specific), one over the per-tower budget. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. 'Built circa 1935' is the register's own estimate. The agency field holds the administrator the register names, a person, not an agency. No corrections proposed. Access is unknown: no source gives visiting rules. The photo credit 'Michael T. Finch, Jr.' on the NHLR page was not added as a photo because no license is shown.

The NHLR detail page was read in full and gives the tower facts. The tie to the Forestry Commission rests on the NHLR administrator line; no source reads that Varnville was one of the Commission's lookouts in service, so the story treats it as likely, not certain. The 140-tower figure comes from the Leesville entry, not from this page. Date reading: 'built circa 1936' is the register's estimate. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. Access unknown. The SCFC history page was not separately read (it did not add anything tower-specific). A WebSearch hit for an FCC tower registration at Varnville (2007) was not used because it is not shown to be this tower. No corrections proposed.

Thinnest of the three. The NHLR page gives name, route, county, coordinates, elevation, registration date, nominator and a photo credit, but no build date, type, agency, owner or condition text. The 76 ft figure is the page's elevation, not tower height, so height_m is omitted. The brief marks status 'standing' and kind 'unknown'; the page does not state condition, so status is left out of facts and the story does not claim it is standing. Two WebSearch calls and reads of the NHLR SC list, the FFLA SC list (no matches), and the Pineville SC Picture Project page (a different tower) found nothing more. The Post and Courier article on SC towers does not mention Vert. Next steps for an editor: ask the nominator Dan Curry about the tower (photo license unknown, so no photo was added), or check whether the Forest Fire Lookout Association profile fills in later. Access unknown.

Build and replacement years are the fiscal-year report windows (FY 1940-41 and FY 1957-58), recorded as 1940 and 1957; the exact months are not in the sources. The history comes through Forest Lookouts' transcriptions of the commission's annual reports, not the originals. Status and access are unconfirmed. A social-media post in search results describes the site as overgrown, but its page could not be read, so it is not cited. Mildred Zeigler's dates are not given.

Brief record checks out: built 1936 and registered October 2, 2012 match NHLR. Left out of the story: a StoryMaps search result (storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/c7196e87d7af47e2a90c4eb79831e87e) says the tower was first built at Fort Jackson and moved to the park in 1940. Fetch returned only the page title, and a WebSearch on the claim found nothing confirming it, so it needs a human check; it conflicts with NHLR's 1936 build at this site. The Friends of Sesqui post is undated in our copy and is the only source on climbing safety; its comment thread (not used) mentions the tower being dismantled, which is unverified. Access level restricted is our inference. No fire history found. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the Register's 1936 build date is a year before the 1937 land purchase in Wikipedia, so the story now says the two are not reconciled. The story also uses the agency's full name and footnotes the park-celebration sentence, which had none.

Register (NHLR) and one HikingWNC listing only; no Forest Service or Forest Lookouts page for this tower was found in the cache (easternuslookouts.weebly.com/whitmire.html returns 404). 'Standing' and the closed upper deck rest on the undated HikingWNC listing, so a current check is worth doing before publication. Staffed-last year is a decade placeholder (1980). OSM node 357098866 (ele 145, tower:type observation) was read but not cited; it differs slightly from the register's 147 m.

Only two sources, and neither gives a current condition. The Former Fire Lookout Sites register has no entry for this tower (firetower.org/lookouts/us/sc/winyah-bay-lookout/ returns 404). Two searches turned up no news or photo report after 2017. 'Standing' is the brief's record; the register's 'presently inactive' is the only support, and status_note says so. The 1938 modified year covers 1938-39 work. The Forest Lookouts page cites a 1939 state report that was not read directly. Recommend a recent photo or local source before publication.

Register, the Former Fire Lookout Sites Bethera entry, and an undated news story cover the history. Current status rests only on the undated news story ('still standing'). The 2024 NEPA page covers two administrative buildings and does not name the tower. Built year 1930 is a decade placeholder for the 1930s. OSM node 357111662 (ele 15) was read but not cited. A current photo or ranger-district check would firm up status before publication.

Only one visit report (September 2020) appears on the Register page, so current condition is unknown. Access is set to restricted from HikingWNC plus the 2020 report; no official closure notice was found. HikingWNC is a hiking site, not an agency. The Index-Journal text is available only as quoted by Forest Lookouts. No photos added.

Brief's facts hold up: 1965 build, 22 ft (6.7 m), standing. The 1964 authorization and the 1965 contract come from a newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not from the newspapers themselves. Staffing is unknown; a search turned up no staffing or fire history. Tower-specific access is not stated: the SummitPost guide covers the surrounding game production area only, so no access level is recorded. The NHLR says the land is managed by the state fish and game department, while the brief lists the agency as the state forestry department; both are recorded. Used 2 web searches, within budget. No photos were added. Two photo credits exist on the NHLR and Rex's pages (Ron Kemnow; Dave Masters), but no image URLs were captured, so none are listed.

The 1939 steel tower and L-4 cab are supported by at least two sources (register and firelookout.com) and the Forest Service. The 1910 first tower rests on the Forest Service page alone; a 1915 newspaper item shows a lookout station by then. Access 'public' is an inference from the register's road note and the Forest Service description of recreationist use; the Forest Service page is undated and nothing says whether the cab may be climbed. Height 9.1 m converts the 30-ft figure.

Rapid City Journal rename article returned HTTP 429 on this pass; not used. Height_m 11.0 and precise elevation carried from the existing record, not independently re-confirmed by a new source this round.

Brochure PDF text extraction was garbled/reflowed in places (OCR-like layout artifacts); only the clearly legible fragments were used. Could not independently verify current rental/visitation status beyond 'public' access level from the existing record.

Two register claims (CCC build in 1941, cabin burned in the late 1990s) conflict with other sources and are reported as disputed. Current staffing comes from an undated Forest Service page. The Aermotor attribution rests on firelookout.com alone. Access 'public' follows the Forest Service page, which describes visitor climbs in the staffed season; drive-up is not described.

The record's height (32.6 m) and elevation (929.6 m) match the sources: 107 ft and 3,050 ft. The 1936 date comes from one source (Forest Lookouts); firelookout.com gives no date. A 1936 CCC or WPA observation tower is described in the camp history (cite 5), but the sources do not say it is the fire lookout, so no event is recorded for it. Access for the tower itself is not stated anywhere we read; the refuge-wide foot-traffic statement (cite 6) should not be read as permission to climb. firelookout.com credits photos to Scott Schroeder; no photo URL or licence was found, so no photos are added. A person may want to check with the refuge whether the tower is open to the public.

Build year of the current stone tower is disputed between 1939 (NHLR, Parkwolf) and 1940-41 (FFLA); a 1939 newspaper excerpt describing a log tower adds ambiguity. Height given in the brief (15.2 m) likely refers to the tower structure; elevation sources consistently give the peak as 6,023 ft, slightly different from the brief's 6,003 ft NHLR figure -- flagged as a minor discrepancy, not corrected since NHLR is the brief's own source.

Build date, builder, agency and staffing are unknown; two web searches found nothing on them. The directory and Wikipedia disagree on elevation and county name. Access level 'permission' follows from the reservation location; no visiting rules were found in the sources. The 1890 event is local context, not the tower's history, and the Wikipedia text cites Jack Utter's book, which was not read. Corrections: county is proposed for review only.

Strongest sources are the NPS Wind Cave assessment (npshistory.com PDF) for construction, use and 1998 access change, and the NPS trail page for current climbing rules. The 1954 newspaper quoted on westlookouts calls the Rankin Ridge watcher a State Park lookout, which does not fit the national park; the story avoids naming that person. No rental or staffing information after 1998 was found; access is recorded as closed to climbing, with the trail open. The NHLR CL100 design label and the NPS 'Standard Steel Lookout Tower' proposal are not in conflict, but only the register gives the CL100 name.

The 1936 build date comes from the marker alone. The height is disputed (100 ft listing vs 108 ft in three sources); a correction to 32.9 m is proposed for review. The CCC camp dates conflict (marker 1925 to 1939 vs brochure 1935 to 1939). A 2025 federal solicitation for fire tower rehabilitation appeared in search results, but its page is behind a Cloudflare check and was not read, so it is not used; it may bear on current condition. Current access is unconfirmed; the marker's daylight-hours statement may be out of date. The tower is not tied to the headquarters building. Another Sand Lake tower (NWR 2) is listed as gone in the FFLA state list and is not this lookout.

The 1966 versus 1975 steel-tower date is the main open question; a Black Hills National Forest history or a Forest Service lookout inventory would settle it. Current access rests on one hiking blog of unknown date plus a SummitPost route description; no Forest Service page for this tower was found, and the Black Hills NF page checked says five towers remain in service without naming them. No rental listing found. The brief's height_m (16.2) was left out of facts because sources conflict.

Build-date conflict across four sources (1935/1939/1939-40/1942) could not be fully resolved within the research budget; flagged in both story and corrections. Worth a closer look at NRHP/npgallery nomination documents if available, which might clarify construction vs completion dates.

Strong record: NHLR, firelookout.com, a long newspaper transcript page and the FFLA list agree on the core story. Open points: the removal year of the upper floors (1973 vs 1978 vs 1970s) and the 1949 vs 1950 build year are reported as ranges. The 1978 removal date and the 1970s date in the 2011 book are from the sources as printed. The travel-site wording about the road is a blog claim, so the story keeps it as a note. The record's height_m 4.3 is unsupported and is proposed for removal. The 1950s-1960s named lookouts are from firelookout.com and the newspaper; names are historical, not verified against Forest Service records.

Built 1935 (brochure and marker agree on the CCC work). Height of 110 ft above ground and 133 steps come from the brochure only; height_m 33.5 is the brochure's figure converted, and 'above ground' is taken as the structure height. 'Steel' rests on one listing (westlookouts). Current condition not verified. Search results said the Waubay tower is a steel tower built by the CCC; only the listed sources were used. The Sand Lake marker also says the Waubay tower is open to the public during daylight hours, but the story uses the refuge's own page.

Thin record. No build date, height or design found in any readable source. Route 296 location comes from a one-paragraph blog post and is approximate. The Tennessee Landforms table lists the tower at 1697 ft and status 'standing'; the 2014 list is the only dated status record. The blog post's address gives a December 20, 2015 date, but the post describes no status, so it is not used as one. A Facebook group thread turned up in search (snippet says '40-foot fire tower built in 19..') but the page could not be read, so it is not used. Access and climbing rules are unknown; the story tells visitors to check first.

Build year is only the decade ('built in the 1940s', Register); no event year was assigned for construction. Access is unknown: no source says whether the public may visit or climb, and the 2006 visit report mentions a climbing sign and broken cab glass, so the story advises against climbing. Record coordinates and elevation (619 m) match the Register. The Eastern US lookouts page gives little beyond county and district. Search snippets (a CCC Camp P-62 Facebook post saying the camp built several area towers) were not fetched and are not used; they do not name Altamont. Worth a human look: whether the Register's 2006 visit still reflects current condition, and whether the Division of Forestry allows visitors.

Elevation disagrees: the Register gives 1,026 ft (313 m) and the Tennessee Landforms table gives 1,020 ft; the record's 312.7 m matches the Register. The story reports both. The Register's 11/26/22 site visit has no findings on the page read. Staffing, access and any current fire-watch use are not documented in the sources read. The record's other_names value 'A' is proposed for removal in corrections. The LS-40 stairway point comes from a general Aermotor history, not from this tower's record, and the story says so. Record coordinates match the Register.

No build date, construction, staffing or fate found. Two web searches returned nothing on this tower. The only status record is the Tennessee Landforms row; the Forest Lookouts Antioch entry is a heading with no text. The record's elevation of 131.1 m matches the 430 ft listing. Leads to try: Tennessee Division of Forestry, Tipton County library or historical society, Covington newspapers.

No register page exists for Avondale on nhlr.org or firetower.org (checked cached TN listings for both; it isn't there), no NRHP nomination, no newspaper hit, and no mention in a general East Tennessee fire-tower news piece that was checked. Web search surfaced an AI-synthesized claim that Avondale is 'also known as Clinch Lookout Tower,' but no primary source for that name turned up (anyplaceamerica.com, the likely origin, returned 403) so it was left out rather than guessed into the story. Builder, year built, agency, staffing and access all remain unknown; a human with access to TN Division of Forestry records or local Grainger County history might find more.

Height (60 vs 100 ft) and county (Hawkins vs Sullivan) conflict across sources; editor should decide height_m and county. Tennessee Landforms also lists a Garden Mountain tower (HWT001, 2405 ft, Hawkins) whose elevation is close to the NHLR 2,393 ft; possible duplicate, not verified. The record's coordinates sit about 2 km from the NHLR coordinates (36.515278, -82.623889). The 1948 and 1953 quotes come from a reprint on the Forest Lookouts page, not the original newspapers. Whether a state 80-foot tower was erected on this ridge in 1955 is unresolved. One web search used for this tower.

Identity conflict to check before publishing. The brief lists Lobelville as an other name, but the Register page does not use that name. The National Register study lists a Lobelville tower and a Linden tower in Perry County as extant on March 26, 2014; the tower list has Lobelville (7-18) removed and Linden (7-19) standing. The Register coordinates sit roughly 6 km southwest of the Lobelville town coordinates on Wikipedia, which does not settle the question. No access information and no visit report were found. The tower's own status after March 2018 is unknown.

Access level 'restricted' is inferred from state ownership and the nomination's account of staff use; no visiting rules were found. Staffing as_of uses the 2021 nomination. The brief record had no height; 60 ft (18.3 m) comes from the nomination. The nomination text gives two construction-related dates (1947 and 1948) and two period-of-significance end dates (1971 and 1975), so check the PDF before relying on either. Story not verified on site. The npgallery entry for NRIS 100006708 returned no content; the tn.gov nomination was read instead.

Two Big Hill towers: this record (Cumberland County, 2,035 ft per Landforms; elevation_m 620.3 matches) and the NRHP-nominated Marion County tower (2,032 ft; built around 1947 per the nomination, date estimated). Do not share history between them; if a Marion County record exists, it should carry the nomination's history. No Cumberland-specific build, builder, staffing or access source was found. A Facebook group post seen only in a search snippet says a Big Hill tower is gated, quarry-owned and not open to the public; it does not name the county, so it is not used. Read and search budgets are used up for this record.

Build date and original owner are unknown; the Register and the 2014 study give no build date. Do not confuse this with the Big Hill Fire Lookout Tower in Marion County, a separate tower listed on the National Register in 2021. The Tennessee State Parks page returned 403 and was not used. Access rests on Tennessee Magazine and the Tennessee Hiking Club; confirm with the park before publishing. No photos added.

Current access level in the brief was 'unknown'; set to restricted based on NRHP note that the cab was locked during survey and the tower is an active state asset rather than a public rental. No conflicting build years found for this tower. No build date, builder, reason for siting, staffing, fires or public access rule appears in any source we could read. The Savannah and Bee Rock names are linked by county and elevation only (774 ft NHLR vs 784 ft Landforms); please confirm they are one tower. The NPS study's table of extant towers as of March 26, 2014 (cite 3) lists Bee Rock, Olive Hill and Turkey Knob in Hardin County and names no Savannah tower. A Facebook group post (Fire Lookout Association-Tennessee) describes the tower as about 60 ft and in rough shape, but the page could not be read, so it is not used. The 2023 visit is the most recent record; the cab condition may have changed since.

Name: the register says Selmer Lookout Tower; Landforms and the 2014 count say Bethel Springs (Landforms MNT005, state number 8-18). The record links them on county and name, which is reasonable but not proven. Elevation differs: 576 ft in the register, 570 ft in Landforms. The register entry has no build field, so no build date is given. The access level 'restricted' is an editorial reading of 'currently being used by the state'; a human should confirm. Two searches were used; the Selmer and Bethel Springs Wikipedia pages were checked and mention no tower. No new photos were found.

Build date, design type and elevation conflict between the register and the NRHP nomination; both kept in the story. Current access and staffing rest on the nomination's 2014-era information, not a current site visit or Division of Forestry notice. The NRHP listing date was not confirmed from the sources read (NPGallery shows only a published date of 3/31/2015), so no nrhp_listed event was entered. No notable fires named in sources. No rental listing found. The record's 1933 'built' is kept; the 1934 completion is added as its own event.

Low confidence. No build date, builder, design or staffing was found for the Sharp's Ridge fire tower in two searches and several page reads. Not used: a 1957 Knox News photo caption (page returned HTTP 403) and a YouTube page with no readable description. Brief's access 'unknown' is set to restricted on the judgment that no visiting arrangement is documented. The 2023 WBIR job concerned a broadcast tower, not the fire tower; it appears only as context. Next step would be Tennessee Division of Forestry records or Knoxville newspaper coverage from the 1940s to 1960s. Elevation sentence reworded in the 2026-10-09 check: Wikipedia gives the ridge's highest ground point (where it places the abandoned tower) as 1,391 ft, and Tennessee Landforms gives the Sharps Ridge site as 1,355 ft. The story no longer says they describe the same point.

The 1961 date rests on two independent short entries that agree. No agency, owner, staffing or access arrangement found after one search. The 2014 list and the undated Landforms entry are the only evidence of condition. Caption credits US Soil Conservation Service in parentheses; photo rights not checked, so no photo added.

Brief corrections: state TN to NC and county NC to Swain. Builder conflict: thebraindump.blog credits the CCC; the page returned 403 and is not cited. Grokipedia and islands.com say PWA; not cited. Current condition is unverified: the newest dated work is the 2014 partial rehab. The Smoky Mountain News feature is undated in the cache and refers only to Barr's 2010 hike and the years after it, so the story gives it no date. The SMN article names Peter Barr, director of the N.C. chapter of the national Forest Fire Lookout Association; he is not identified with the NHLR nominator. 'Medium to strenuous' is from the Smokies Guide; Wikipedia gives only the roughly 2,300-foot rise, so the story no longer cites it for 'strenuous'. No source read states whether the stairs are currently safe or whether climbing is allowed, so the story advises checking with NPS. A Smokies Friends page from 2023 says the tower remains standing as one of four original park towers, but its URL is not in the cache, so it is not cited.

Three sources, two of them listing only. Build date and builder not found after two searches. The encyclopedia entry is local and undated; its 'still exists' line is the only current-condition evidence. OpenStreetMap node 356888183 tags it tower:type=observation with lattice construction and 451 m elevation; not footnoted because the OSM page was not cached as text.

Two sources only, and the county encyclopedia is secondary. No build date, design, use or staffing found; a second search and a guessed encyclopedia URL (404) gave nothing. The NRHP multiple-property PDF lists Smith Knob in its tower table, but the table's meaning (surviving or not) was unclear, so it is not cited. The brief's record (Scott County, 504.1 m, standing) is consistent with both sources; no correction proposed. Next step would be Division of Forestry or Scott County newspaper records. The restricted level is an editorial judgment drawn from the Division of Forestry operation. The footnote now supports only that operation, and the story says no public visiting arrangement was found.

Thin record. The only dated source is the 2014 extant list in the Division of Forestry multiple property document; the Tennessee Landforms list is undated and says its history is still being gathered. Two web searches found only town, county and fire department pages. The cached NHLR Tennessee register list does not include Smithville. Access and climbing status unknown; the story tells visitors to check first and not to climb.

Thin record. The register gives only 'late 1950s' for construction, so no built event was written. The brief's 2019 NHLR registration was not seen in the pages read, so it is not cited. Page reads for this tower reached the six-read budget.

The Register's Sneedville page does not name an administering agency. A search snippet pointed to an easternuslookouts.weebly.com Sneedville page with a Division of Forestry District 1 heading, but the fetched copy did not show it, so it is not used.

Thin record. The only dated source is the 2014 extant list in the Division of Forestry multiple property document; the Tennessee Landforms list is undated and says its history is still being gathered. Only the Register registration page and one Landforms row say anything specific. No build date, design, staffing, visit report, or access rule was found in readable sources. Two Facebook posts from the Clinch-Powell History page came up in search with claims about an early 1950s build date and radiological monitoring for Oak Ridge; neither page could be opened, so the claims are unverified and are not in the story. Access, staffing and fire history are unverified. The tn.gov state forest page failed to load (connection reset) and the Overton County News history returned HTTP 429. Open question: Wikipedia names a 'Goodpasture Mountain Firetower' and gives Goodpasture Mountain the same 1,493 ft figure Tennessee Landforms gives for Standing Stone. We could not confirm these are one tower. The Tennessee Landforms code 'GB2402 4-11' is not interpreted. The brief's elevation (455.1 m) matches the 1,493 ft figure.

Status conflict to check by a human before publishing: the 2014 Division of Forestry extant list and the Tennessee Landforms list both say standing, while a photo caption on the telliquah.com Starr Mountain page calls the fire tower abandoned. That caption is undated and is the only abandonment source. Elevation is 2,205 ft on Landforms and 2,200 ft in the mountain-bike guide. The Forest Service Starr Mountain land purchase page (https://www.fs.usda.gov/r08/cherokee/projects/archive/61680) describes about 153 acres on Starr Mountain next to Gee Creek Wilderness; it does not mention the tower, so the tower site's owner is unknown. Agency is inferred from membership in the Division of Forestry list, not stated for this tower. The cached NHLR Tennessee register list has no Starr Mountain entry. No build date, builder, height or current access rules found.

Status is the open question. Only TN Landforms places a Stringtown tower in White County, and it gives no build date or design. The 2014 extant list and the NHLR Tennessee list both omit it. Elevation in the record (610.8 m) matches TN Landforms' 2,004 feet. Next steps: check the current TDF tower inventory or a recent site visit, and a county newspaper search for construction history. Web searches returned only cemetery and genealogy pages.

Build date, builder, staffing and fire history are not in the NHLR entry, the Forest Lookouts listing or the tnlandforms inventory. Two web searches returned only statewide background (CCC tower counts, a 2015 Division report title) that is not cited. Aermotor is hedged by the register ('believed'). The access sign comes from a register entry of about 2018-2019; verify on site or with the Division before publishing. Record fields design and height_m are still null; design is filled here from the register.

No build date, builder or designing agency found in the sources read (NHLR detail page has no Built field). The agency is not established: the 2006 visit notes a TN Dept of Forestry sign and locked shed on site, but no administration statement was found, so no agency fact is recorded. The only physical description is a 2006 visit report; the Tennessee Landforms list (undated snapshot) shows it standing. The 100-ft height is the visit report's figure, converted to 30.5 m. OpenStreetMap tags it tower:construction=lattice; not used because it is user-edited and does not give a date.

Only two sources say anything useful: TN Landforms (name, county, elevation, standing) and the 2014 extant list in the NRHP multiple property document. No build date, design, height, owner or access rule was found, and web searches returned only genealogy pages. The record's NGS register entry (state number GC 2588) rests on the TN Landforms code 'GC2588'; no source we read confirms it as an NGS designation. Agency is left out because the document does not name an owner for this tower. Next steps: a TDF records request or a county newspaper search for construction and fire history.

Build date is not confirmed. The only 1955 source is a newspaper line, quoted by Forest Lookouts, saying one tower was to be erected here; no completion notice was found. The brief's height_m 24.4 is the 80-foot purchase type, not a measured height for Theta, so it is left out of facts. No staffing, fire history, access or visit information was found in the sources read, so those keys are omitted. Agency and District 7 come from the Forest Lookouts page. Searches: 2 (websearch.py). Page reads: about 4 cached pages plus the MPS PDF. Untried lead: 1955-56 Maury County newspaper coverage or Tennessee State Library and Archives records for the completion date.

Height 70 ft converted to 21.3 m. The 2018 WKRN report and the Register disagree on where the tower came from; the story says so. Access level 'private' is inferred from private farm ownership plus a 2018 visit report; no current access statement was found, so please check before publishing. Staffing and notable fires are not in any source read. No new photos were found.

Thin record. No build date, builder, height, staffing, fire history or access statement was found. Standing rests on the Tennessee Landforms table plus a 2020 NHLR site visit; the Register does not say 'standing' in words. The brief's agency field is consistent with the Register's administrator line. Access is left out of facts because nothing was found.

Build year and design come from the NRHP registration form, which says ca. 1933 in its description and 1933 in its period of significance. Two 2021 news items were tried: the Overton County News returned HTTP 429, and the Chattanoogan page had no readable text, so neither is cited. Some news coverage spells the maker Aeromotor; the form says Aermotor. Staffing, notable fires and public access are not in the sources. The form gives 80 ft total height; the record's 24.4 m matches that, but the form does not say whether it is to the cab floor, so no height fact was added. Ownership conflict is recorded in resolved_conflicts. Fact check 2026-10-09: the story gives the 1,863 ft figure as elevation, dates the build to around 1933 to match the form's ca. 1933, and drops the unsupported description of the current use as working.

Two independent sources agree the Viola tower stood in Warren County (TN Landforms and the 2014 extant list). Nothing found gives a build date, design, height, owner or access rule. Record coordinates (35.56585, -85.86738) sit about 3 km north of the Wikipedia town center (35.538, -85.861); not checked against a map of the tower. The TN Landforms code '5-3' is unexplained and not used in the story. Agency is left out because the document does not name an owner for this tower. Web searches returned only genealogy and a Delaware tower page, which is a different Viola.

No build date, builder, staffing, fire history, access or visit information was found. Status rests on the 2014 extant list and an undated Landforms listing. The Division's ownership of this tower is not stated on any page read; the MPS covers Division towers and lists this one, so the story does not name an agency field. The November 2023 woods fire is on Walnut Mountain but the report does not tie it to the tower; it is used only as local context. Brief field 'registers: NGS None' is not in the facts schema and was not verified. The Tennessee list in the NHLR crawl cache (76 entries) has no Walnut Mountain entry; a live check is worth doing. Brief coordinates and elevation match the Landforms GPX. Searches: 2 (websearch.py). Page reads: about 6, including the MPS PDF. Note: a central_us_lookouts cache file titled Walnut Mountain is a different site in Oklahoma and was not used.

Status is the open question. A current visit or a dated source would settle it. The Register's 'Privately Owned' line is the only ownership statement. Height 45 ft converted to 13.7 m. No build date, builder, staffing or fire record was found. The countyoffice.org directory mentions a Waynesboro tower, but it returned 403 and was not used. Access level 'private' follows the Register.

No build date, builder, staffing, fire history, access or visit information was found in the sources read. Status rests on the 2014 extant list and an undated Landforms listing. The MPS covers Division towers and lists this one, so the story describes it as one of the Division's towers only by that list; no agency fact is recorded. The MPS says two earlier wooden towers in Hickman County (Moore's Switch and Cobel) were replaced by steel towers; it does not say Weatherly was one of them or connected to them. Unfetched lead, not used: a search result (data.capecodtimes.com, a bridge inventory mirror) titled 'NATCHEZ TRACE PARK over WEATHERLY FIRE TOWER ACC' suggests the tower access road passes under the Natchez Trace Parkway, which would bear on access. The page is behind a bot check, so nothing from it is cited; a human check is worth doing. Brief coordinates and elevation match the Landforms GPX. Searches: 2 (websearch.py). Page reads: about 3 plus the MPS PDF.

Current status is disputed: NHLR (2023 visit, registered Dec 2023) describes it in place; tnlandforms.us lists it as removed with no date. Construction date unknown; the 1955 item only says it was to be erected by early winter. No staffing, access or rental information found in two searches and the cached pages. Access key omitted rather than guessed. The NHLR record reads 80 ft, which matches the record's height_m of 24.4. Two searches used; the Wikipedia article for Westpoint has no tower mention.

No source beyond tnlandforms.us mentions this specific tower by name; the register has no build year, design, agency confirmation beyond the district-tower numbering convention, staffing, or access information. Checked nhlr.org and firetower.org (FFLOS) crawl caches for Tennessee and the local raw-page caches for 'white house'/'whitehouse' — none has an entry for this tower. Two WebSearches turned up nothing tower-specific beyond tnlandforms.us. The 'agency' fact: fact-check spot-checking (2026-10-04) found the source page does directly name 'Tennessee Division of Forestry (208 tower sites c. 1976...)' alongside the district-tower numbering explanation, so this is a direct naming rather than an inference as originally noted. No corrections to the tower record are warranted — tnlandforms is already the record's source for name/location/county/elevation/status.

No build date, builder, or purpose found on the NHLR page or the tnlandforms table. Two web searches gave nothing on this tower. Results were unrelated genealogy pages and a TowerDex FCC-registry entry for a 275.9 ft structure in Williston, which is probably a communications tower, not this lookout. Ebenezer identity with this site is unconfirmed. Access level left unset: the Register calls the site an active TN Forestry site but describes no visiting arrangement. Possible follow-up: Tennessee Division of Forestry records for Fayette County, Fayette County archives, Tennessee State Library and Archives.

Register says the tower originally stood on Walden Mountain near Harriman; a WebSearch named Walden Ridge as the nearby feature, unconfirmed, so the story keeps the Register's wording. Elevation conflict: Register gives 958 ft for the farm site, Tennessee Landforms lists 1,506 ft for Windswept; not resolved, flagged in story. No build year found in any page read. Status standing rests on the Tennessee Landforms list alone. Brief access 'unknown' is now private per the Register's farm and owner wording. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the story now says the Register credits new private owners, not that the farm is private, because the sources do not state that.

Location conflict left open: Tennessee Landforms gives 36.1499,-84.7282 and 1,506 ft (459 m); the Register gives N 35.93667, W 84.06655 and 958 ft (292 m). The record's coordinates and elevation_m were not changed. Height 18.3 m is converted from 60 ft. Owner names in the Register were left out of the story and quotes. Used 2 WebSearch and 4 page reads. The NPGallery Tennessee Division of Forestry fire lookout MPS PDF (64501237) covers ten other towers and does not mention Windswept. No recent source on condition or public access was found.

Current access is unverified: the only access evidence is a 2006 visit report (cab locked; a sign allowed climbing at own risk). Access key omitted rather than guessed. Staffing data is from 2006 only. Height is in conflict across 50, 60, 80 and 100 ft, so no height_m is set. Replacement date conflicts (1930s per Register, unknown per study). The record has no height_m and the NHLR elevation (2,252 ft) differs slightly from the record (686.4 m, which matches). Two searches and about six page reads used.

Build years 1961-1962 and the Aermotor belief rest on the register entry alone; no second source was found. The Luminary name is unexplained in all sources read. A social media search result called the site abandoned; it is unreliable, was not read at source, and is left out. Access is not established. The state-forest rule applies only if the tower is on state forest land, which is not confirmed. Record fields design and access are unfilled; design is filled here from the register.

Restoration date and date of ownership change are not in the sources read. Rental status not verified. Register gives the owner and nominator as the same person (Kent D. Taylor). Record built year 1960 corrected to a 1942 first tower and a 1960 replacement. Tennessee Landforms elevation is 1800 ft; the Register gives 1,778 ft, which matches the record's 541.9 m. Two searches and about four page reads used.

No source read gives a build date for the Alto tower. The 'ALTO 1948' on the survey station is a survey marker stamp and is not used as the tower's build year. Staffing facts come from 1946 and 1952 newspaper items as transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page; the 1952 Benge item is the last staffing mention found. 'Standing' comes only from the FFLA Texas list, which is undated. The story says nothing about public access beyond the survey description's gate reference, which is undated, since no source gives current access. The Rusk Cherokeean and Alto Herald originals were not checked; Portal to Texas History may hold the Rusk Cherokeean and could settle the build date. The Alto photo already in the record is not repeated. No new photos added.

Thin record. The Forest Lookouts Arp page carries only a header (Smith County, Texas Forest Service) with no history, design or height, so the story is shorter than the usual target by design. No source read gives a build date, staffing, fire history or current access. The 'Standing' status is from the FFLA Texas list, which is undated. A search turned up the Arp Volunteer Fire Department (smithcountyfire.org), a different organization, which was not used.
