Thin record. The only detailed source is a 1972 National Geodetic Survey description reprinted on the Forest Lookouts Bronson page. It gives the structure, paint, cab, about 110 ft height and location, but no build date, staffing, fire history or current access. The height is converted from the 110 ft figure in the description (33.5 m). The road directions in that 1972 description appear in the story only as a caveat: they may be out of date and are not a current access source. A Visit Sabine County Facebook post appeared in search with a claim that the tower was most likely erected in the early 1940s by the Texas A&M Forest Service, on former Kirby Lumber Company land. The page text was not readable (the fetch returned only the title), so the claim is not used and is a lead for a human to check against Texas Forest Service records or Kirby Lumber archives. The record's agency value ', Texas Forest Service' is corrected in corrections. No photos added.

Thin record. Sources: a 1948 NGS station description reproduced on a volunteer site (not read from NGS itself), the FFLA list (Standing), an undated Texas Escapes travel page, and the TSHA community entry. No build date, staffing, fire history or access found, and no photo with a usable licence found. The O'Quinn part of the name is unexplained in every source read. An Angelina County PDF (angelinacounty.net/files/pdf/rfc.pdf) describes a proposed county radio tower on Central ISD land just off US 69 near O'Quinn Road; it does not say it is this lookout's site, so it is not used. The record's height (33.5 m) matches the survey's 110 feet. TSHA (cite 2) puts the community eight miles northwest of Lufkin on US 69, against the survey's ten miles airline; the story gives both figures and does not choose between them. Editor may want the Texas Forest Service or a local history source for the build year and the name origin.

Thin on current condition and access: the newest evidence is the March 2019 Register drone photos and video, and the FFLA list (undated) marks it Standing. The 1970 Texas Forest News scan is OCR text with broken word spacing, so quotes are copied as printed. The article places the planned tower about four miles northwest of Chandler; a Facebook post seen only as a search snippet (not opened, fetch returned a login page) gives six miles and a November 1970 dedication. That snippet was not used or cited. Register coordinates (32.340344, -95.528777) were not checked against Chandler's town centre. Access, staffing after 1970 and the Texas Forest Service's current role for this tower are unknown; a Texas Forest Service or Texas Historical Commission check would help.

Thin record. Sources: the 1958 NGS station description (via a volunteer site), the TSHA community entry, a Forest Lookouts caption (#50), and the FFLA list (Standing). The record's height_m was null; 30.5 m is proposed from the survey's 'overall height of about 100 feet', which is a survey figure rather than a measured one, so it is a fact, not a correction. TSHA gives Farm Road 2517 for the community while the survey gives Farm Road 123 for the route from the village; these are not necessarily in conflict. No build date, builder, staffing, fire history or access found. Confidence low.

Origin is disputed and not settled. FFLA lists East River, Harris County (gone); Texas Highways and Bowman say the tower came from near Conroe. The 1974 newspaper item speaks of a tower to be built on the museum site, not of a move. Bowman's 1976 move date is the only move date found. The Texas Forestry Museum website returned no text when fetched, and the Lufkin Daily News tower article returned HTTP 429 and was not read; the museum's own history may settle the origin. Record county, coordinates and status match the FFLA list. The 100-foot height is from press and writeup descriptions; the overall height and whether it is the original cab are not confirmed. Agency is from the 1974 notice of intended ownership, not a current source. Bowman's column is dated February 28, 2010 and was updated December 6, 2012, so the access and climbing status is only as recent as that update.

Thin record: two sources. The 1958 and 1963 descriptions are of the original Elysian Fields site, not of the Winston Ranch tower, and the sources do not say which structure was moved. The agency fact is the Texas Forest Service named beside the National Geodetic Survey in the survey page's header; the page does not state ownership, and the story words it that way. Both the FFLA list and our record spell the county Nacagdoches; the correct spelling is Nacogdoches (Wikipedia), so the correction is proposed for human review. The TSHA Elysian Fields town entry was read and has no lookout mention. Winston Ranch owner, access and condition were not found; the search returned no other source for this tower.

Two Etoile sites: FFLA Loc 1 (31.36111, -94.38861) is gone and Loc 2 (31.33156, -94.36711, the record) is standing. The 1949 Coast and Geodetic Survey description names Etoile Lookout Tower No. 6 but does not say which site it was, so the record is unchanged. Edward Cavallerano's book (SearchWorks record) was not read. Used 2 WebSearch and about 9 page reads, over the per-tower budget. Nothing found on build date, design, height, staffing, fires or access.

The only lookout source is the Forest Fire Lookout Association list, which is undated and has a blank NHLR/FFLOS column for Grapeland. Grapeland is not on the Forest Lookouts Texas list. Two WebSearch calls turned up no lookout reference; the local history pages read (TSHA, EastTexas.com, Wikipedia, TxGenWeb) mention no tower. Design, agency, year, height and access are unknown. No photos found.

Thin record. The 1935 NGS description (via a volunteer site) places the station about seven miles north of Jasper; the TSHA entry places 'the Horton lookout tower' three miles to the south, reference point not stated, in the mid-1980s. The sources do not show these are the same tower or what the three miles is measured from, so the story does not link them. The record's status_note matches the FFLA asterisk footnote; no correction proposed. No build date, height, staffing, fire history, cab-removal date or access found. A YouTube video titled 'Horton Fire Lookout Tower Jasper County TX' appeared in search results but was not read. Confidence low.

Register (firetower.org) and FFLA list disagree on the location and status of the standing tower; no build date found. Distance of about 3.4 km is computed from the listed coordinates. The 1957 quote is from a Marshall News Messenger item reproduced on the centraluslookouts page; the newspaper itself was not read. Searches for a Jimplecute article on a tower move found nothing. Related record us-tx-jefferson (Loc 1) says relocated while FFLA says gone and the register says standing downtown; that record needs a separate pass.

Thin record. Readable sources were the Forest Lookouts Karnack page (header only, no history), the FFLA Texas list (status and coordinates) and an undated Texas travel page (general context). Not reached: Texas Forest Service pages and NHLR or FFLOS pages for this site. A library catalog page describes the book Fire in the Piney Woods (Texas lookout towers, the forest service, and the Civilian Conservation Corps) as a lead, but its text was not read; the Duke University Press abstract returned HTTP 403. The FFLA list shows two Karnack entries: Loc 1 gone, Loc 2 standing. The sources do not say whether these are two towers or two sites for one tower. The record's 95 m elevation comes from OpenStreetMap; it was not verified here and is not in the story. Access is unknown and no access fact was added. Fact check 2026-10-09: the travel page says the towers came before airplanes but ties the word long to the earlier tree-climbing sentence, so the story drops long from the tower claim.

Record name is Kirby Forest; the Forest Lookouts page calls it Hyatt. The only current status is the FFLA list (standing). The Find a Grave memorial (1940-1980) was added by a contributor in February 2026; its citation names Hyatt Cemetery but does not say which record gives the dates. If 1980 is the end of the tower, the FFLA listing is wrong. The Tyler County entry is dated January 1, 1941 but does not name Hyatt, so it is not evidence of the build date. No reliable build date found; the 1943 newspaper item shows only that the tower was in use by then. No access information found, so no access or visit facts are recorded. Two WebSearches used. A site visit or landowner check would settle both status and access.

Tower is on the E.O. Siecke State Forest, renamed in 1951; the record's name Kirbyville is the historic one. Record height 24.4 m matches the 80 ft given in 1926 and by TFS. A 1948 newspaper said the tower would be raised to 120 ft; no later source confirms it, and the TFS release still says 80 ft. The 1927 count (175 fires, fall 1927 season) and the TFS count (135 in the first year in use) appear to cover different periods. The 1926 and 1927 newspaper items were read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. No current photo or condition report found; standing status rests on the FFLA list and TFS saying the tower still exists. Public climbing is not permitted per TFS.

Two November 1960 reports name different mountains: Latch Mountain (Joe Schuler's place) and Chamberlain Mountain (O.V. Schuler land). They may be one tower or two; the 1966 report calls the tower the Latch tower. Unresolved record conflict on location: FFLA gives 32.69691, -95.08512, and the second coordinate set in the record is 32.6968, -95.06911, about 1.5 km east. Not checked against a map or a source that gives coordinates, so no location correction is proposed. The Facebook post is undated and is the only present-tense mention found; it is a community group post, not an official record, and only its preview text was readable. No photo or visit found. The county correction (Upshire to Upshur) is typographic and should be easy to confirm.

No source read gives a build year, height or design. The marker is the only source that dates the tower, and it gives the in-use years 1955 to 1969 only. The Forest Lookouts page is nearly empty apart from the name, county and agency. A Waymarking NGS benchmark page (BL2173, title mentions 'LIBERTY HILL LOT 1966') came up in search, but the cached page held only its title, so it is not used. The hmdb marker has 2020 photos by James Hulse; not recorded because no license is stated. Access is unknown: no source says whether the tower may be climbed. NHLR and FFLOS register pages were not checked. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 5 page reads.

Generic name ('lookout tower') and no town, county, state or owner on the map. The OSM tag is observation, not fire lookout, so this may not belong in the lookout set. The brief's Texas placement and coordinates (33.03 N, 97.08 W) are not confirmed by any page read; the OSM page names no state, so the story no longer says the outline is in Texas. A WebSearch hit for a 150-ft Grapevine Main Observation Tower in downtown Grapevine was a search snippet only, not read in full; it does not appear to be this record, but that is not verified. Used 2 WebSearch calls; page reads: OSM way (twice), FFLA list, NHLR list. Suggested check: the OSM way's location on the map, or a county record, before keeping it in the set.

NHLR (decommissioned 1970) and Texas Escapes (functioned into the 1980s) disagree on when the tower stopped operating; noted in the story rather than resolved. The on-site historical marker (hmdb.org #31698) returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, so its exact inscription is not cited here. Texas Escapes is a general-interest history site, not a primary source, so the Wesley Love / WPA narrative rests on that one article; a Texas Historical Commission marker file or a Jacksonville Daily Progress archive piece would strengthen it. A draft citation to 'Forest Fire Lookout Association (firelookout.org)' claiming its Texas lookouts list records this tower as standing has been removed: the cached source is actually the Former Fire Lookout Sites register (firetower.org, a sister site of NHLR, not FFLA), it catalogs decommissioned/removed lookouts, and its one Texas entry is Jefferson Lookout Site, not Love's Lookout. The source neither supports the claim nor matches the cited publisher, so both the footnote and the sentence were dropped.

Build year and height come from the NGS datasheet quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the datasheet's own PID and page were not fetched. The Forest Lookouts page gives no coordinates, so it is not confirmed that its tower is the Loc 2 site on the Forest Fire Lookout Association list; the brief's Loc 2 identity is kept but unverified. The CCC camp link is inferred from the 1933 date and the camp's general work only; no source ties the camp to this tower's construction. Access is unknown. Used 1 WebSearch call and about 3 page reads plus the shared Texas index and FFLA list.

Only tower record is the Forest Fire Lookout Association one-line listing (standing, Newton County, coordinates). No build date, height, design, staffing, fires or access found in the sources read. The Texas Escapes narrative also gives the 1834 land grant as 1934; its quoted marker says 1834, and the story does not use the grant year. Lead: the Cavallerano book Fire in the Piney Woods (muse.jhu.edu/book/137054) is described as covering every Texas fire lookout tower; not accessed, and it may hold the build record. Worth asking the Texas Forest Service or Texas Historical Commission. Used 2 WebSearch calls; page reads: FFLA list, HMDB marker, NHLR list, FFLA p=784 (table not in text), Wikipedia, Texas Escapes. Verification 2026-10-09: story now says 'unincorporated community' (Wikipedia wording) instead of 'small community', and drops 'named for the community', which no source gives.

Thin record: three sources and no build date, design or history. The community history (1843 church, 1847 furnace) is context, not tower history. Record height and elevation come from OpenStreetMap (lattice tower tag, 151 m) and were not used because no readable historical page supports them. Access and landowner are unknown. A Texas Forest Service history or a newspaper search for Lake O' the Pines or Marion County could add a build date.

Height 6.0 comes from the OSM height tag, which prints as '6' with no unit; metres assumed. The brief's status 'standing' is not supported: OSM maps the object, not its condition, so it is corrected to unknown. The name suggests a Martin Luther King Jr. link, but no source says so. The latest edit note mentions downtown walking paths; the city is not named. The OSM page names no state, and the brief's Texas placement is not confirmed by any page read, so the story no longer says the outline is in Texas; the story also drops a speculative line about whom the name honors. Used 2 WebSearch calls: one for a Waco 'MLK Lookout' (no record found), one for Waco's Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park (event pages only; a snippet gave a 300 MLK Blvd address, not verified). Page reads: OSM way (twice), FFLA list, NHLR list. A city parks record would settle whether this is a fire lookout at all.

The 1936 date comes from a June 1936 newspaper item saying the tower had been erected; no later construction record was read. The 1936 item calls the agency the Texas Forestry Service, a branch of A. and M. College; the Forest Lookouts page and the FFLA list use Texas Forest Service. Standing rests on the FFLA list only. A texasescapes.com article says some East Texas towers can still be found near Mount Enterprise; it is undated and general, so it is not used. No access source found. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 3 page reads plus the shared FFLA and Texas index pages.

Thin record. The FFLA list is the only tower-specific source and gives no build date, builder, design, staffing or access. Bowman's East Texas lookout page is about Lufkin and other East Texas towers, not Neches, and must not be used to date this one. The story now calls it a web page, not a column. The 2025 Cavallerano book is the best lead; only its MUSE publisher summary was read. An undated 2011 'Texas lookout towers' list in the crawl cache has a 'neches' entry (TFS-style number TX095) with garbled coordinates; its source URL could not be recovered, so it is not cited. Record is consistent: standing, Anderson County, matching coordinates.

Only the Forest Lookouts transcription page (newspaper clippings 1937-1966) and the FFLA Texas list were read. The 1937 and 1954 items are transcriptions; the original newspapers were not checked. The 1937 articles call the agency the Texas Forestry Service; the page header uses Texas Forest Service. A Facebook group post seen only in a search snippet, an aboutus.com page (elevation 137 ft, HTTP 429) and an NHLR entry (connection reset, guessed URL 404) were not read. Access level could not be determined, so facts.access is omitted. Check the NHLR/FFLOS for a register entry and current condition.

Only the NHLR page describes the tower itself, and it hedges with 'believed'. No build date, builder, staffing, fire or access record was found in NHLR, TSHA, firelookout.org, or the Forest Lookouts regional page (which shows only the name). NHLR says 'Texas A&M Fire Service' for the repeater, probably meaning Forest Service; the story quotes it as the Register's wording. height_m is 70 ft converted. Brief coordinates match firelookout.org. Access is left out because no read source states it; brief 'unknown' stands. Not checked: Texas A&M Forest Service records or local newspapers. Confidence medium because registry and standing agree across sources, but history is thin. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'Sawmills came first' overstated the TSHA entry (which gives 1850 as the earliest date; a church and school followed by 1854-55), so it now gives the 1850 date; the Register footnote was removed from the advice sentence; the farm-road and registry-number evidence was added.

Almost no tower-specific history exists in the sources read. The Forest Lookouts page gives only a status note, and the FFLA list gives a status and coordinates. No build date, builder, height, staffing, fires or access were found. Two searches and five page reads were used. The NHLR Texas list (five registered towers: Chandler, Love's, Pine Mills, Spring, Woodville) does not include this tower. Next step: local Henderson County newspaper archives or a Texas Forest Service history for the tower's build date and use. The brief's agency field held the status note; see corrections.

Read: the Forest Lookouts page (1928 Alto Herald and Forest Worker items, 1942 NGS station description), the FFLA Texas list, the HMDB CCC marker, the Pine Cliff Resort page (commercial; used only for the State Highway 7 access, the tower's place in the recreation area and the 'last standing' phrase), the USFS Ratcliff Lake page and the Recreation.gov listing (no tower mention). Two searches and five reads used. Not found: staffing, notable fires, whether the tower may be climbed, current owner of the tower itself. The HMDB marker says CCC workers built fire towers without naming this one. Check the Bird Mountain tower (Anderson County, listed Tower Gone) for its own story. The brief's 27.4 m height is supported by the 1928 reports; the 1942 survey gives about 100 ft.

Status conflict. The FFLA Texas list says standing; I saw no date on that list. Our crawl data for the Forest Lookouts record reads gone/dismantled, but I found no sentence on the Salem page or the Texas list that says so, so the 'gone' reading is unsourced. The only page text read is the 1965 bid notice to remove the old tower and erect an 80-foot replacement four miles NE of New Salem. It does not confirm completion. The record's height_m 24.4 comes from that 80-foot figure and is unverified as built. The FFLA coordinates were not checked against the notice's New Salem location. Build date of the older tower unknown. Not read: the original Cherokeean notice (Portal to Texas History may hold it) and any Texas A&M Forest Service records. Ask Texas A&M Forest Service or Rusk County about current status before publishing any visit guidance.

Agency conflict. The Forest Lookouts Texas list credits the Texas Forest Service. The 1952 SFASU photo record (creator United States Forest Service) places the site in Davy Crockett National Forest. Unresolved; a Davy Crockett National Forest office or Texas A&M Forest Service history record could settle it. No build date, design, height, staffing or access found. The FFLA status list shows no date that I saw. TopoQuest gives an elevation of 341 ft (not used in the story). The 1953 Grand Prairie Daily News item was read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not in the newspaper itself. No photo added: the SFASU page text read has no image URL.

Very thin record. Smith Ferry is not registered in the cached National Historic Lookout Register or FFLOS listings for Texas, and no construction date, design, height, staffing, or fate (standing/removed/burned) beyond the FFLA list's bare 'Standing' turned up in two web searches plus the cached regional lookout lists. The Texas Escapes citation is general East Texas context (phase-out to aerial patrol), not Smith-Ferry-specific; flagged as such in the story. Worth a follow-up with Texas A&M Forest Service records or Tyler County historical sources if a human researcher has more time/budget.

Only FFLA gives tower-specific information, and it gives no build date, builder, design, staffing or access. The Community Impact article (published May 6, 2026, per its dateline) gives office context only and does not mention a lookout tower (checked, no match for 'tower'). The story gives the groundbreaking as April 29 and does not say construction is still under way, which the article does not establish. The FFLA Bastrop entry (gone) is a different site and is mentioned only to prevent confusion. Cavallerano's 2025 book has a 'Lost Pines' appendix that may cover Bastrop County; it was not read. Record is consistent: standing, Bastrop County, matching coordinates.

No newspaper, NRHP, or forest-history coverage found specific to this tower; it is recent (built 2023, NHLR-registered Jan 2026) so that may simply not exist yet. The NHLR nominator, Alfred Francis Gessel, shares a surname with a contact address once suspected on the Timber Lane Utility District site, raising a guess that he may be a district official involved in bringing the tower to the park — but this was never sourced (the district-facilities page carries no contact names or emails) and has been dropped from the story entirely rather than left as insinuation. Climbability and drive-up access are unconfirmed; the park's own page references a 'Fire Tower Flyer' that was not reachable in this research. One correction applied: the NHLR elevation figure (113 ft / 34 m) is not labeled by the register as site elevation vs. structure height, so the story no longer asserts which it is. The district-facilities source was dropped (it supported neither the Fire Tower Flyer mention, which is on the parks-and-trails page, nor the contact-name claim, which isn't on the site at all); the FFLA citation is renumbered [^3] accordingly.

Thin record. Only county, agency, FFLA standing status and coordinates were found. Searches surfaced only unrelated Shelby County fire news. Best lead: Cavallerano's Fire in the Piney Woods. The Project MUSE summary was read; the full text was not, and may need institutional access. Texas A&M Forest Service history pages (tfsweb.tamu.edu) returned HTTP 403 to fetch_text, so were not read. The FFLA list shows no date that I saw. The story is intentionally short (about 125 words).

Build date is known only as 'the 1930s' (NHLR); events[0] uses 1930 as a placeholder for the decade, and the story says 'in the 1930s'. NHLR and firelookout.org name the agency Texas Forest Service; the Pine Mills entry names Texas A&M Forest Service. The sources do not reconcile these. The Tyler County Heritage Society has a 'Fire Tower' artifact (index dated January 1, 1941); only a preview was readable and it does not name this tower, so it is not used. No access or visit information found, so access is omitted. Brief coordinates differ from firelookout.org by about 0.0003 degrees, immaterial. Brief status and registration year agree with sources. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the Register footnote was removed from the advice sentence; the company name is given as in the Register ('Emsco Oil Derrick Co.'); the Santa Claus wording is now quoted in full and the Register's administrator line is quoted.

Two small date conflicts in the sources, both noted in the story rather than resolved: last staffed year (NHLR: 1968; Deseret News: 1969) and the restoration year before the 2008 closure (NHLR: 1986; Deseret News: early-1980s renovation, reopened 1987). Nothing in hand to adjudicate either. The record itself checks out against all sources on name, location, build year (1937) and status. The tower is now a staffed-by-volunteers interpretive/tour site rather than an active detection post, which the current record's staffing/access/visit fields didn't yet reflect. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found a third, previously unflagged conflict: NHLR gives elevation as 8,819 ft, but Wikipedia, Wikidata and willhiteweb all give 8,834 ft; now flagged in the story and as a correction above rather than resolved. Also corrected three footnote misattributions in the original story/JSON draft: the '360 square miles' view figure and the above-ground-living-quarters uniqueness claim were cited partly to NHLR, which does not state either; and the NRHP listing date/reference number was cited partly to NHLR, which gives only the 1978 nomination, not the 1980 listing date or reference number. Willhiteweb separately gives a 1935 build year, at odds with the 1937 given by NHLR, Wikipedia, Wikidata and Deseret News; left unflagged since the story never cites willhiteweb for the build year and the other four sources agree. Also fixed a pronoun error: the story referred to the current volunteer tour guide as 'him', but the cited Deseret News source names her as Clare Boerigter ('her third season').

Thin record. Brief's height_m 24.4 matches the 80-foot figure in two sources. No build date, staffing or access level is given by any source, so none is recorded. The FFLOS list gives status only. The Weebly entry is a short notes block.

Two conflicts are unresolved: height (100 ft in Weebly vs about 125 ft in the 1942 survey) and fate (2015 scrap auction listing vs standing in 2019 and 2023). The 1933 entry is an under-construction report, not a completion date, and the Weebly page presents it as the same tower without proving it. Access is restricted by fence and signage, and the visit report judges the steps too poor in shape to be regularly climbed, so the story does not encourage a visit. No photo added: the Register's photos carry no licence statement in the text. Brief's 30.5 m height is kept, as it matches the 100-foot figure.

The brief had no height. The 35-foot figure is the Register's, converted to 10.7 m. No source states that the public may drive or walk to the tower, so the record gives no access level; the public trails listed are the preserve's, not the tower's. The latest condition record is the May 2018 visit report. The Register has a photo path (nhlr.org /images/Lookout_Photos/US907_Bald_Knob/Scholetzky1.jpg) but no licence is stated, so no photo is added.

Two substantive sources: the NHLR entry and a 1929 newspaper item quoted on Forest Lookouts (the newspaper itself was not opened). Build year is unresolved: 1933 (register, 60 ft) against October 1929 (62 ft); the story says so and the record's height_m 18.9 follows the 62-foot figure. Record agency 'Arthur Stiltner' is the register's 'Administered by' line, a person rather than an agency; a human should decide the agency field. Nothing found on staffing, fires, present ownership or condition. A web search snippet said the Virginia Department of Forestry once ran the tower and it is now private, with standing recorded as of March 26, 2008; no page I could open states this, so it is not in the story or facts.

No build date in any page read. Height conflict unresolved: the register and the Forest Lookouts header say 80 ft (record height_m 24.4); the 1964 survey description says 100 ft. Ownership change date not found. The Forest Lookouts page also gives driving directions to the tower through a gate and along a private road; they are deliberately left out of the story, which says the tower is private. Do not confuse with Apple Orchard Mountain (Bedford County, listed gone). No staffing or fire history found. Present condition not verified. The Bedford city history page that a search returned covers fire departments, not this tower, and was not used.

Only one period source: the 1963 Coast and Geodetic Survey station description, reproduced on the Forest Lookouts page. No construction date, builder, staffing, or fire history found in that page, the FFLOS Virginia list, SummitPost, or two WebSearch queries (neither returned a history). The NHLR and FFLOS caches hold no page for this tower. 100 ft is converted to 30.5 m. Access is private per SummitPost; the 1963 gate-and-trail directions on the Forest Lookouts page are deliberately left out. Next checks if wanted: Virginia Department of Forestry records, Russell and Buchanan county newspapers, and an NHLR listing check.

Standing is confirmed by firelookout.org. The 1958 report and 1964 NGS note are quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, which credits the 1958 piece to the Kingsport News; the original article was not checked. The NGS station is BIG KNOB, VA/SCOTT. The 1964 note also measures the station mark from the tower's legs (10.3 ft from the southeast leg, 4.8 ft from the northeast leg), so the mark sits on this tower's site; the note still gives no construction date. The 1930/1933 date is on the survey mark (a standard disk set in bedrock), not the tower, and nothing in the sources dates the tower from it. Do not use the 1964 access description (locked gate, 3.25-mile trail) for visits; it is historic and the tower is private. High Knob (Wise/Scott counties) is a different tower. No design, height, or build date in any source read. Fact-check 2026-10-08: 'earliest record' became 'earliest dated record of the tower in these sources'; the claim that nothing ties the survey mark to the tower was removed because the 1964 note does tie them by measurement; the Register footnote was removed from the advice sentence; the access and survey-mark quotes were added as evidence.

Big Walker is an observation tower and tourist site, not a fire lookout, per the Forest Fire Lookout Association's 'Obs Tower' code and the sources. The editor should decide whether it belongs in Firefinder. Access is a fee-based public visit per Wikipedia; hours and fees were not verified. The record's 'access unknown' is now resolved to public with a fee. Not checked: a separate OSM node named 'Walker Lookout Tower' (node 358265378, ele 763 m) is a different site and was not researched.

Thin record. Only the NHLR entry and the FFLA list were usable; the Forest Lookouts Birdnest page has a header and no body text. No build date, height or design found. The 2009 report's 'aerometer' is probably Aermotor but is not stated, so no design is recorded. 'Unstaffed' comes from visit-report impressions in 2017, not an agency record. The newest visit is from 2017, so current condition and standing are unverified. Access is not stated by any source read. Record elevation_m 10.1 matches 33 ft. A web search snippet mentioned a Franktown location and a 2008 status note; no page was read to confirm it, so it is not used.

Register says the tower is privately owned and no longer a lookout; no date for that change, no owner named. Forest Lookouts names VDOF as agency, so the record's agency field may be stale. No staffing, fire or access sources found; two searches turned up nothing on the tower's history. A search also turned up a 125-foot Southside Electric pole in Blackstone, which is not this lookout. The 1942 date may be the build year or first record; the sources do not say which.

Standing rests only on the Forest Fire Lookout Association Virginia list. The Forest Lookouts page is a name-and-county stub with no tower details. TopoQuest gives the summit (711 ft, Buckingham County, Dillwyn map sheet), not the tower. A search snippet mentioned a row reading Private (formerly VDOF), Standing (2008) for this mountain; its source page could not be opened (firelookout.org/lookouts/lo-virginia.html returns 404), and the wording is not in any Buffards page read, so it is not used. Two WebSearch queries were run; neither returned a history. No NHLR or FFLOS page for this tower is in the cache. Owner and access are unknown. Next checks if wanted: the Association's Buffards detail page, an NHLR listing, Virginia Department of Forestry records, and Buckingham County historical sources.

Built, replacement, cabin, 1989 dedication and registration all agree across the NHLR page, the Forest Lookouts page and the Patrick County Chamber page. The Chamber text repeats the NHLR description, so it is not independent confirmation. No staffing or access source found. A Martinsville Bulletin article (martinsvillebulletin.com) returned HTTP 429 and was not read. The record's source_pages list nhlr.org/lookouts/us/va/blakey-ridge-fire-tower/, which appears to be a different site (Blakey Ridge, Madison County); it was not used and should be checked. No photos added: the NHLR page credits no image URL that I could find.

The 2017 visit report is nine years old; condition may have changed. Land ownership is unresolved: the register says Jefferson National Forest, the 1964 survey description says private property. No build date or builder found. The Tower No. 59 number appears only in the 1964 description. The visitor listing is user-written and its route may be out of date. Recommend the Forest Service (Jefferson National Forest) confirm the land status and current condition before publishing the access note.

Only the two FFLA Virginia lists were read. Two web searches found no news, agency or county record of the tower or its move. A search snippet mentioned an older Virginia listing with VDOF ownership and a removed status; it was not fetched and is not used. Distance of about 16 km between the Capron and Southampton points is computed from the listed coordinates. The Southampton Ag & Forestry Center's location and any access information remain unverified.

Thinnest of the three. The FFLA list is the only tower-specific source and gives name, county, coordinates and status. The Forest Lookouts Upper Essex entry has a heading, the county and a region label (VALLEY RIDGE) only; it carries a photo whose caption, credit and licence are unknown, so no photo is recorded. The story now says the entry gives the name and county with no history, without saying 'only'. The Virginia Department of Forestry and NHLR Virginia listings were not checked for this site. Name variants: Caret (FFLA) and Upper Essex (Forest Lookouts) are treated as one site, which is an inference from the matching county and name. Suggested next steps: Virginia Department of Forestry history and Essex County newspaper archives.

Existence and standing rest only on the Forest Fire Lookout Association Virginia list, which also lists Caret (Upper Essex) as a separate standing tower. The Forest Lookouts page is a name-and-county stub. Wikipedia's Center Cross page is an unincorporated community in Essex County with no tower detail, so it is not cited. Two WebSearch queries returned a TopoQuest place page, a Browne State Forest page that gives a Center Cross address but no tower mention, and a registered antenna structure and an early-1800s house at Center Cross, neither of which is the lookout. A search snippet gave a row reading PRIVATE (Essex County) (formerly VDOF), Standing (2008), but its source page could not be opened and the wording is not in any Center Cross page read, so it is not used. Owner and access unknown. Next checks if wanted: the Association's Center Cross detail page, an NHLR listing, Virginia Department of Forestry records, and Essex County records.

Only the NHLR page gives history; the second and third searches found no independent source for the 1930s date or the 1974 watching arrangement. The Register says only 'the 1930s', so the built event uses year 1930 as a stand-in for the decade, and modified uses 1980 the same way. Coordinates appear on the FFLA Virginia list, but the NHLR says the owner asked that they be unlisted. The story omits them and the record should be reviewed. Owner and watching family are not named in the story. The brief's 'Private owner' and standing status are supported.

Only readable source is the FFLA Virginia index (the standing list at firelookout.org/?p=3654 agrees). No history, build date, builder, height or staffing found. Searches surfaced an older 2011 'Charles City' database entry (Providence Forge quad, private, formerly VDOF, 'Standing (2008)') and a 420 ft Virginia Electric and Power structure at Roaches Corner (built 2009). Neither was readable or cited, and the 420 ft structure is a utility tower, not a lookout; a human should confirm the tower identity before any edit. Record fields match the listing, so no corrections proposed. Page reads: 7 (brief budget 6), mostly dead or duplicate links (lo-virginia 404, towerdex 403, duplicate DHR page). Searches: 2. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the NHLR expansion had no cited source, so the nhlr.org Virginia index was added as source 2 and footnote 2 was added to the story.

Built year and registration date and design come from the Register's own fields. Access and condition rest on one 2010 visit report, which is sixteen years old. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with permission. The 1941 built date and the visitor's pre-1945 recollection are compatible but only the Register field is used as the date. Visitor report names are left out of the story. Second search returned only general material; no independent history found. Elevation in the brief (1017.4 m) matches the Register's 1,017 m. The story does not include coordinates.

The 1937 dispatch is the only dated primary-type source and does not name the tower; the Crafton Gate link rests on the Forest Lookouts page. Build year is inferred from the dispatch and the register's 1930s, so the event is flagged as approximate. No staffing, fire, condition or access sources found in two searches. Phenix Fire Tower is mentioned by the register but was not researched.

Standing status rests on the Forest Fire Lookout Association list; the Register does not say standing in words. Staffing 'seasonal' comes from the 1955 newspaper about the Richardsville station, presumed to be this tower's site; no later staffing source. Brief's access 'unknown' corrected to private. A 2019 Facebook group post (Abandoned in Virginia) mentions an old fire tower on the Richardsville road; social media, not used. Coordinates withheld by owner; do not publish a location. No photos added; the Register credits a photo to Kristin Reynolds but no image URL was read. Not verified: condition, current owner's name, any closure or public access.

Standing comes from the Forest Fire Lookout Association list. The photo caption (Flickr, Earl C. Leatherberry) is the only source for no longer being used as a lookout, for the antennas, and for NRHP contributing status; Wikipedia's Cumberland Court House Historic District article and the DHR district page were checked and do not mention the tower. The 2019 unstaffed finding is from one visitor's report on the Register, not an official survey. Access is left out of facts: the Register's sign and directions fields say 'Unsure' and no source states public access. SAH Archipedia (VA-02-CB4) returned HTTP 403 and was not read. A Facebook post in Abandoned in Virginia mentions the tower; social media, not used. Brief's record height 25.9 m matches the 1941 survey; the 2015 registration and 1941 build year match the Register. No photos added: the Register credits a July 2019 photo to James Hull, but no image URL was read. Not verified: current use beyond the caption, owner's statement, antenna operators.

Thin record. The Register gives only the decade for construction and no staffing dates or access information, so no access level is recorded. The Register's and the Association's coordinates differ by a few metres; the brief's coordinates were not changed. The Association's unconfirmed-sites list has a Dinwiddie entry flagged 'same as Dewitt?' as a possible duplicate; not checked. No Forest Lookouts page for this tower was in the cache. Facebook and YouTube mentions were seen in search results only and are not cited.

Index row and FWS About Us page read in full; ODU species list grepped for fire tower captions only. The ODU captions do not show the tower's location, builder or date, and it is not confirmed that the photographed tower is the listed one. The Suffolk News-Herald 2011 fire coverage returned 403 and is not cited. Not confirmed whether the tower lies inside the refuge, so access is unknown and the story gives no visit advice beyond asking staff. No events or facts added because no readable source supports them. Searches: 1. Page reads: 3, with the index shared with the other towers. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the ODU source title was 'A to Z Index' (search-result link text); the page heading is 'Great Dismal Swamp Species List' and its title tag is 'Great Dismal Swamp', so source 2 was corrected. Source 3 title was set to the FWS page title tag. Story wording that copied the FWS and quote phrasing was reworded.

Thin record: only three sources read and the eastern lookouts page for this tower is a heading only (name, county, forest). No staffing history, no fires, no visit or access information was found. Not to be confused with other Duncan Knob sites in the George Washington National Forest near Mount Jackson and Massanutten (about 38.7 N, -78.6 W), which are different places; this record is the Bath County site at 38.164, -79.705. A community Facebook post about a former attendant was not used because only a truncated snippet was readable. The access field is omitted because no source says whether the public may climb the tower.

Only the two FFLA Virginia lists and Wikipedia's Rassawek page were read; two web searches on the East Leake move found no dated or sourced account. The record us-va-east-leake-loc-1 says the Loc 1 tower was moved to Rassawek, but the FFLA list does not name which East Leake point Rassawek came from. That claim is unverified. Search snippets mentioning an older listing for East Leake (South Anna, VDOF, removed) were not fetched and are not used. Distance of about 16.5 km between East Leake (Loc 1) and the Rassawek point is computed from the listed coordinates. The name Rassawek belongs to a sensitive Monacan archaeological site; the story reports only what the sources state.

Thin record. The only history is two newspaper reports from 1967 and 1969 (Bluefield Daily Telegraph, as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page) plus the FFLA listing. No build date, height, design or access information found. Not in the NHLR or FFLOS Virginia listings in the local crawl. Brief's record had no height; NHLR gives a 90-foot tower, so height_m 27.4 is added. Staffing and condition come from two visitor reports on the Register (2008, 2018), not an official survey. Thin record. Build date is 'early 1930s' only; no staffing, fire or access information in any source. Only the FFLA directory line and the Forest Lookouts county index support this record. Not on the NHLR Virginia list. The brief's county, status and coordinates match the FFLA list. Only the FFLA listing (standing, Lee County) and TopoQuest (Lee County, 2,519 ft, named Hunter Lookout Tower) confirm the tower. Wikipedia names the gap, not the tower. Only the FFLA listing (standing, Buchanan County) and RoadOnMap (a place-name site naming Keen Mountain Fire Tower, 2,710 ft) name the tower. Build year not found. The CCC is named by a 2014 blog and the 1991 state survey gives only a statewide CCC total (88 lookout towers through 1941), not a date for this site. Hiking guides disagree on the structure, as the story says.

Two sources only, and the NHLR page carries nearly all the history. The 2014 county survey is quoted by NHLR, not read directly. Height converted from 80 ft to metres. Access, staffing and current condition are not documented, so no access key is given. Two WebSearch-equivalent searches and four page reads were used.

Ownership conflict: the Register (undated page, registered 2015) says the Virginia Department of Forestry still owns it; the 2015 chapter report lists it as private with land for sale. Not verified: current ownership, whether the tower has been moved or removed since 2015, or whether the land has sold.

Original Long Mountain history rests on the FFLOS register alone. The Rhudy move and the Rhudy standing claim rest on the FFLA lists only; no Rhudy-specific page was found in two searches. Build year and builder rest on one register entry that conflicts with the CCC's dates; no second source found. The CCC Company 2359 article from The Central Virginian turned up in search but returned 404 on fetch, so it is not cited. The Louisa County 1995 survey was checked and does not mention the tower. Height converted from 100 ft. Consider adding a built event as an editor's call; the record had none.

Coordinates: the Register says they are unlisted at the owner's request, yet the record's lat/lon matches the FFLA Virginia list and the Wikidata point. Built date is only the spring-1938 announcement; no completion report found. Location descriptions conflict (see resolved_conflicts) and the record coordinates were not tested against them. Built year is only 'early 1930s' in the county text; the 1930 event year is a placeholder. The 1990 staffed_last year is also a placeholder for 'until the 1990s'. Thin record. The only sources are two FFLA lists that give name, county, coordinates and a standing status. No build date, builder, owner or staffing dates were found; the story says so. Searches returned hike guides, a Facebook post and a YouTube result. Thin record. Only the register and the forestry page were read. The brief's '1961 built' is the NHLR erection date at Partlow; the tower stood at Prince William Forest Park from early in WWII (FFLOS build year 1942). Two registry sources and one 1953 newspaper item quoted by Forest Lookouts; the newspaper itself was not read. No source read covers fires the tower spotted, staffing after 1953, or current access. Do not confuse with the Red Oak Knob fire tower in West Virginia's Monongahela National Forest, which is a different structure. Two searches and about six page reads turned up no build date, designer, staffing record or fire history. The Long Lines page is a hobbyist site, so treat its wording as a lead. No staffing history, fire-watch dates, or height figure was found in the sources read, so facts.height_m and staffing are omitted. The register's purpose (fire spotting plus recreation) and the county library's (tourism) differ in emphasis. Elevation differs: NHLR gives 3,304 ft (1,007 m), which the record and story use; Wikipedia gives 3315 ft for the same peak. Not reconciled. Build history: the NHLR detail page gives no build year. Roof: the 2008, 2010 and 2012 chapter reports call for repair or replacement; the 2022 report says replaced 'last year', read as 2021, which is an inference. Staffing: the NHLR visit report has a Staffed? question; not used as a fact. Budget: four fetch_text page reads (NHLR, Forest Lookouts, the 2025 chapter report, Wikipedia) plus one blocked NorthWoods page; two WebSearch calls; the other chapter reports were read from the local cache with pdftotext -layout. No new photos added; the record photo is from the NHLR (Jack Kelley, all rights reserved).

Steel tower date is unresolved: the state record says a steel tower from Gilson Mountain went up in spring 1956, while the NRHP nomination says a private organization built the present tower in 1966. The NRHP title is taken from the nomination header. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

Record height_m 21.0 (from OpenStreetMap) does not match the 45 ft 9 in height the January 1939 paper gave for the planned replacement. Left out of facts and corrections for a human to settle.
