Brief check: 'still closed in the 2021 report' is verified (cr-vt-2021.pdf: 'continues to remain Closed'). Access changes from the brief's 'unknown' to 'closed'. Gaps: (1) No staffing years anywhere in the sources read; the NHLR 'about a decade' is the only statement, so no staffed or staffed_last event is recorded. (2) Current status after the 2021 report is unknown; no reopening is shown but none is ruled out. (3) The Valley News column is undated in the copy read; 'about 10 years back' for the NorthWoods work is relative to an unknown date, so no year is given for it. (4) The column says 'It was sold to a paper company in 1961' right after describing the warden's cabin. The antecedent of 'It' is ambiguous (cabin or tower or land), so the story leaves that sentence out. TPL's page says International Paper Realty sold the 14 parcels in the 2005 deal; the two may or may not be linked. (5) The column's 'light copper roofs' detail is also left out for the same reason. (6) A search snippet quoting a NorthWoods trail director about summit cabins being removed or burned was not from a page read, so it is not used. (7) Do not confuse this with New Hampshire's Mount Monadnock. (8) TPL spells the mountain 'Monandnock'; the quotes use the NHLR spelling. (9) NHLR photos are credited to Craig Hamelin; no image URLs were added. Budget: 6 distinct pages read (one, the easternuslookouts.weebly.com Monadnock page, returned only navigation and is not cited) and 1 WebSearch.

Only the association's list (cite 3) says the tower was relocated, and the list gives no detail. The record's note that it moved 'a short way, to a new spot on the same site' could not be checked: the association's detail page is not in the cache, and no read source describes a move. The record's height_m 7.6 is the 25-ft figure from the state park for today's observation tower, converted to metres; the parent record (us-vt-mount-ascutney) carries the same 7.6 m against a 54-ft 1940 steel tower, so the parent height may need review. The parent also says 'relocated' while the association lists the original as 'Tower Gone'. A WebSearch summary attributed construction to CCC Company 129 (1933-1938); no page I could read states that, so it is not used. The county correction rests on the Forest Lookouts page, which reads 'Windsor County'; the association's list repeats the typo.

Brief events for 2013 (footing repairs), 2014 (FFLA grant), and 2018 (glass removed; steel stairs) were not confirmed in the sources read and are left out of the story. The 2016 Register visit reports most of the cab glass already missing, which sits awkwardly with a 2018 glass-removal date. The FPR park page is undated, so the mid-December closure cannot be dated; do not treat it as current without checking. The Forest Lookouts history gives the wooden tower 30 ft in 1949 and 40 ft in 1935; the NGS 1942 survey describes a wooden tower about 60 ft tall on Hogback Mountain, which may be a different structure. Elevation matches the brief (2,316 ft, 706 m). The FPR release names the park as Molly Stark State Park; Forest Lookouts calls it Molly Stark State Forest.

Brief's 2010 're-wooded' wording is not in the register text read (corrected). Not verified in pages read: the 2012 'ski area workers' and certificate detail, and the June 19, 2023 NHLR registration date (the grep did not return the date line), so neither is in the story. Climbing rules for the cab are not stated in the sources read; the state page implies public visits. Build date conflicts (1922/1924) and the summit-name conflict are reported in the story. Fact-check 2026-10-08: story now says the state describes spectacular 360-degree views, attributes the 1951 chimney to the register's lookout cabin and flags that the register does not say it is the watchman's cabin, and footnotes the wood sentence. Pages read: 8, over the 6-page budget because the NHLR and Eastern pages are long.

Construction date is unresolved. The 1924 Commissioner of Forestry report already describes an octagonal stone tower, while a trail guide and Wikipedia credit CCC work in the 1930s. An earlier tower may have been rebuilt by the CCC, but no source we read says so. Wikipedia's park photo caption calls the summit building a 'CCC-built shelter', which may or may not be the tower. Groton State Forest history guide and Living New Deal pages returned HTTP 403 and were not read; a search snippet from Living New Deal gives 1935, unverified. Whether the 2002 NRHP listing of park CCC facilities includes the tower is not confirmed. Status 'standing' rests on the FFLA list alone. Wikipedia gives the summit at 596 m (1,956 ft), which is the mountain's height, not the tower's; the record's elevation_m is null. No staffing or fire history found. Interior and climbing access not found.

Build date 1943 and staffing come from 1943-1947 newspaper items transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page; not checked against the Reformer itself. The only current evidence of the tower is the FFLA 'Standing' entry; no recent condition or access report was found. Access is unknown: the site is town watershed land on Pleasant Valley Road, and no public-access rule was found, so no access level is recorded. Height is not given in metres because the 34-foot figure's reference point (ground or cab floor) is not stated. The record's kind 'three_story' and county Windham match the sources; no corrections proposed.

Two open conflicts are reported in the story: the move year (1943 vs 1944) and the 1931 tower design. The brief's height_m 24.0 is not supported by any page read, so it is left out of facts; no source found gives the steel tower's height. Staffing evidence is a 1959 newspaper item and the Register's October 2016 visit form; no current staffing source was found. Access is public per the state page; no closure notice was found. The Register lists the summit site at 2,947 ft while the state page gives 3,037 ft. No photos added. Forest Lookouts page also holds 1938 and 1947-1957 maintenance notes, not used.

The only source that places a tower here is OpenStreetMap, which names it a Lookout Tower and tags it observation. The FFLA Vermont list I read has no entry for Stave Island, and the local NHLR and FFLOS caches hold no record of it, so it is not confirmed as a fire lookout. Status 'standing' in the record rests only on the OSM point existing, not on any report of its condition. The OSM point is several hundred metres from the seaplane base coordinates in AeroCopilot (44.5959, -73.3476), so it may be a separate structure. Recommend a satellite check and a local source before any fire-lookout claim; the record's name and kind may need review. Access is unknown and no visit guidance is given.

Several sources disagree on dates and heights (see resolved_conflicts). The 'today' access rests on an undated USFS trail page. The NRHP nomination is dated March 1990 (Hugh H. Henry), before the 1992 listing. A Stratton Mountain Resort hiking page (search snippet only, not fetched; the fetch returned no text) says the tower was manned until 1979, which conflicts with the nomination's 1982; it is not cited and remains unverified. No rental listing found; the cabin is a Green Mountain Club shelter, not described as rentable. The NRHP ID 92000687 and the 1992 listing are from the brief and the NPGallery detail page; the listing year is from the GMC page. Consider updating facts.height_m if the USFS 70 ft figure is confirmed for the renovated tower.

Everything before 1973 comes from a transcription of state reports and a 1950 newspaper notice on the Forest Lookouts page, not the originals. Current status rests only on the FFLA list. The sale to a private owner means no public access; the owner's 2019 email is quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, so treat that as the owner's stated wish. The 1915 tower's structure type is not given. Record location and county (Essex) match the FFLA list; no corrections proposed.

The 1936 building question is unresolved: a 2019 plan citing a 2009 USFS source says it still stands, while the register and firelookout.com say the L-4 was replaced in 1975. Staffing rests on one 2025 hiking guide and an undated register entry. Unread search snippets, not used in the story: SummitPost and an Alamy caption give 1976 for the R-6 cab; a hiking site mentions a 1924 occupant and 1935 radio; Trailchick says staffing was seasonal in the past. The record's 1936 built event is the first L-4 cab, not the cab standing today. Page reads for this lookout: four.

Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. Elevation conflicts across four sources; NHLR figure kept. TrailChick describes climbing the tower; the story reports that its 2017 visitor did not climb to the top and does not claim that tribal permission is needed to climb. Named 1943 teacher omitted from the story. Access rules and TrailChick's permit detail come from a 2017 visit updated in 2023; check the Colville permit page before relying on it. Living New Deal not used.

The NRHP listing (NRIS 90001915, 12/27/1990) describes the lookout on its original Badger Mountain summit. This record links it to the Columbia Breaks site, where only the cab is said to be displayed, so the listing may not describe the current exhibit. The kind 'ground' on this record is not confirmed by any source read. The NRHP says the summit was donated around 1941, while the FFLOS dates the build to 1941; the house's build date and move date are not settled. Parent record us-wa-badger-mountain (status relocated) was not edited.

Current status is the main uncertainty. The most recent visitor source read is the WTA page, which says the tower has been deconstructed (its image file name is dated 2024); the TrailChick visit is from 7/02/18. No 2025-2026 status source was found, and the search summary also reported no rebuild. The record's status note says FFLA marks it as temporarily removed; the FFLA lookout list was not read, so that claim is unverified here. The first-tower date conflict (1929 vs 1938) is real: the Register and firelookout.com (1938, 73-foot pole) vs Forest Lookouts and TrailChick (1929, 80-foot timber). The record's 1938 is kept. A Washington state preservation office article, 'Umatilla National Forest & FFLA Give 80 ft. Tall Gift', was found by search but returned 403, so it is not cited; its search summary gives 1956 for the 82-foot tower and attributes the damage to a 2013 snowstorm, which conflicts with the 2010-2011 tree strike in other sources. A human should check that article directly. Record claims of FFLA grants of $500 in 2013 and 2014 were not found in the pages read and are not in the story. Staffing: none reported after 2014; the Register describes 'standby status' without a date, so no staffing fact is recorded. Pages read: 7 including one 403. One web search used. No photos added; NHLR and TrailChick carry photos but licence information was not in what was read.

Summit elevation conflicts. The Register gives 6,007 ft (1,831 m), matching the record's 1830.9 m. Firelookout.com and TrailChick give 6,135 ft. Left out of facts. Access level 'restricted' is an editorial judgment from the state-land road, the DNR emergency-use cab and the usually locked catwalk. No source states a public access policy, so check with DNR before publishing. No rental found. 'Unstaffed' rests on the June 2018 Register visit report and Will Hite's 'not staffed for decades'; nothing newer. TrailChick shows a May 2026 update date, but its photos run to 2021 and its condition text predates the repairs. Will Hite contradicts itself on tower height (40 feet in the 1960 entry, 20 feet in the fire section). Photos on firelookout.com and TrailChick were not traced to a licence, so none added. The record's 'L-4' design is only the 1934 cab.

Record height_m 94.5 is wrong for a ground house; correction proposed (omit). Elevation differs by source: register 5,154 ft (record 1570.9 m matches it); National Forest Foundation and the 1968 newspaper say about 5,310 ft; firelookout.com says 5304. Not reconciled. Staffing: the 1930 and 1931 K.I. Peters notices conflict with the May 1960 notice calling Burley the first lookout in the Randle District; not reconciled. The 1968 name is Darleen in one Daily Chronicle story and Charleen in another; unresolved. Distance: the 1960 notice says 28 miles south of Randle, firelookout.com says 10 miles SSE; the record coordinates match the register. A search snippet (TrailChick) suggests a tent camp in 1930 before the 1934 cab; I did not open that page, so it is unverified. The National Forest Foundation article is undated; its two-year restoration timeline may be out of date, and no rental was found open. Status: standing is supported by the 2026 Forest Service page. Page reads used: 6. WebSearch used: 1.

Two independent descriptions (register and firelookout.com) agree on the 1934 cab and the 1951 sale and move; the place-name link is weaker. The association gives the standing cab as 'Reynaud'; the register and the relocation list say only 'a ranch 4 miles up the Twisp River'. The story now says no source ties the Reynaud name to the ranch, so whether they are the same place is unconfirmed. A WebSearch summary of a 2021 Methow Valley News item (https://methowvalleynews.com/2021/07/14/valley-life-twisp-20/) reports a 1933 purchase, a 1951 public-auction sale to a named Reynaud family member, and a 2003 move to a Reynaud Loop Road overlook. I could not quote it: the cached copy (data/raw/web/0478968c70039e53367ece9e7e875ff6d28d43f5.bin) is gzip-compressed and fetch_text does not decompress it, so the text came back as binary. If fetch_text is fixed to gunzip responses, that article should be re-read; it may correct the location and add the 2003 move. The 1934 date is the register's; the 1933 purchase is unverified. Methownet's 'End of Lookouts?' page returned 404 and was not used. No photos added.

Built date is disputed: the record's 1938 (Wikidata, matching the NRHP) against a 1936 first tower and 1939 replacement in the FFLOS and FireLookout.com. The NRHP listing (NRIS 90001912, 12/27/1990) describes the summit site before the 1995 move, so it may not describe the current exhibit. Visit Wenatchee places the center on US Highway 97 while the center's own page says Highway 97A; the story omits the route. Parent record us-wa-chelan-butte (status relocated) was not edited.

The 1985 sale and move are stated the same way on three pages (register, firelookout.com, relocated list), though the first two share wording and likely a common source. The only current-tense claim, that it still stands at the farm, is the register's 'where it stands today'; no news item or recent photo was found to confirm it, and the register's text is undated. The association lists it standing, but that list does not name the farm. height_m 12.5 is the register's 41 ft converted to metres, not a figure a source gives in metres. The register's photos (1940s and early 1980s) are already on the parent record us-wa-chewelah-peak, so no new photos were added. A 1948 newspaper quote on administration (Willhite) was not used. The parent record shows status 'relocated' and FFLA 'Tower Gone' for the original, which is consistent. Several Willhite staffing names are on the page; none is used here.

Height is genuinely disputed across three sources (90 ft Umatilla NF inventory, 94 ft Kresek, 82 ft firelookout.com) and I left height_m out rather than pick one. The 'built 1938' field in the current tower record looks like an error against the CCC narrative that NHLR itself tells (1933 tower / 1935 cabin) - see the proposed correction. A same-named 'Clearwater Lookout Site' in the FFLOS register (firetower.org) is a different, unrelated former lookout near the Olympic Peninsula (~-124.3, 47.6) and was not used here. Distance from Pomeroy is also given two ways (15 mi per firelookout.com, 25 mi per the rental listing) - left out of the story as not load-bearing. Fact-check correction (2026-10-04): the draft had attributed firelookout.com's 82 ft figure to 'the Fire Lookout Museum' - that credit line is actually for the 1997 photo on that page, not the height, so the story and this file no longer carry that attribution. Also removed an unsupported claim that the tower is closed to 'climbing' (no cited source says this; the OSM node carries access=no but no climbing tag), and lightly reworded one sentence in the story that paraphrased willhiteweb.com too closely.

Current use is disputed and not resolved: the register text (undated, also on firelookout.com) says staffed most summers; the Willhite page (undated text, photo captions 1934 and 2016) says it appears recently abandoned; TrailChick (visited May 2019) does not say. Check with the Colville Tribes before publishing either claim. The $80/yr permit comes from a TrailChick page updated March 2026; verify with the Tribes. A search summary claimed the Colville Tribes staff the tower periodically, citing a photo entry; no page read confirmed it, so it is left out. Access note in facts is permission per the record. Record fields height_m and status are unchanged (45 ft tower height is not converted because the register does not say whether it runs to the cab floor).

The brief's status note (tower still stands, cab gone) and its 4.9 m height describe a pole tower that the NHLR and WillhiteWeb say is gone; corrected. The FFLA Washington list page the brief cites (firelookout.org/lookouts/us/wa/) was not read, so the source of the brief's wording is unchecked. The staffing history comes from newspaper items reprinted by WillhiteWeb (1915, 1919) and FireLookout.com's personnel list (1923, 1929); the 1919 item is written in the future tense, so the story says 'set to run' it. The Slagle brothers are undated, so no events entry was made for them. The 1960s burning and 1970s decommissioning are not pinned to exact years, so no event was made for them either. The weebly page's 1913 and 1915 newspaper items were not used. No photos added. Current access into the cabin is not confirmed. Confidence is medium: the cabin's facts agree across sources, but the pole-tower dates conflict.
Build-year conflict (1932 vs 1934) resolved by reporting both with their likely explanation, per brief's own flagged conflict.

Height 42 ft converted to 12.8 m. Brief elevation matches NHLR; other sources differ by about 30 to 35 ft. Current status is from TrailChick (updated March 2024) and firelookout.com ('as of last report', undated). Ramblr (2019) and geocache pages were not read. The stair removal is undated. Access is drawn from WTA and TrailChick; the story does not encourage climbing. No corrections to the brief.

Reads: register, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts page (two passes on the cached page), FFA Washington list, WillhiteWeb Forks page, museum exhibits page; one WebSearch. A WebSearch hit on WillhiteWeb's Deming page (sumas_mountain_271) was not read and is not used. Record check: the Forks record's county (Clallam), coordinates and standing status match the FFA list. The register's Date Registered value did not appear in the cached text, so the March 26, 2012 date in the us-wa-deming record is unverified. The record has no year for the relocation; the story adds 1985 for the cab move. Height is left out: the 75-foot and 40-foot figures belong to different towers, and the source tower for the cab is disputed. Access 'public' rests on the museum display page; the museum invites visits, but no hours or climbing rules were found. Story is about the lookout, so the original Deming site is covered only as the place the tower came from.

Build year conflicts: NHLR says 1933; NPS inventory form, Seattle Times and firelookout.com say 1932 (the NRHP record also keys 1932 as its significant year). Distance to the site conflicts across three sources. Elevation differs (NHLR 5,982 ft; Seattle Times 6,102 ft; the NPS form's elevation is garbled in the OCR). The Seattle Times profile is undated in the copy read, so the staffing as_of is undated. No source states whether the cabin is open to visitors, so access level 'restricted' is an inference from its active NPS-staffed status. The brief's agency 'U.S. Dept. of the Interior' is the department; the operating bureau is the National Park Service. No specific fire the lookout helped fight appears in the sources read, so no fire events were added. Not checked: whether the NRHP nomination (NRIS 88003451) gives a different build year; the nomination PDF was not retrieved. Owner-supplied photo credit on the NHLR page ('courtesy of Jim Henterly') has no image URL, so no photo entry was added.

Unresolved: the end of the Aircraft Warning Service use. Willhite Web quotes a 1944 report saying the last day was Oct 5, 1942, but also names lookouts in 1943, and Wikipedia's article is cited for the WWII use without a date. Trail length conflicts (10 miles per Willhite Web, 13 miles per NWHikers). Elevation conflicts (NHLR 5,728 ft; firelookout 5,753 ft; the brief's 1745.9 m matches NHLR). Current public access is not confirmed; the Willhite page is undated. The NRHP number 07000736 comes from the brief, and the Wikipedia article gives the same number.

Good spread of sources for a rental-tier lookout: NHLR and firelookout.com agree on the 1935 build; NHLR and willhiteweb.com separately confirm WWII Aircraft Warning Service use (firelookout.com's cached page does NOT mention AWS use, despite an earlier draft citing it for that claim -- fixed during fact-check). willhiteweb.com (a hiking-guide site, used here beyond its usual access-only role because no better source turned up) supplied the Ogilvie staffing anecdote and the 1967 Evergreen Fire, which also matches the burn-scar language already in the record's own rental.description. The NRHP-date conflict is more interesting than first flagged: NPGallery's own asset page gives 1987, but BOTH Recreation.gov and willhiteweb.com independently say listing came out of the 1990s restoration -- two popular secondary accounts agreeing with each other against the primary NRHP record. Left as a flagged conflict rather than guessing; someone with the actual nomination PDF could settle it. Elevation also differs by about 100 ft between NHLR (5,483 ft) and Recreation.gov/willhiteweb/firelookout.com (5,587 ft, three sources agreeing), noted but not changed. Fact-check also caught that the story's claim about the 2026 closure reason was wrong: the live Recreation.gov listing attributes the current closure to a winter-flooding road washout (hoped fixed for the 2027 season), not a wildfire as an earlier draft stated -- corrected. Also removed an unsupported claim that the U.S. Forest Service nominated the property for the NRHP; NPGallery's page does not say who nominated it. No new photos found beyond what the record already has.

Access is not established. The sources describe the lookout as an active detection site used for emergencies and say nothing about public visits, so access is recorded as restricted with that note. Build date: 1938 for the current structure per two sources; a 1931 newspaper item on the Weebly site points to an earlier station, and this is reported as a conflict. Elevation: 1651 m (5,417 ft) on the register versus 5,491 ft on firelookout.com and the Methow Valley page; the Methow page's elevation line uses a prime character and was not quoted. The Methow page has the 2021 fire and paint details; the 2021 fire is recorded as a fire event. Read budget: seven page reads, one over the six-read cap. The seventh was a TrailChick grep that added no story facts. The OpenStreetMap way page and the firelookout.org Washington list were read only to check the record, not for story facts. The 1932 fire report and the 1962 weather-station note that appear in search results were not read and are not used.

Reads: register, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts page (two greps on the cached page), Waymarking lookout page (returned only its title), WillhiteWeb (full page), Waymarking Orient town page (returned no matching text). Two WebSearches: one for the Orient cab, one for park access. The FFA Washington list was reused from the Deming pass. Access 'public' rests on the cab's placement in a community park and the 1985 plan for a historical point of interest; no fetched source gives visiting hours or confirms public entry, and the Waymarking text that mentions the park being open to the public was seen only in a search snippet and is not used. Sibling record flag, not a correction to this one: us-wa-first-thought height_m 21.3 (about 70 feet) fits the 1925 pole tower, not the 40-foot 1947 steel tower the L-4 cab came from. Whoever edits that record should check it. The record for this Orient entry has no height, so none is given here.

Reads: NHLR, Former Fire Lookout Sites Register, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts page, both Association chapter-report PDFs (six reads). The Association's Washington list was reused from the Deming pass. No WebSearch used. Record checks: county Stevens, coordinates (FFA list) and standing status match. Sibling record flag, not a correction to this one: us-wa-flagstaff has height_m 15.2 (50 feet), which matches the 1952 tower on the Forest Lookouts page, not the 40-foot 1971 DNR tower that was dismantled in 2013. That sibling record also lists status relocated while the Former Fire Lookout Sites Register lists the site as gone, and its conflicts list records the NHLR as showing it standing when registered. Whoever edits that record should check these. Whether the tower or only the cab was re-erected in Northport is unresolved in the sources; the story says so. Access 'public' rests on the town-park placement; no hours or climbing rules were found. The 2011 report's broken word in 'Department ofNatural' is avoided in the quotes.

The record us-wa-flattop-mountain carries the 2026 FFLOS entry (US 171, WA 507). A separate record us-wa-flattop (Flattop Lookout Site, FFLOS 2012, US 1315 WA 215, gone) appears to describe the same summit. Editor should consider a merge. Built date: the 1946 year comes from firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb; the NHLR entry gives no built year. Cab size conflicts (12 vs 14 feet). Replica status: the CBFIC page calls its structure a replica of the top story, built partly from the old wood; a search snippet also mentions a dispute over whether it is a moved original, but that claim was not read and is not used. The Mount Adams lookout is a separate structure and is not covered here. WillhiteWeb's 'Location Today' note describes the summit without a date, so the current condition is dated only to that visit. CBFIC hours and visitor access were not verified; the story gives no hours and does not recommend a visit. The register's 2005 visit report is the only source for that year's condition. The record's kind two_story describes the original summit cab; the CBFIC replica is one story. No new photos.

Access is the weak point. Only TrailChick (visited 2017) and Huckleberry Press (April 2022) describe the road, and no DNR notice was found. The level is restricted because of the gate and because nothing says the cab is open. The 1950s replacement is given as 'the 1950s' with no event year. The 1942 AWS dates come from NHLR and the Rex's page. Coordinates in the brief (48.855779, -118.632521) are within about 10 m of TrailChick's (48.855745, -118.632588). Two other pages (firelookout.com and ramblr.com) were seen in search results but not read. Read budget: five pages and one search.

The brief says 'None relocated' with no year. The 1986 date comes from NHLR and Okanogan Country, which agree. The 1950s date for the L-4 cab is only a decade in both sources, so no year is given for the cab's tower. The story covers the cab only; the summit history is in data/stories/us-wa-franson-peak.md, where the 1934-vs-1986 build-year conflict is still open. The Molson Museums' hours and fees come from their own page and should be rechecked before a visit. The cab's exact display spot was not confirmed on a museum page.

Current staffing and rental status not found in sources read. The most detailed account is TrailChick's 2017 visit with a 2021 drive-by. The 1957 'Mrs. Harry A. Gavin' and 1960 'Mabel M. Gavin' items are linked to Mabel Gavin of the 1952 listing by inference only; the story says 'appear to'. Search budget: three WebSearch calls used against a budget of two.

Record height_m 27.0 is not supported by any page read. The register and firelookout.com give a '15' timber' tower, which may mean tower height or cab size, so no height was written. Forest name: the register says Okanogan National Forest; the current name was not confirmed in a page read. Staffing status is undated (WTA). Lightning Bill spelling varies: WTA uses 'Lightning Bill'; OutdoorsNW writes 'Lighting Bill'. A 2023 Cascadia Daily News item (search snippet only, not read) reportedly says the lookout has been back in use since 2021; not used. Page reads for this lookout: five.

The brief's 'relocated' event has no year; 1969 is from four sources. The story is about the moved cab; the original site is us-wa-goat-peak-2. The replacement-date conflict (1956 WTA vs about 1960 register and firelookout.com) and the WTA-only L-4 interim cab are unresolved. A different Goat Peak lookout, an NHLR entry in the Methow River valley dated 1923 that appeared in search results, was not used and should not be merged with this one. The geocaching page for this lookout returned only its title, so it was not used. No public access was found.

Exact year staffing ended within the 1980s is not pinned down by sources (firelookout.com only says 'into the 1980's'); treat the 1980 staffed_last event as approximate. Brief's height_m (omitted in facts) and elevation (1623.4m / 5325ft per brief) vs. Wikipedia's 5,485 ft (1,672m) elevation figure disagree slightly; not resolved here, flagging for editor.

The brief's R-6 design is documented in NHLR for the 1963 wooden tower; I found no source that gives the cab type of the 1986 steel tower, so the facts field describes the predecessor's cab. Same-name Gold Mountain in Kitsap County (leslieromer.com; firetower.org Gold Mountain Lookout Site, 1947 and 1965 towers) is a different site and must not be merged. Staffing and permit details come from TrailChick (visited 2019; page updated March 2024); confirm the current permit and staffing with the Colville Tribes before publishing access advice. The firelookout.org Washington listing was not verified for this tower. Blog-level sources were used only for access and staffing.

The brief's height_m of 2.4 is wrong for a 100-ft tower; corrected to 30.5. The elevation disagreement (541 ft NHLR vs 480 ft TrailChick and a blog) is unresolved. No source explains why or by whom the tower was built, and the outcome of the 2002 sale is unknown. Access depends on JBLM Training Area 4 schedules and a Range Control permit, which I did not verify with the base. The substack post is undated and was used only for access and elevation.

Access upgraded from 'unknown' to 'public' based on USFS statement that visitors are welcome inside during the day when staffed/open; no camping or potable water at the site. Build-year conflict (1955 vs 1956 for the current tower) resolved by reporting both. Fact-check 2026-10-04: two footnotes in the story misattributed claims that are sourced to [1] (Snoqualmie Fire Lookouts Association) to [2]/[3]/[4] instead -- the 'early-2020s renovation' claim and the 'no camping on the deck' claim both trace only to the SFLA page, not to NHLR or firelookout.com; footnotes corrected.

The NHLR lookout page gives coordinates and an elevation of 5,901 ft for the original mountain site (the former-site record gives 5,947 ft); the museum coordinates in the record are kept and no elevation is set. The former-site record (US 1449, WA 349, registered 2012) belongs to the sibling record us-wa-graves-mountain and is not merged here. The 1955-56 lookout names on WillhiteWeb are omitted for privacy; the 1944 couple is described without names. Search snippets from Visit Northeast Washington (Facebook, Instagram) say visitors can climb the stairs; those pages were not readable, so climbing is not stated. The WillhiteWeb sidebar (elevation 2,793 ft, Pend Oreille County) looks like another page's template and is not used. No photo URLs were added.

Brief lists NRHP added date as implied by 1988-numbered reference (88000117); Wikipedia infobox gives exact date Feb 22, 1988, which resolves the record. Access is wilderness hike-in, not drive-up; no mileage figure verified beyond a secondary fan site's '17 miles east of Darrington' claim, which was not cited as fact in the story.

Read: firelookout.com, TrailChick, WillhiteWeb and the firelookout.org list (plus a weebly index page that only lists Colville Indian Reservation). The site is a combined guard station and lookout cabin, not a tower; the record's kind 'ground' fits the vocabulary. Standing status and the rental are supported by WillhiteWeb (undated) and Campflare. No staffing history and no fire history were found in the pages read, so staffing is left out. Height is unresolved: the tower record gives height_m 13.7 (~45 ft), but both NHLR (~63 ft) and firelookout.com (67 ft) describe the current 1964 tower as much taller; 13.7 m may describe the earlier 1932 tower instead. NHLR page lists the lookout as 'Available for Rental,' but this looks like it may be a generic NHLR field rather than confirmed current rental booking info; I described it cautiously as an emergency shelter and flagged the discrepancy in the story rather than asserting a formal rental program. Did not find a source confirming the current (2026) status of the restoration — last confirmed info is the NHLR's 2024 note that the cabin was still off-site. Worth a follow-up check with the Gifford Pinchot NF or NHLR for an update before calling it 'restored' outright.

Record height 9.1 m is the 1933 tower (30 ft); the standing 40-ft tower is about 12.2 m. Height is unresolved (100 ft in the register and two guides; 110 ft in the 1937 plan and 1960 inspection), so no height_m is given. Unresolved: first-structure date (about 1923 per Register and Willhite; 1921 newspaper item; Hiler's 1930s to 1958 for the earlier cabin). Elevation differs across sources: 4,800 ft (register; record's 1,463 m matches), 4,811 ft (trail guide summit) and 4,831 ft (fire lookout page and 1960 inspection, which refers to the old tower). Core history (1926 cupola, 1950 L-4 cab, 1980s last staffing, 2008-2011 restoration, 2012 back in service) is consistent across the Register, Forest Service, Snoqualmie association and TrailChick. No photos added; photo licences were not in the text read. Read: firelookout.com, TrailChick (first 3,000 of about 5,200 chars), WillhiteWeb (first 3,000 of about 4,500 chars; the access section after that was not read), Wikipedia (excerpt), the firelookout.org list (Kitsap line), and the weebly index (menu only). Record height 1.8 m is wrong; the tower is 40-41 ft. The Methow Valley News article linked from NHLR (story.php?id=3883) returned HTTP 404 in the cache, so it was not read. The record calls this the Long Mountain lookout, but the steel tower's first home was Spades Mountain (1941). Construction dates conflict: first lookout 1928 (register, TrailChick) vs 1929 (Forest Service, firelookout.com); current tower 1961 (firelookout), 1962 (register Built field, Forest Service) and 1967 (register cab note, TrailChick, which calls 1967 the current structure). Build history is disputed for the years before 1937 (1916 camp, 1922 tower on a log cabin, 1928 planned house, 1931 cupola). Build years (1937, 1954, 1974) and the 2022 registration are well supported. Record height 50.0 m is wrong (41 ft, about 12.5 m). Built year 1966 in the record is disputed: 1965 per two sources. Elevation 1145.1 m matches NHLR only. The 2021 Green Ridge fire account (lookout saved by fire wrap and retardant drops) rests on one blog, TrailChick; check against Forest Service fire reports. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found the original story had miscited and conflated two of its numbers. (1) The 'five miles northwest of Yelm' location sentence was footnoted to the register (firetower.org), which actually says only 'Olympia, Thurston County' and never mentions Yelm; the Yelm distance comes from firelookout.com instead, so the footnote has been corrected to cite that source. (2) The steel tower's '118 ft' figure, footnoted as the IslandWood rebuilder's figure for the *same 1968 tower* the register puts at 112 ft, is actually that source's figure for the *rebuilt* Canopy Tower as it stands today at IslandWood -- and that source gives two different figures for that rebuilt height (125 ft and 118 ft) in two different places on its own page. The rebuilder's page gives no height at all for the original Fort Lewis tower, and separately dates its construction to 1966, not 1968 (a discrepancy the original story missed entirely). The story and this record have been corrected to state these distinctions rather than conflating them. Also fixed: the rebuilding firm was called 'Sahale Snowkites & Climbing' in the original story and source list -- that name does not appear anywhere on the cited page, which identifies the firm as 'Sahale LLC' (operating as Seattle Bridge Builders LLC); corrected throughout. No staffing, named lookouts (other than 2010 FFLOS nominator Irene Potter), or fire-detection history for the Rainier site turned up in any cached or web source -- this appears to be a genuine gap in the record, not a search failure. The sibling record us-wa-rainier-lookout-site-at-islandwood gives height_m as 125.0, which is almost certainly a feet-to-meters unit mixup (125 ft, not 125 m, matching the 125 ft figure found on the rebuilder's own page) rather than meters; worth a human look at that record, though it is outside the scope of this task to edit it.

Brief height 125.0 is a feet figure entered as metres; corrected to 36.0 m (118 ft, the rebuilder's 'stands today' figure). The same Sahale page also says 125 ft, so the current height is not settled. Built date conflicts (1966 Sahale vs 1968 register/firelookout.com) are both kept. Firm name: the cited page says Sahale LLC (Seattle Bridge Builders); the sibling record's 'Sahale Snowkites & Climbing' is not on that page and should not be reused. The FFLOS register entry US 559, WA 5 belongs to the gone Rainier Lookout Site record (us-wa-rainier), not this relocated tower. No staffing, fire history, or public-access information found in any page read; the sibling record reports the same gap. The Canopy Tower sits at IslandWood Environmental Learning Center; no access level set because the sources do not say whether the public can visit. Verification 2026-10-09: the story now attributes 'all-steel' only to firelookout.com (the register says 112' steel); the 1968 replacement sentence cites the register; the 3D model claim is tied to the Sahale page's reference to old plansets. Both 1966 and 1968 dates remain reported.

Height: record 4.0 m is unsupported; sources give a 10-ft tower (proposed 3.0 m). The record's 1910 'built' event is the first cab; the present tower (1959) is added as its own event. Dates for the first cab (1910 vs 1913) and the restoration crews (2007-08 vs 2010) conflict; both are reported. Access is marked restricted because the road is gated and no source documents public entry to the cab. Rental is a plan in the sources (2010 quote, undated pages); recreation.gov and the Forest Service were not checked, so a human should confirm current rental and access status. All source pages are undated except the 2010 PCT quote. PCT Washington's 1913 first-cab date and 1938 garage date were added on this check. The WTA route is 3.1 miles plus 0.3 mile to the gated road (about 3.4 miles), and the story now ends that figure at the gate. No climbing advice is given.

Dates are the hardest part of this record. The 1918 shipment is quoted from a 1918 Oregonian item reprinted on Washington Lookouts; that page calls the destination Red Mountain, and Willhite says the house ended up at Red Top, so the link is plausible but not certain. The 1952 L-4 cab is consistent across four sources. The abandonment year is not given beyond the 1970s, so no event was recorded for it. Sources do not agree on whether volunteers staffed the lookout in 2017; the story says so rather than choosing. The brief's record (1952 built, 1997 registered) is consistent with the evidence, so no corrections were proposed. The WTA page describes the trail as an easy hike; the record does not need it. Willhite Web and TrailChick are personal trip-report sites, used for dates and access details only. The Washington Lookouts page is a secondary compilation; the 1918 and 1926 items are quoted from it. Several local pages list the same site under the name Red Top Mountain.

Only the register page is specific to this tower; the reservation origin is the register's belief, not a documented fact. The HistoryLink essay on Washington lookouts and the Aermotor PDF were read; only the Aermotor PDF gave model context. Search hits for 'Rocky Butte' lookouts in California and Oregon are unrelated. The Wenatchee World caption (photo credit Earl Cater, who also nominated this tower) describes a 130-foot North Douglas County Lookout west of Rocky Butte, which may be the source of confusion for the record. The brief's events line 'None relocated (Moved to Rocky Butte from a site not recorded.)' is malformed; see corrections. The brief lists the agency as Unknown, and the register does not name one, so no agency is recorded. No access information was found.

Build year disagrees: 1964 in the register, firelookout and TrailChick, 1965 in the 2018 tDAR study; story states both. Record height_m 10.7 looks like the 1927 pole tower (35 ft); facts.height_m set to 3.0 for the present 10-foot tower, please confirm the cab-floor height. The 2018 visit report on the register says Staffed? No, and the 2018 TrailChick visit says last staffed 1976; no later staffing source found. No current rental or open-to-visitors information found; the 2022 Forest Service project page does not say the cab is open. Access note is inferred from road-access statements, not from a Forest Service visitor page. The 2017 restoration partner is named only as FFLA in TrailChick; no expansion was found in any source read, so the story keeps the acronym.

Only the 2021 blog says the Quinault Nation donated the cab in 2000; the other sources say only that it was moved. Museum hours and current condition are not verified; the museum homepage we read had no lookout detail. The county in the record (Pierce) is for the current site and was not checked against a source; the original site is in Grays Harbor County per Former Fire Lookout Sites. The access level 'public' is inferred from the museum park setting and one visit.

Staffing rests on the 2024 TrailChick page and an undated firelookout.com page; no 2025 or 2026 source was confirmed. The 2019 tours come from TrailChick only. The record's 3.0 m height has no source in the pages read and is proposed for removal. A search summary said some sources describe staffing as only occasional; I did not read that page, so it is not used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'several structures' was replaced with firelookout.com's 'over a dozen' count, because the register's wording ('over a different structures') gives no usable number. The TrailChick citation for the one-of-two claim was corrected to TrailChick only, and the 'visits are guided tours' sentence was narrowed to what TrailChick describes.
No source gave an exact trail name/mileage within budget; left access as general trail note rather than inventing specifics. No distinct fire events found tied to this lookout specifically.

Access is by Yakama Nation tour only, so the story says so and does not invite visits. The TrailChick sentence says it helped open and close Satus, which may be a copy error on the Signal page; the story flags it. The firelookout.com staffing note is undated, and no 2026 status was found. A search summary described a staffing quote from the Yakama fire office; it was not read, so it is not used. The record's height_m of 2.4 looks like the cab width and is proposed as a correction. No new photos: the register's photos are credited to Christine Estrada and no image URLs were read.

Built-year conflict resolved: 1917 cupola was replaced by the 1933 L-4 now standing; brief record's 1917 'built' event should probably be relabeled or a 1933 'rebuilt/replaced' event added. Did not verify current staffing status beyond what NHLR/firelookout.com state.

The brief's height_m of 41.0 is a unit error: the source gives 41 feet, so the correction proposes 12.5 m. Staffing is the open question: the register, Willhite and firelookout.com say not staffed since around 2010, while the Forest Service campground page says staffed in summer; that page is undated. Elevation differs (register 5,944 ft, Willhite 5,961 ft). The 1925 lightning death is in two newspaper reports quoted by washingtonlookouts.weebly.com, which disagree on the date and spelling. The NHLR's 'Staffed? No' and visitor comment are undated. A WebSearch snippet about a 2025 rental listing was not confirmed and is not used. The brief's status and access were not verified beyond these sources. Willhite's 1909 cabin placement is 'about half a mile southeast' per firelookout.com, so the 1909 event note is attributed to that source. Fact-check 2026-10-08: 'four lookouts' is now footnoted to the register's 'fourth lookout to occupy the site'; 'rough road' and 'advises' were narrowed to Willhite's 'rocky' road and 'probably needed' wording.

The tower's current condition at Camp Waskowitz rests on an undated Forest Lookouts line that it is used for educational purposes; no recent visit or photo was found. Highline's own pages were not fetched. The access level 'restricted' is inferred from the school-program operation, not from a stated visitor policy. The 1942 entry is recorded as Aircraft Warning Service activation; the sources do not say how many people staffed the site. Wikipedia is used as a lead for the camp; its statements were not checked against the sources it cites.

Could not fetch the 2010 Wenatchee World burglary article (HTTP 429, cached twice already); it would add a concrete incident if a human can retrieve it. Record's 'built 1947' is confirmed; the 1925 'camp' predecessor is new context not in the tower record's events list.

The tower record also carries an FFLA-sourced relocation event claiming Stranger Mountain was moved to 'Crystal Ridge' (linked to id us-id-stranger-mountain-at-crystal-ridge, in Idaho). Neither NHLR nor FFLOS mention Crystal Ridge; both describe only the single 2008 move to the Colville fairgrounds. This looks like an FFLA data error (possibly a different lookout sharing the 'Stranger Mountain' name) and is worth a human look before publishing the Crystal Ridge link on this page.

Sources disagree on what moved. The 2008 chapter report says the cab; Kresek's account (NHLR) says the whole cab and catwalk came off a 40-ft tower with the legs reset on piers; the lookout sites register says the tower. The register's chronology puts the 1983 cab on a 42-ft tower, so the 40 vs 42 ft conflict is unresolved. The record's relocated event has no year; sources give 2008. The move reason also differs: a Homeland Security facility (NHLR crane caption) vs electronics interests (2008 report). Current condition is not established. The only condition note on the register is an undated visit report by Rod Fosback, written after the 2004 visit; it says the structure is still very sound but describes vandalism. It does not say where the structure was, so the story does not place it at the fairgrounds. Visitor access was not found, so no access facts are given. Two search summaries claimed a 1959 original tower and other details that are not on any page read; not used. Mountain site story is us-wa-stranger-mountain.

Core facts (1936 build, L-4 cab, staffed into 1938, abandoned, standing) agree across four sources. Access level 'permission' rests on the Colville tribal-land permit note, which appears on TrailChick's Strawberry and Whitestone Ridge pages, not on a Strawberry-specific rule; verify with the Colville Confederated Tribes before relying on it. Record elevation 1786.4 m is close to TrailChick's 5,863 ft (about 1,787 m); left unchanged. A 1934 newspaper item quoted on washingtonlookouts.weebly.com/strawberry-mountain1.html refers to a 'Strawberry Mountain' listed under the Colville National Forest (39N-30E-33), a different site, so it was not used. The 1938 abandonment year is an approximation: sources say the tower was abandoned after staffing into 1938.

Record matches NHLR on elevation, registration date (July 1, 1995) and the NRHP number. The record's 1933 build year is kept as NHLR's figure; Willhite and firelookout.com say 1932 at Lion Rock, which is noted in the story and the resolved conflicts. Staffing (every summer) comes from undated NHLR, firelookout.com and Willhite pages; no 2025-2026 staffing source was read. A Wenatchee World search snippet says the lookout is staffed annually, but that article returned HTTP 429 and was not read. The 2025 Lower Sugarloaf fire threat is from firelookout.com only. The NRHP entry was read as the NPGallery summary page; the full nomination was not read. Access is public: a gated spur road with a short walk, per WTA and Willhite. No climbing advice is given.

Status corrected from standing to abandoned (last used 1970s; upper stairs removed), proposed for human review; facts.status set to match. Height disagrees: 20 ft in the register and Fire Lookout; 22 ft on the Washington lookouts site; TrailChick gives 20 ft in its history text and 22 ft in its data box, so height_m is left unset. The lookouts history site also quotes a 1933 newspaper item about a named individual's illness while stationed here; deliberately left out. Laurence Davies is named only as known 1959 personnel from Fire Lookout. The last-used date is given only as the 1970s, so no exact staffed_last year was entered. Access is marked restricted based on the gated road and removed stairs. Coordinates and 1959 build year match the record; elevation 1976 m matches the register's 1,976 m.

Build year conflict (1932/1933/1934) across three sources, flagged rather than resolved. Brief's own record used 1934; that matches firelookout.com but not NHLR or Wikipedia/NRHP, worth a corrections note if the editor wants to standardize.

Dates agree across sources: D-6 cupola 1929, L-4 cab 1949, cab remodel 1989, NHLR registration 2015. The brief's height_m 3.0 is the concrete base, not the tower; see corrections. Frank Hohenadel's start year is unclear ('194?'). No rental or closure information found. Do not confuse with the Oregon Table Rock Lookout on the NHLR (/lookouts/us/or/).

Staffing is genuinely disputed: the register text is older and TrailChick (March 2024) is newer. A search summary mentioned Forest Service staffing for a few months a year; that page was not read, so it is not cited. The 2026 HistoriCorps sessions were scheduled for September; completion was not checked. The brief had access as unknown; it is set to public on the strength of the hiking route, but the 8.24.26 closure shows access can change. The brief's elevation (1701.4 m) follows the register; the other sources differ. Fact-check 2026-10-08: WTA also says 'The structure is staffed intermittently during the summer, and shuttered for the rest of the season.' That is a third staffing account, which the story does not yet mention; the editor may want it in the staffing paragraph. The 'combined' forest claim now rests on HistoriCorps, not the register; the two Thorp sessions are listed as separate ranges, not one run; and 'hike in' is now sourced to TrailChick with its road directions.

Build/staffing date ranges genuinely conflict between NHLR and the NRHP nomination (via Wikipedia); kept both in the story rather than resolving. Current record's 'built 1931' and 'abandoned 1942' event years fall within these ranges and are not contradicted, so no correction filed.

Record location (48.52702, -117.452515) and the 1959 build year match NHLR, so no corrections. Elevation: the record's 1660.9 m matches NHLR's 5,449 ft; firelookout.com, Will Hite and TrailChick give 5,474 ft (about 1,669 m). Left out of facts. TrailChick's coordinates differ slightly from the record. The record's 2005 and 2009 restoration events, and the 2009 date for lightning protection and the rental program, could not be traced in the sources read. Will Hite dates the lightning protection and reroofing to summer 2007, so the 2009 entry needs checking against its source. Access 'restricted' is editorial: locked gate, locked cab, walk-in only. TrailChick's note that the catwalk was open in 2018 is not a standing permission, and the story does not encourage climbing. Rental status is unconfirmed: the 2017 chapter report gives plans, Will Hite gives 2007 preparation, and no current listing was found. The Colville 2017 report says two lookouts were in the rental program but does not name them. Will Hite gives five days of 2017 work; the chapter report gives a one-week session. Not contradictory, but noted. Photo licences (NHLR 2018 photo by Jarred Roberg; firelookout.com photo from the Fire Lookout Museum and Rex Kamstra) were not checked; no photos added.

The NHLR registration date (April 13, 2022) was supplied in the queue brief but I did not independently re-verify the exact date text on the live NHLR page beyond the description text captured; treating source 1 and 3 as the same underlying page. No source gave a precise current rental/booking status, so I avoided claiming one; described it only as occasionally volunteer-staffed per NHLR and Wikipedia's 'visitor contact point' language. 2026-10-04 fact-check: the 'seven lookouts once stood' detail was previously cited to sources 1/2 (NHLR/Wikipedia), which don't contain it; it's actually from source 4 (TrailChick) and has been re-cited there. The windstorm/deadmen, visitor-contact-point, and Landmark District sentences were cited to source 3 (the NHLR duplicate), which doesn't contain those details; re-cited to source 2 (Wikipedia), which does.

Build year, height, staffing and NHLR registration agree across four or more sources. The record's access level 'permission' is not stated by any page I read; check with the reservation before publishing that level. No notable fires or design history turned up in the sources reached, so the story is short. A Cheryl Hill search result for a Tower Mountain was an Oregon lookout (92-foot Aermotor tower, 1935) and was excluded.

Brief's design L-4 describes only the 1933 cab (corrected). Brief's built 1966 is the current tower; the site's lookout dates to 1933 (corrected). Brief's 2005 'restored' is overstated: the chapter report says local management and some maintenance (corrected). Ownership is unresolved across sources: NHLR lists WDNR as administrator with private owners; firelookout.com says state then private; TrailChick says privately owned as of March 2026. Story reports the conflict rather than picking one. The washingtonlookouts.weebly.com and willhiteweb.com pages were not read beyond their indexes. Not read: the 2014-2021 staffing reports for this tower; none were needed.

Cabin dimensions conflict slightly: NHLR says 14x14 ft, Recreation.gov's current listing says 16x16 ft -- could reflect a later rebuild/remodel or simple inconsistency; reported both without resolving. Height_m omitted: no source gave a tower/cab height figure (it's a low groundhouse, brief gave no height_m either). Access level recorded as 'public' via paid rental, but note the 2013 report on lightning-protection non-compliance and the active 2026 wildfire closure -- actual availability fluctuates and should be checked against current Recreation.gov status before publishing anything time-sensitive. Fact-check 2026-10-04: elevation also conflicts across sources -- NHLR itself states 6,511 ft, while firelookout.com and Recreation.gov both state 6,654 ft. The story's opening sentence cited NHLR for the 6,654 figure it does not support; citation corrected to firelookout.com + Recreation.gov (the two sources that actually give that number).

Current record's design L-4 belongs to the 1933 first lookout; the 1963 tower is a 14x14 DNR cab. Height (20 vs 42 ft) and distance between sites conflict across sources. Staffing info is thin: one 2003 NHLR visit, a 1955 Daily Chronicle item reprinted by Washington Forest Lookouts, and TrailChick's 1938 and 1967 reports. No fire history found. Access is restricted; the story says do not climb.

Built year 1964 and the Spokane Mountain replacement agree across the register and firelookout.com. Elevation is unresolved: the record's 1021.1 m matches the register's 3,350 ft, but TrailChick gives 3,464 ft and firelookout.com gives 3413 ft; the record was left unchanged for a human to check the datum. The access level 'permission' is not stated by any source read; it reflects tribal administration and should be confirmed with the Spokane tribal administration. The staffing 'as_of' 2024 is taken from TrailChick's last-updated date (March 24, 2024). The 1962 letters are quoted on a lookout-history site, not from an archive; the 40-foot tower was only a proposal and the built tower is 53 ft. The reasons for the site change (electric service, reservation coverage, wider views) are sourced to the December 1962 letter and TrailChick, and the story now states them.

The 1985 built year and the staffing and permit facts agree across sources. The first-cabin date is disputed (1932 on firelookout.com, 1935 on the register and Forest Lookouts) and the story reports both. Elevation needs a human check and was not changed: the record's 1396.6 m matches the register's 4,582 ft, but TrailChick gives 4,760 ft and the 1960 inspection report gives 4762 ft (about 1,451 m). The record's 1985 built year and the R-6 correction both come from the register. Staffing 'as_of' 2022 is the register's registration year, which is when it said the tower remains staffed every summer.

Early dates conflict: 1934-35 for the CCC cab and wooden tower (register, 1960 inspection report, 1935 newspaper item) versus 1938 (Firelookout.com, TrailChick photo caption). The steel tower is dated only to 'circa the 1960s' by the register; the exact year was not found, so no event year is given for it. The brief's 1960 built date and 2.1 m height are both wrong per these sources. The Colville Reservation status (administration, permission from a private landowner) is taken from the register. Access is permission-only in the record; the register's stair-to-platform note is reported but not endorsed. The 2024 staffing as_of comes from TrailChick's page (last updated March 24, 2024).

This record duplicates us-wa-whitmore-mountain (verified, with register number US 1565, WA 92); the story follows this record's subject, the 1934 L-4 cab. Build dates conflict (1934/1935 against 1938) and the story says so. Steel tower height conflicts (53 against 67 feet). The staffing 'every summer' claim comes from the register and two guides. The $80 annual pass is from a tribal PDF whose URL timestamp dates it to April 2024; recheck the price before publishing. Access is reservation land: visitors need a use pass, and SummitPost warns that access for non-tribal members can change. The story does not encourage climbing.

Not a fire lookout. The record sits in the fire-lookout set but describes a city birdwatching tower; suggest hiding it. The OpenStreetMap way is tagged building=yes, man_made=tower and tower:type=observation. The City of Auburn park page returned an empty page from our cache, so the tower's current condition and rules are unverified; the record's status 'standing' is unchecked.

Two consistent sources agree on all key dates; did not pull firelookout.com or NRHP PDF since NHLR and Wikipedia already agree closely. Access note on snow/ice-axe conditions worth flagging to editor for a seasonal access warning on the listing. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story's September 15, 1994 NHLR date was cited only to Wikipedia, which does not state it; corrected the citation to also point to the NHLR listing itself, which does.

Built date and 2009 staffing end rest on the state record (WHS HI234013), which says it is based on DNR records. NHLR agrees on the October 1939 build date and the 100-foot design. The 1932 predecessor is unconfirmed: the 1934 survey description (weebly copy) and the directory's 'Bagley - first' entry (gone) both suggest an earlier tower, but neither says it was replaced. Access is not set: no source read gives current rules, and the We Wisconsin travel article's claim that only the Mountain tower is publicly climbable implies but does not state that Bagley is closed. Status 'standing' rests on the WHS record (not demolished) and the directory. The DNR statewide decision (WPR) is undated in the copy read; the 2015 date that appears in the Beaver NHLR record and in a search snippet was not confirmed here, so no year is attached to the decision. Do not confuse with the Mountain Fire Lookout Tower (WHS HI28224; NR-listed 2008, built 1935 per that record); a search snippet mixed the two. The WHS HI28224 record lists the Mountain tower in Oconto County, the same county as Bagley. NHLR misspells the county as 'Wisconson'; not quoted. NHLR photo credit: Brian Ziegler; no image URLs added. Budget: 7 distinct pages read (one, HI28224, is the Mountain tower and is used only for disambiguation), 2 WebSearch.

Thin record. The build date (November 1933), design, and 2015 staffing end all come from NHLR alone. The 2015 date was not confirmed by a second source; WPR says the DNR will stop using all 72 towers but the copy read is undated, and a search snippet with a December 2015 date was not from a page read, so it is not used. Standing status rests on the firelookout.org directory, which gives no date. The survey station description (weebly copy) names the landowner; the name is deliberately omitted here and the quote uses only 'ON LAND OWNED'. The survey description is dated 1934 on the page read ('DESCRIBED BY COAST AND GEODETIC SURVEY 1934'); the story uses that date. Look-alike warning: the Pembine/Paust Tower (WHS HI234017) matches on month, year and architect (International Stacey Company). Its original site differs, but the record also says it was moved in 1991 to a current site whose location is not given on the page read; a duplicate check against the Beaver record may be worth doing. No access level is set: the We Wisconsin article's claim that only the Mountain tower is publicly climbable is not enough to say the Beaver tower is closed, and the survey description's gate and road directions were left out so as not to guide a visit. The brief omitted the 2015 staffing end; it is added here. Budget: 6 distinct pages read (one, WHS HI234017, is a different tower used for the look-alike note; the We Wisconsin and WPR pages are shared with the Bagley work) and 2 WebSearch.

Thin record. Only FFLA listings, a Forest Lookouts page and a TopoQuest map name were read; web searches for build or staffing history found nothing usable, and no search snippet is cited. The TopoQuest 'Bennett Lookout Tower' point is about 16 m from the FFLA 'Bennett – first' (gone) point by our calculation, so the map name may belong to the first tower; not corrected in the record. 'Standing' is the FFLA listing only, not a site check. The Wisconsin 2015 DNR closure is not applied: no source says whether Bennett was a DNR tower.

Thin record. The bearing sources are the FFLA list (standing, coordinates), TopoQuest (county, elevation), a Central US page that holds only a title and county, and a statewide WJFW article. No build date, builder, design, staffing, fire history, ownership or access was found, so no facts block is written. The WJFW article says 72 towers were decommissioned in 2015; whether Blue Hills was one of them is unknown. A Rusk County museum post mentions CCC work near the Blue Hills area but does not describe this tower, so it is not used. Used 2 web searches and about 4 page reads.

Built year and height disagree between the register (1932, 70 ft) and Forest Lookouts (1933, approximately 73 ft). The 1950s cab fire has no exact year in any source, so its burned and rebuilt events carry no year. Access is recorded as private from one 2018 visit note; no current access policy was found. Clark County runs a Bruce Mound recreation site, but no source ties it to the tower. A Clark County history page on the 1948-2013 recreation area was read but not cited, since it does not mention the tower. The register's photo credit (Brian Ziegler) has no image URL I could find, so no photos added.

Build year 1932 and standing status are consistent across the register and the Forest Fire Lookout Association. Not found: any post-2015 fate, current staffing, or public access information for Brule. The 1950 staffing comes only from a photo caption. The land-manager conflict (DNR vs National Forest) is unresolved; a DNR or Forest Service records check would settle it. No photo URL was available for the 1950 image, so none is listed.

Build year conflict: register says November 1933, Central US Lookouts says 1935. Register is more specific and the brief agreed with it, so the story uses 1933 and flags the gap. A Wisconsin Field Guide Facebook post describes a long-serving Buckeye lookout nicknamed Percy; that page returned only its title, so it is not used. Not found: post-2015 fate, current access, or climbing information.

Only the FFLA line (coordinates, Tower, Standing) is confirmed for this site. The record's elevation_m 409 comes from an OpenStreetMap node, but the OSM page as fetched showed no elevation text, so it is unverified and left out of the story. Cataract is described in search results as a place in the Town of Little Falls; that was not confirmed on a page I read, so it is not used. No build date, builder, height, staffing, or access rules were found. The Wikipedia page for the community and Door County Pulse were not used. Greenfield and Norway Ridge are other Monroe County towers listed by the FFLA; they are not part of this record. Current state is unconfirmed. The registry still lists Cedarville as standing while marking the Middle Inlet tower gone, so the Cedarville entry may be stale. A recent photo or county record would settle it. The DNR closure is dated by the FOX 11 article (December 17, 2015).

Identity of the 80-foot tower is unresolved. The 1933 Oshkosh item names no site; the Central US and clamlakewi pages place it under Clam Lake, and the 1932 completion report and AHI date this tower to 1932. facts.height_m 24.4 comes from that 1933 item and the record, so treat it as probable, not confirmed. Used 1 web search and about 6 page reads.

Thin sourcing: the register is the only detailed source and it says construction year and height are unknown. Search results also return the 'Clevedon Lookout Tower' (the Sugar Lookout) in Clevedon, Somerset, England; those pages are unrelated and were not used. The 1958 Cleveland fire tower reference may or may not be this structure; left unresolved in the story. No staffing, access or visit source found; none recorded. The 1991 record is about the Park Falls Ranger Station tower cabin and says 'the fire tower was moved' from Connor Lake in 1973.
