The 2015 article's year is inferred: the printed page has no date, but it cites a Dec. 16 DNR release and 2016 retirement. Current condition and access are unknown. The lake is spelled two ways across sources.

Only pre-2016 sources were found for this tower. Its post-2016 status and access are unknown, and no source says whether it was among the 72 closed towers. Visit and access fields are left out on purpose. The registry lists it standing, which may be stale.

Two register-level facts only: 1937 build for the Wisconsin DNR and the 2017 registration. No staffing, fire history or sale year found in the sources read. The FFLA 2021 divestment count covers Wisconsin as a whole and does not name Dairyland; its 39 total includes towers that reverted to the Menominee Tribe, USFS and Department of Military Affairs. Access is undocumented; the record's access 'unknown' could now read 'private'. The NHLR photo credit (Brian Ziegler, all rights reserved) is already in the record.

Build year 1939 and DNR administration come from the NHLR register only; no builder or staffing history found. Ownership of the mound is disputed: thelandman.net (a rock-formation guide, not authoritative) says private land, while the Town of Rome operates the recreational area that contains it and the register lists the DNR as administrator. Climbing status and cab condition are unknown. The register gives 80 ft, not a height to the cab floor, so no height_m was set. The Town page's opening date is loose ('weather permitting').

Built date, design, cab, and CCC-era use rest on the NRHP registration form (dated August 2006, listed 2007) and agree with NHLR and Wikipedia. The end of staffing is disputed (1973 vs 1957 as period end) and is reported as disputed. The restoration claim comes only from NHLR, undated. Access is from Travel Wisconsin; no FS page for this tower was read. No rental info found. Two WebSearch queries via websearch.py; about six page reads plus the nomination PDF. The Wisconsin Historical Society record NR2273 and a Price County Review article about former Fifield lookouts appeared in search but were not read. The NRHP date is July 3, 2007 per Wikipedia while the form's Keeper line reads 7-1-07; the story says 2007 only.

Two sources disagree on timing: SummitPost says a 2015 announcement set closure for 2016, while WJFW says the towers still in use were decommissioned in 2015. Both are kept in the story; not reconciled. Location is unresolved: FFLA lists a separate 'first' Flambeau Ridge site, marked Gone, at 45.28101, -91.20750, about 0.7 km east of the standing tower's record coordinates. The 1935 report says the tower moved north, but the standing coordinates sit south of that site, so we could not tell which site the 1931-35 tower used. Record coordinates left unchanged. Access and visit facts come from SummitPost (2019) and are not confirmed for today. A 1975 report of a fall from the tower names a private person, so it is left out. Used 1 web search and about 5 page reads.

Register and FFLA agree on county, designation and standing. The 1939 build date and 84-foot height come from the register alone. No Flannagan-specific history, staffing, access or post-2015 status was found in two WebSearch queries and the sources read. The WXPR article is statewide context only and is not used as Flannagan's history. The 84 ft figure is overall tower height, not cab-floor height, so it was not entered as height_m.

The Wisconsin AHI record (HI234016, surveyed 2017) is the only detailed source: 1934, metal, observation/fire tower, International Derrick and Equipment Company in the architect field, DNR staffing as needed until at least 2000, not demolished, not on a register. Standing status rests on the FFLA list (undated) and the AHI non-demolition note. Height, owner, access and fire history were not found after two searches. Next places to try: the AHI site file held by the SHPO, the Polk County Historical Society, and the DNR. The St. Croix 360 article is about the Gordon tower in Douglas County; it is cited only for the statewide 2015 DNR decommissioning and does not say whether Frederic was included. The 431 m figure is the OSM elevation tag at the tower's point, not tower height. Search snippets were not quoted.

Searched for a local/CCC construction story (Adams County Historical Society 'Friendship Sesquicentennial' page) but it discusses Friendship Mound's sheriff's radio tower and a lighted star, not the fire lookout, and has no bearing on this record; not cited. No source found on who built it, current public access, or whether it is climbable, so those fields are left unknown rather than guessed. Fact-check 2026-10-04: removed several story sentences that went beyond the cited source (an invented etymology for the 'Skyline' name, a claim the design was 'widely used' by the state forestry service, invented reasoning about dry grass/wind/debris burning driving spring staffing, and an invented claim that decommissioning was 'in favor of aircraft and other detection methods') — none of this appears in the NHLR page text. Also note cite 2's FFLA list spells the feature 'Friendship Mound (Skyline)', slightly differing from cite 1's 'Friendship (Skyline)'; not treated as a correction since both clearly refer to the same tower.

The 1932 build date comes from the register alone; the Forest Lookouts Glidden page gives only the county heading. Two WebSearch queries found no Glidden-specific history, staffing, access or post-2015 status. A WebSearch snippet pointed to a Wisconsin Historical Society record for a 'Glidden Ranger Station' built 1934; that is a different kind of building, was not read, and was not used. The 80 ft figure is overall tower height, not cab-floor height, so it was not entered as height_m.

The register is the only source for the first site (about 736 ft) and the later move; no other source I read mentions a move, so that claim is single-sourced. The record's agency is the former operator (WI DNR); the current owner is the Friends of the Bird Sanctuary per the 2021 news report, and the record's ownership 'unknown' could be updated, but no correction is proposed because the record does not claim an owner. The 2015 decommissioning and 2017 NHLR registration match the record. Staffing and climb schedule details come from 2021-2022 reports and may have changed; the 2026 status of the open-climb schedule was not checked. The Airbnb listing was not read directly (JavaScript-heavy), so the rental is supported only by the 2021 article and the FFLA rentals list. Four web reads, one WebSearch (the second was not needed).

Build year (1933) and height (approximately 84 ft) rest on one compiled entry on the Forest Lookouts site, which cites no underlying record. Two web searches found no second source for the build date, builder, staffing or condition. The brief's agency value '18N' is a land-survey location and is corrected above. Next places to try: the Wisconsin Historical Society AHI, DNR fire tower records, and the Monroe County Historical Society. Access is unknown; the story says nothing about visiting beyond checking with the land manager.

Build date is unknown per NHLR, so no built event. Status 'standing' rests on the firelookout.org listing; the NHLR page does not state status. The county article prints no year; it describes the towers after the DNR decommissioned them. Its 'off Highway B four miles east of Hayward' tower is matched to Hayward only by inference, so access stays 'unknown', which matches the tower record; the fenced-and-locked description may not apply to Hayward. Staffing and fire history for this tower not found. The 60-towers-manned figure is a statewide quote from DNR's Trent Marty in the Sawyer County Record article [2], not a Hayward-specific fact. Search results included a Wisconsin Historical Society record for the 1928 DNR ranger station, which is a different building and was not used.

Only two listings were read: the FFLA Wisconsin list and the OSM node (ele 380, tower:type observation). Two web searches found nothing on Highland's history. An Upper St. Croix article (stcroix360.com, 2018) came up in one search, but it is about the Gordon tower, not Highland, and is not cited. Next places to try: the Wisconsin Historical Society AHI, DNR fire tower records, and the Douglas County Historical Society or Forestry office. Confirm the tower's identity against the Douglas County forest records before relying on the coordinates. Access and ownership are unknown.

Built 1949 and the 2015 decommissioning are well supported. Sale date and buyer are unknown. The register says the tower was built for a standard design by the Wisconsin Conservation Commission; the 1949 newspaper header names the Wisconsin Department of Conservation, so the builder agency is not settled. The register photo captions disagree with their file names (caption 'August 1952 photo' vs file 'hodag_tower_april_30_1952'); both NHLR photos are already in the record. A WJFW article describes its author and a friend climbing the tower, with no date or permission stated. The story cites it for that account; it is not evidence of public access. The record's 36.6 m matches the register's 120 feet; the register does not say whether that is to the cab floor.

Only two FFLA listings (standing, coordinates), a Wikipedia community page and a WXPR statewide article. Web searches found no construction or operating history. A Historical Society search turned up a different tower (Iron River, Bayfield County, 1934) and a TowerDex communications structure in Iron Belt; neither is the lookout and neither is used. The FFLA Wisconsin condition-report PDFs for 2017 to 2025 (cached) were searched for all three names and do not mention Iron Belt. Whether Iron Belt was a DNR tower is unknown, so the 2015 closure is not applied to it. 'Standing' is the listing only, not a site check.

Height is unresolved: the state file and Central US Lookouts say 100 ft, the register says 79 ft 6 in (about 24 m). The record's height_m 30.5 follows the 100-ft figure and was not changed. Builder is unresolved: register says the Conservation Commission, Central and the state file say CCC. End year is unresolved: register says 2015, Journal Sentinel says towers leave service in 2016. No current access source was found; the FFLA standing status is undated. The FS statement covers the forest's 14 original towers, and Iron River's membership in that group is unconfirmed. Three websearch calls were used on this tower (budget two). No new photos.

History is thin: the only build year, design and registration facts come from one NHLR entry. The Forest Lookouts page for Jack Pine (centraluslookouts.weebly.com/jack-pine.html) shows only a header, so it was not cited. A Wisconsin Historical Society post in search results mentions a 1935 CCC move and a 1936 cabin, but the page returned only a login stub and does not name the tower; it was not used. Mountain Fire Lookout (Forest Service) was built in 1935, which may be what that post describes. Whether Jack Pine was among the 72 DNR towers in the 2016 plan is not confirmed. Staffing, fires, access and visit details not found. The anyplaceamerica and peakery pages were not cited; peakery lists no climbs.

The 1934 build year rests on one amateur-run site; NHLR gives no year. The CCC link is supported by NHLR, the Taylor County article and the HMDB marker. No height, staffing, fire history, access or visit information was found in the sources read. The Forest Service pages searched covered the Mountain Fire Lookout, not this tower. Reads: NHLR, Forest Lookouts, Taylor County article, HMDB, firelookout listing.

Thin sourcing. Two WebSearch queries plus cached pages (FFLA Wisconsin lists, OSM node, WXPR 2015, FFLA 2019 chapter report) yield only name, county, coordinates, standing status and OSM elevation. No build date, builder, design, height, staffing, access or rental source found. Record matches FFLA and OSM on name, county, location and status; no corrections proposed. Search returned TopoQuest place pages for other features (Basswood Lookout Tower, Langlade County); not cited. WXPR date comes from the article URL (2015-12-21). The WXPR and FFLA 2019 items are statewide context only; neither names this tower. Leads to try: Wisconsin Historical Society Architecture and History Inventory, WDNR tower divestment records, Langlade County forestry or historical society. Confirm land ownership before any access advice.

The 1934 date is an upper bound (in place by 1934), not a known construction date; the brief's 'built 1934' should be read that way. Not found: current staffing by the Tribe, any tribal statement on the tower, or visitor information. Access is private property, so the story advises permission only.

No source gives the year the current 68-foot tower was built. The La Crosse Tribune Jackson County article (a search hit on local decommissioning) returned HTTP 429 twice and the 2015 Post-Crescent article returned 403, so neither was read. The register's 'Administered by Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources' may be stale given the statewide decommissioning; worth checking who now owns the site. The statewide decisions in the newspaper and WPR pieces are not Knapp-specific, and the story says so. The brief's record for this tower has no errors found.

Thin record. Kolpack-specific facts come only from the NHLR detail page (build month, height, registration, administrator) and the FFLA state list (standing). Two searches found no newspaper, DNR or staffing source for this tower. Access, staffing and any rental are not established, and the story says so. Worth a search of the Shawano County Historical Society archive (its digital archive appeared in results) before a fuller history. The record's 'access: unknown' stands.

Thin sources: one undated inventory list (FFLA) and one Forest Lookouts page. Build year, design, height, operator and current condition are all unknown. The record's agency field holds 'Menominee Indian Reservation', which is a place, not an operator; confirm with the tribe before using it. Two WebSearch queries and one Wisconsin Historical Society fetch returned nothing about this tower (the HI22302 record is Bass Lake, Florence County, not this tower). The OpenStreetMap node 353894126 tags it ele=327 m; not used in the story. Not checked on the ground.

Tower history not found: no build year, height, builder, design or fate. The WHS station record (HI20350) describes a ranger station, not the tower, and we did not confirm the tower sits on the same site (record coordinates 45.46458, -91.13424; station address W8945 Highway 8 not geocoded). Related WHS records HI20346 (garage, 1934) and HI20348 (oil house, 1937) are the same station and were not used for the tower. A search snippet claimed a staffing roster and that only three Rusk County towers were in active use; that came from an undated document we could not fetch, so it is not used. Blue Hills (Rusk County, also listed standing) is not researched here. Access unknown.

Thin record. The NHLR detail page carries nearly all tower-specific facts, including a description that the tower has not been in active service for decades; that description is undated and I took 2017 (registration) as its as_of. A Clio entry for the tower was found but is a user draft, so it is not cited. The WJFW feature covers the 2015 decommissioning only in general terms, and the 2015 APG article (Price County Review) could not be fetched (HTTP 429). The name 'Tomahawk Lake Lookout' appears only as a historical name on the register; the record uses 'Lake Tomahawk Lookout'. Access and rental are not established; the story says so and advises against climbing. The register's damage description is the reason.

Location conflict unresolved: record shows FFLA 45.98554, -91.80243 against central_us_lookouts 45.98306, -91.81611 (about 1,092 m apart). The Forest Lookouts page we read does not show coordinates, so we could not check the second point. No build, design, height, staffing or fate found. A search snippet linking Lampson to Brooklyn Township and a 1903 schoolhouse is about the community, not the tower, and is not used. Access unknown.

Built year 1932 agrees across Forest Lookouts and the Wisconsin Historical Society record. The newest evidence of standing is the 2024 survey date on the WHS record plus the FFLA list; no current photo or condition report was found. No staffing, notable fires or access rules were found in the sources read. The laonahistory.com site has a wildfire news index that might hold tower material; I did not follow it up. One WebSearch used for this tower, plus one before it. No new photos.

Thin sourcing. Two WebSearch queries plus cached pages yield only name, county, coordinates, standing status and OSM elevation. No build date, builder, design, height, staffing, access or rental source found. Record matches FFLA and OSM on name, county, location and status; no corrections proposed. Lead not used: a search snippet described a Town of Lawrence tower south of Glen Flora in an undated Rusk County ranger-station document, but the cached copy of the page it linked (a UW-Madison library page) does not contain that text, so it is not cited and may or may not be this tower. The NHLR is the only source that describes the tower itself (build, move, design, registration). The FFLOS listing confirms it stands (cite 5), and the 2019 Journal Sentinel article gives the same 1935 move year (cite 4) and describes the tower as still standing. Wikipedia and the Tower Heritage Center cover the ski hill, not the tower. The 1935 move date predates the hill's motorcycle-race years (1938-1940) and its 1941 ski-hill establishment; no source read explains when the tower reached the hill or where it stood before, so treat 1935 as the Register's and the Journal Sentinel's claim. The NHLR credits the 'Wisconsin Conservation Corps'; the sources read do not expand that name, so verify the builder before publishing. Staffing and fires are not in any source read. Climbing: the 2019 article calls the Mountain Fire Lookout Tower the only Wisconsin fire tower open to the general public for climbing and does not mention climbing at this tower, so access is unstated rather than confirmed; the brief's access 'unknown' is kept as unknown.

Identity is solid: the WHS record, Forest Lookouts, FFLA and OSM all describe the same Bayfield County tower with the 1932 build year. Condition is the open question. The brief's standing status rests on the FFLA list, which conflicts with Forest Lookouts (abandoned). The NCTA event page text I read has no visible date, so treat it as a listing rather than proof of a recent visit. Does not say whether climbing is permitted. The brief's agency '44' is a location fragment, corrected to unknown. No fire, staffing or photo evidence found. One WebSearch pair used (two searches total for this tower).

Thin sourcing. Two WebSearch queries plus cached pages yield only name, county, coordinates, standing status and OSM elevation. No build date, builder, design, height, staffing, access or rental source found. Record matches FFLA and OSM on name, county, location and status; no corrections proposed. The central US lookout list page names Lugerville (Price County) with no detail. Search returned the Fifield tower (Price County, a different structure) and Wisconsin Historical Society records for Lugerville houses; neither describes this tower, so neither is cited. WXPR and FFLA 2019 items are statewide context only. Leads: Wisconsin Historical Society Architecture and History Inventory, WDNR tower divestment records, Price County Historical Society, Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest office (to check whether the tower sits on national forest land). Confirm land ownership before any access advice.

The tower history rests almost entirely on one long NHLR narrative (with photographs credited to WI DNR and the USFS, not fetched). The Park Falls origin is a visitor comment and is uncorroborated; the register's own 'likely surplus' is a suggestion, and the story labels both. Date conflict to watch: the register puts the 1939 tower's destruction in September 1941, while a Chequamegon Bay history PDF (chequamegonbay-history.com, ChequamegonCJ134WindsAndFloods.pdf) describes a late August 1941 cloudburst and windstorm across the Ashland area. That PDF does not mention this tower, so the register's date stands, but it is unreconciled. The 'Staffed? No' line on the register is a visit-report field and is not quoted, because the page text splits it across lines. Access level is not established; the record's 'access: unknown' stands. Possible mention of a Marengo tower near Mellon in a Facebook group post was not used.

Brief height_m 3.0 is wrong; NHLR says 94 feet. Status is the open question: FFLOS (cached read) still lists it standing, but the DNR auction (ran Aug 18 to Sep 2, 2021, now CLOSED) offered it for removal by Dec 8, 2021. The auction shows a plan, not a completed removal; the winning bidder is not named in the catalog. Excerpt read of the 2021 FFLOS report does not name Matson. Location: the catalog address reads 'Fire Lane Road/Helf Road, Plover, WI', while NHLR places the tower in Marathon County and the catalog text says Marathon County owns a small building near the tower; the Plover address is not reconciled and the story says so. Before publishing a status or location, check DNR divestment records, a recent photo, or the NHLR update history. Staffing is documented only through 2009; no fires are named in any source read.

The 1922 windmill and 1934 steel tower come only from the 2021 county forest plan, which itself relays earlier county plans; no primary record was reached. Status 'standing' rests on the FFLA lists alone. Staffing, current access and visiting rules are not in any source, so they are omitted rather than guessed. The brief's access 'unknown' stands. No corrections to the current record. Possible follow-up: a Washburn County or Wisconsin DNR page on the tower's current condition or public access.

Thin record. Forest Lookouts gives only the county, and the FFLA lists it standing without a register number. OSM supplies the name and 571 m elevation, which matches the brief. The brief's agency (null) and access (unknown) remain unchanged. The Wisconsin Historical Society search for Ashland County fire towers did not show a Mellen entry, and the NHLR guessed URL returned 404. A local source (Ashland County or the Wisconsin DNR history) is needed before the story can say when it was built or who staffed it. No photos found.

Build year is disputed: register says 1951, City Pages says the tower dates from the 1940s. End of service is disputed: register says staffed until 2015, City Pages says decommissioned in the early 2000s; the statewide 2015 announcement fits the register better. The City Pages copy I read is undated and I did not confirm its original outlet. Lease and renovation details come only from City Pages. No public access or climbing source was found. The 1958 photo and register photo credit (WDNR/John Hunt) are already in the record, so no new photos. Two websearch calls were used on this tower.

Brief's 1932 build is supported by the 2008 nomination (prefab 1932, pier dated 10/22/32 at the original site); the 1935 date in the Forest Service page and Wikipedia is the relocation year. Brief record lacked the 1935 relocation and the 2008 NRHP event, both added. Access and seasons come from the Forest Service page; staffing from the NHLR 'Staffed? No' field and the nomination's 1960s end of use. NHLR gives no Built field. One WebSearch via websearch.py; about six page reads including the nomination PDF (one GetAsset ID returned no text). No photos added.

The 1934 build year and DNR staffing to 2015 come from one state inventory record, not a second source. The 1916 Forest Lookouts entry conflicts with 1934 and may describe an earlier structure on the site; left open. The state record places the tower in Boulder Junction township and on Plum Firetower Road, and that is what the story says. Current access and visiting rules are not in any source, so they are omitted. Cross-check: WJFW dates the statewide decommissioning to 2015, while the Saddle Mound story says 2016; that discrepancy is for the editor to settle across towers. Leader-Telegram article on the 2015 closure returned HTTP 429 and was not read.

The NHLR page is the only tower-specific source. The Forest Lookouts page supplies the 1927 proposal only. The 1940 survey is cited as the NHLR quotes it; the survey itself was not read. The Register does not say whether the 1939 tower was moved or whether a new tower went up in 1951, so the story keeps both dates and says the sources disagree. The 64-foot height in the brief is a proposal, not a built tower. Agency is supported by the statewide DNR decommissioning statements, not a tower-specific deed. The sources read do not name the current owner or say whether the tower was sold after 2015. Access, climbability and rental are not in any source read, so no access level or visit fact is recorded. No photos added. Not verified: whether the tower has been moved, sold or restored since the 2017 registration. The 39-tower figure in the 2021 chapter report includes towers conveyed to the Menominee Tribe, USFS and the Department of Military Affairs, so the story says landowners, not private landowners.

Only location, elevation and standing status are sourced for this tower. No build date, builder, design, staffing or access appears in any page reached. A Leader-Telegram article on the 2015 closures, which quotes a long-time North Mound staffer, returned HTTP 429 on every attempt and was not read; it is the best lead for this tower's history and worth a retry. The name 'North Mound' versus 'Kokaly' and the Eau Claire County entry need a check against a Wisconsin DNR or Clark County source. Story is short because the evidence is thin.

Thin record. The NHLR page is the only tower-specific source; the Forest Fire Lookout Association list confirms the county and standing status. The 1932 build year, 2008 cab replacement and 2022 sale status come from the NHLR alone. The sale status is as of early 2022 and no later record was found, so the sale may have completed or changed. Agency is inferred from the statewide DNR decommissioning statements, not from a tower-specific record. No height appears in any source read, so no height_m is recorded. Access, climbability and rental are not in any source read. No photos added. Not verified: whether the sale completed, who owns the tower now, or its current condition.

Thin record. The NHLR page is the only tower-specific source; the Forest Fire Lookout Association list confirms the county and standing status. The NHLR gives the build date only as late 1930s, so no build year was entered as an event. Height is converted from the NHLR's 100 feet (30.5 m). Do not confuse this with the Millston entry on the Forest Fire Lookout Association list, which is marked gone at a different location (44.16192, -90.65797). Agency is inferred from the statewide DNR decommissioning statements. Access, ownership and rental are not in any source read. No photos added. Not verified: current condition, sale status, or any move since the 2018 registration.

Brief record checks out against the sources (1932 build, 595 m elevation, WDNR administration, standing). Access: the 2019 article says the fire tower is not open for climbing and that the observation tower beside it can be climbed; the Register says the adjacent wooden observation tower is open to the public. The story points visitors only to the public observation tower. Staffing and fire history are not in any source read. Not used: the Central Lookouts page carries an unsourced 1983 photo caption about the observation tower and Timms Hill Park, and an NGS description mentions a benchmark stamped 'OGEMA TOWER 1934'; Wikipedia's Timms Hill article says a public lookout tower is atop the hill without saying which one. The 1982 date comes from one survey history; the 1983 caption on the Central Lookouts page is not a source for this story.

Few sources. No staffing names or specific fires were found for the Pembine tower. The Register and the Historical Society agree on the 1990 sale and the 1980s service end, and disagree on the build year by one year. Wikipedia is a lead only; its park facts are stated as Wikipedia's. Whether the tower can be climbed is not stated anywhere; the story tells readers to ask the park. A Geocaching page repeats the Register's text and was not used as a source.

Built year 1934 is corroborated by two sources (WHS record and Forest Lookouts). The brief's agency field reflects only the Forest Lookouts page; the 2015 Star News article says the Medford DNR branch manages the tower, so the agency is contested. Access level and current condition are not in any source read, so access is omitted. No NRHP listing was found.

Two sources. NHLR is the only source for the 1936 build date, the 1960 end of use and the 1978 purchase and donation; FFLOS only confirms standing. Unresolved lead, not used: a Facebook group post, seen only as a search snippet and not readable, says a 90-foot first fire tower stood on Military Hill in 1927. Only two sources were usable. No Wisconsin Historical Society record or NRHP listing was found for Pipestone. No build year exists in the sources; the 'likely after 1940' statement is the register's own inference. The FFLA standing list is undated. Built year 1932 rests on a May 1932 newspaper item quoted by a Forest Lookouts page; the original newspaper was not read. The Star News reprint (Dec 2015) is the only source with a build date, oversight and staffing detail. The article contradicts itself on who runs the tower (DNR Prentice station vs federal Chequamegon National Forest land), and the Forest Lookouts Wisconsin page agrees with the federal version. Thin record. The Register entry is the only detailed source; the 1946 photograph record is the only staffing evidence. The WJFW feature covers Wisconsin towers in general and does not name Rock Falls, so its 2015 decommissioning is not applied here. No source on current access, condition or climbing; the record keeps access unknown. Build year, builder, design and current status were not found. The 100-foot height comes from a 2008 job notice, which does not say whether the figure is tower height or height to the cab; the record's 30.5 m matches. The FFLA listing is undated. Checked and not relevant: Wisconsin Historical Society records HI234014, HI234018 and HI234019 are other towers; towerdex.com returned 403. Two lists place this tower and nothing else is documented: no build date, builder, fire history or owner. Cannot confirm whether it is one of the DNR's 72 towers. Needs a Menominee County history or Wisconsin AHI record and an owner check before any access or condition claim.

Only two lists document this tower; no build date, owner, history or access source. Neither the DNR article nor the WJFW piece names Shelton, so it is unknown whether it was one of the DNR's 72 towers. Do not add access or condition claims without a new source.

The Michigan origin rests on the FFLA entry alone; no Michigan source was reached (the michiganfiretower.com homepage has no Silver Lake match). Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap name this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. The list has no NHLR or FFLOS entry for it. Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap name this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. Build year not confirmed: the 1926 Milwaukee Sentinel item says work would start soon, and no completion date appears in the sources read. Only the two FFLA lists have anything on this tower, and they agree. Two web searches found no other Timberland tower record. Coordinates are the association's and were not checked against a map. The story is short because the evidence is thin; a Burnett County or Wisconsin DNR source would be needed to add history.

Four sources plus the Register. The 1932 item is the earliest date found; the Forest Lookouts page files it under Clark County but does not say the Twin Mounds entry is this tower, so treat 1932 as a 'by' date. The WJFW and Door County Pulse articles are statewide; neither names Twin Mound. Door County Pulse gives no year, so 2015 rests on WJFW and the Register. Nothing readable says whether the tower is open to visitors, has been sold, or has been rented since 2015; JSONline and AnyPlaceAmerica returned HTTP 403, and a Facebook group snippet about a retired tower in the Clark County Forest was unreadable and not used. The OpenStreetMap node gives 399 m against the Register's 398 m, which is not material and was not used. No photos added. Thin record. NHLR is the only detailed source, and it gives design, administrator, the October 1936 build, and the August 2017 registration. The statewide list confirms standing. No staffing, fire, access or rental information was found. Unresolved lead, not used: a Wisconsin Historical Society Facebook post, readable only as a search snippet, describes a 1932 Aeromotor tower moved by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1935 with a cabin built in 1936; the snippet does not name Villas, so it is not used and should not be assumed to be this tower. Current ownership after the state's 2015 decision is unknown; NHLR still lists the DNR, which may be out of date, and the Register does not say whether Villas was one of the 72 towers. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the NHLR coordinates (N 45.236839, W 089.307953) and the OpenStreetMap node (45.2368463, -89.3079481) agree, so the 506 m node is the same point; the 13 m elevation gap is unexplained, and the story says so. The story's 2015 wording now dates the decommissioning (WJFW) rather than a Wisconsin decision, since the Door County Pulse article is undated. No photos added.

Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap describe this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. The list name is Washburn (Bayview); the OpenStreetMap name is Washburn Lookout Tower, and its coordinates match the list. What Bayview refers to is unexplained in the sources read. Two WebSearch rounds found only directory entries and records for other towers (Iron River, Bayfield, Long Mile). The Wisconsin Historical Society record HI24653 is Iron River, not this tower. A Forest Service PDF named Longmile as a surviving Bayfield County tower; it is not established that this is the Bayview site, so it is not used. The Washburn city page was read but its county line did not match the grep and is not used. Budget: 2 WebSearch, about 6 page reads.

Sources agree on 1936 and 100 feet. The Forest Lookouts page spells the forest 'Chequamegan'; the brief copied that spelling, so confirm the forest's correct name before publishing. No staffing, fire or access information was found in the pages read. An OpenStreetMap node (353893853, ele 455, tower:type observation) was checked and could support elevation if needed, but it is not cited. Search results listed Wisconsin Historical Society photo assets for the tower and a tower cabin; they were not opened, so no photos are listed.

Brief's county (Columbia) follows the Register; Central US Lookouts and the FFLOS list say Adams. Build date 1958 is right per the Register, but a lookout structure dates from 1934. The 2015 statewide decommissioning is dated by NHLR and WJFW; the Door County Pulse piece gives no year. No fire, staffing-roster or photo sources found. Access upgraded from unknown to restricted on the Register's private-land note. A Wisconsin Public Radio article was read for context but is not cited. WebSearch used twice.

Build date (Nov 1939), design (79-ft Stacy) and registration come from the NHLR page alone. No owner, access or fire sources found. A geocaching listing (GC30CBZ) in search results describes a 100-ft Aermotor built by the CCC; its page returned no readable text, so it is not cited and the Register's figure is used. OpenStreetMap node 353893837 gives 572 m elevation against the Register's 575 m; not material. The Register's 'staffed intermittently' wording is cited, not expanded. WebSearch used twice.

Brief's 1940 build date is wrong: NHLR says the date is unknown and likely after 1940, so the correction was applied to the story and events. Worcester is not named in the statewide decommissioning sources, and no staffing, fire or access sources were found; the story says so. The Central US Lookouts Phillips page has only a header and a county line, no tower text. The FFLOS and NHLR agree on Price County, standing status and the 100-ft height. WebSearch used twice.

Build date and height rest on the register alone; no second source for the 1939 date was found. Staffing, access, and rental are not covered by any source checked. The 1977 item is quoted on Central US Lookouts; its newspaper name is printed as Wausaw on that page, so the paper is not named in the story. A 1940 Wisconsin Historical Society photo of a Tomahawk forest protection headquarters came up in search, but it does not mention the lookout, so it was not used. A USDA Forest Service PDF named in a search snippet returned 404 and was not used.

Build date conflict left open: e-WV says a fire tower was erected at Watoga in 1926 (unnamed); the Pocahontas Times says the CCC built the Ann Bailey lookout in the 1930s. The construction material and the naming rest on one local article. Not used: grokipedia.com (unvetted encyclopedia copy claiming 1935 and CCC Company 1525), eathealthy365.com (claims a 1970s restoration; no primary source), and a WPA state files PDF on archive.org (text did not extract; its naming passage was seen only in a search snippet). A guessed westlookouts.weebly.com page returned 404. Whether the tower can be climbed is unknown; call the park before any visit. The West Virginia Outside post says WVDNR publishes no length for the Ann Bailey route, but the official trails page lists the Ann Bailey Trail at 3 miles; the story uses the official page. Two web searches used.

Sources conflict on the build date (Register: early 1930s; Forest Lookouts: a 1923 53-foot Blaw-Knox tower and a February 1930 'new steel fire tower') and on height (47 vs 53 feet). The story says so and does not pick one. Unresolved: whether the 1923 structure is the tower standing today. The Register's visit and access details are not in the record. The cabin rental is supported only by the June 2021 article; check current booking before publishing. The record has no built year; none is proposed as a correction. No corrections proposed. Not verified on site.

Build date (circa 1926) rests on NHLR and one 1926 newspaper item; Wikipedia's 1939 is a weaker later bound. Condition is from a single 2017 NHLR visit and Wikipedia's 2016 status. The repeater project was approved in 2010 and the tower was not removed (Wikipedia). The Reddit and FFLA items were not used: a 1988 transfer to the Forest Service is unverified. Access: hiking via a gate and 3/4-mile walk; no climbing.

The 1931 build and 1943 move agree across the Register, the Dolly Sods site record and the Forest Service history, so the history is well supported. The cab collapse year is 2010 in two sources and before October 2015 in the Register. Current condition rests on the 2020 Register visit report and a 2013 travel post; not checked on site. Access (grassy road off Forest Road 19) comes from the 2013 travel post only. The Reddit and abandonedonline pages were not used. Nothing in the 1976 newspaper item was used beyond the employee's remark. No new photos with image URLs were added.

Only two sources, both lists or registers; no state disposal record was found. height_m is the 60-foot figure converted. The NHLR photo credit (Rocco Germani) has no stated license, so no photo was added. The visitor comment is an NHLR contributor's text, not an official record.

Brief record checked: the 1933 build, 2015 NHLR registration, elevation and coordinates match the sources. Brief status note (cab gone) is supported by the FFLOS asterisk legend and the Register. Construction date and design are well supported by the register and a local site. Current condition rests on the 2021 register visit; no 2025-2026 report was found. No source read gives a build date; the 1913-14 warden report is the earliest mention. The 1926 and 1938 newspaper items are only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the originals were not checked. Brief correction: the record's 1946 'built' is the move date; the original build was 1925 at Carlin Hill (firetower.org). The brief's 'standing' status is supported by the FFLOS list and the 2017 maintenance note, but the current condition is not confirmed. The brief's 914.1 m elevation matches NHLR's 914 m rounding.

Three sources only, one of them a list. No build date, staffing or fire history in any source read; two web searches added nothing usable. The move to Pocahontas Co. H.S. rests on a single FFLA list entry with no date. Register and FFLA agree the original is gone.

Build year not pinned. Clio gives only the 1930s. Wikipedia's infobox lists the governing body as the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources; not used here.

Thin record. Status and coordinates come only from the FFLA list; no NHLR page for this tower is in the crawl cache. No height in the brief; the 1952 'about 65 feet' figure may describe a later structure than the 1924 tower and is kept in design text, not height_m. Heights disagree: 75, 79, 85 and 88 feet across 1936-37 items and the Register; the story reports the spread and does not pick one. Thin record. No build year found: the register says the CCC built the 86-foot tower but gives no date, and two WebSearch queries found no construction history. Unread leads: e-WV Fire Towers (wvencyclopedia.org/entries/2115), e-WV Flat Top Mountain (entries/2123), Wikipedia Flat Top Mountain (West Virginia). Searches found no 2024-2025 access notice. The WBOY article on climbable WV towers does not mention Point Mountain. Ownership: the NHLR names the WV Division of Forestry as administrator; the Monongahela National Forest list in a search summary was not read and was not used. Budget: four fetch_text page reads (NHLR, FFLOS, firelookout WV list, WBOY), one failed fetch of a WV tower list PDF (DNS error), two WebSearch calls, and one local read of the cached Forest Lookouts page (eastern_us_lookouts/point-mountain.html). No photos added.

Current use is well sourced by the Forest Service release of September 8, 2026: the cab and campsite are open for rental, booked on Recreation.gov, with the 2027 season April 15 to November 30. The Recreation.gov listing itself was not read, so check rates and dates there before publishing. Open disagreements, left in the story: location (register says east of Cowen; Forest Service says about 12 miles south of Cowen) and cab size (register 14 by 14 ft; 2023 news 12 by 13 ft). The register's 80-foot height is also used by the 2023 news report, so it is treated as settled. The record's access 'unknown' is now given as public (rental). No corrections proposed. No photos added: the register's May 2022 photo is credited to an individual with no licence shown. The rental release does not say whether the tower itself may be climbed, so the story does not advise climbing it.

Build date 'by 1925' comes from the FFLOS Randolph County record; NHLR's Built 1999 is the relocation year. The record's events list 1999 as built and should be corrected. A WBOY search snippet places the tower 'on top of Cheat Ridge' in Pocahontas County; the page was not read, so the Snowshoe Mountain location rests on NHLR. The 80-foot height is from one history page only. Access: private resort ground; no climbing.

Stub-level record. Standing status and coordinates come from the FFLA list. The name match to Mapcarta's Slaty Lick Knob Lookout Tower is inferred from the coordinates, not confirmed by any agency. The local GNIS peaks file lists Slate Lick Knob at 39.4223, -78.7903; it is not cited because the GNIS page fetched without usable text. Slate Lick does not appear on the Forest Lookouts or NHLR West Virginia lists as crawled. Build date, design, builder, staffing, access and fires are unknown. Mapcarta's 'Slaty' spelling should be checked against a county or Forest Service source before the name is changed.

Date the wooden lookout came down is not found, so no removal event is recorded. Whether the 1969 observation tower replaced it is inferred from the register wording and not stated outright in any fetched source. The brief's elevation (1482.2 m) is the summit height, not a tower height; no height key is given. Brief status corrected: the FFLA list reads Gone. Two WebSearch results (a Monongahela guide saying the stone tower stands on a former wooden tower site, and a 1938 photo of a fire tower) were not fetched, so they are not used. The FFLA list's Gone status and the register's wording fit together, so the record is not contradictory once the observation tower is separated from the fire lookout. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

No construction date found for the current tower; the earliest dated references are a 1916 station with a watchman and a 1926 tower on telephone lines. Staffing is recorded as unknown: the 1947 'in charge' item is not evidence of current staffing. County conflicts (Greenbrier per NHLR; Nicholas per the lookout list and the forest-lookout site). Elevation also differs: NHLR gives 3,112 ft (949 m), while the 1916 report gives 3,158 ft for the station. A Facebook post in search results (WV fire lookouts) asks whether the tower was removed; only its title could be read (login wall), so it is not used. Check status before publishing. Search results also return a different Sugar Grove tower in Berne Township, Fairfield County, Ohio (110 ft, Lancaster Eagle-Gazette, 2017); it is not this tower and must not be merged into this record.

Access and visiting status unknown; the register says emergency use only on Beaver Coal Company land, and no public visiting or rental information was found. The newspaper clippings are secondhand, transcribed on the Forest Lookouts site, not checked against the original papers. The build year conflicts (register 1934, clippings Jan 1935). A Facebook group post claiming a 2012 observation could not be read, so it is not used. Mapcarta gives 2,654 ft elevation against the register's 2,637 ft; not used. No record corrections proposed.

The NHLR says originally built in the 1920s by the CCC; the state history credits the Civilian Conservation Corps with forest work but places a 1924 tower on Michael Mountain. Search snippets from theclio.com/entry/45123 and wvencyclopedia.org credit the CCC with building the 1935 tower, but those pages were not opened and no quote was recorded. Read on the 2026-10-08 fact-check, easternuslookouts.weebly.com/thorny-mountain.html (not cited in the story, not an NHLR or state source): a '1935' entry says the lookout duties were transferred to this site from Michael Mountain, which bears on the 'Michael Mountain link is not confirmed' sentence; a November 28, 1937 Bluefield Daily Telegraph item says a new tower with observer's cabin atop a '40-foot steel framework' was 'completed recently' on Thorny Mountain, built by CCC labor. The story does not use either item. The editor should decide whether the 1935 date, the 'not confirmed' sentence, or the height note needs them. Staffing not recorded: the NHLR shows 'Staffed? No' but the quote is split across lines. Six page reads used. No photos recorded. Elevation on the NHLR page is 3,385 ft (1,032 m), consistent with the brief.

Built year conflicts: register 1937 vs park page and trail blog 1935; the January 1937 item supports 1937 (described as yet to be erected). Access conflicts: park wording 'open' vs register fence and trail blog 'not open for climbing'; recorded as restricted. No fire or staffing history found. easternuslookouts tick-ridge1.html covers a different Tick Ridge in Carter County and was excluded. A Facebook group post and a Historic Wayne County post could not be read in full, so they are not used. The record's 80-foot height and 1,367 ft elevation fit the sources; no record corrections proposed.

Closure and access are well supported by the 2025 news report, which is a Wyoming News Exchange piece; the Forest Service order itself was not read. Build year is disputed (1939 vs. completion October 1940). Elevation differs between NHLR (9,383 ft) and firelookout.com (9492'). The 2014 report says Historic Core; the 2025 article says HistoriCorps; the story treats them as the same group but that is not confirmed. Not read: Living New Deal (403 error), a Sheridan Press closure article and a 2024 Cowboy State Daily piece (search snippets only). No last-watch date found; the 1980 end date comes from the 2025 article. No photos added; NHLR photo credits not checked.

Thin on history: only three pages read and no fire or rental record found. Do not confuse with the Bighorn Mountains Black Mountain (Sheridan County, BHNF, built 1939 by the CCC, now boarded up); the Sheridan travel-history article and the Road Trip Ryan page describe that tower. Staffing dates in the register come from the 2018 visit and may have changed. Personal names of past lookouts are kept to the published lists.

No source checked actually states a 1950 build year for the current tower; both NHLR and Recreation.gov agree on 1963, so the earlier draft's claimed 1950/1963 discrepancy was unsupported and has been removed. No clear record of when active staffing ended beyond NHLR's '25 years then standby' note, and no date given for when that standby period began.

Thin record. Read: the firelookout.com page, the FFLA Wyoming list and the Wikipedia article on the reservation. Two web searches found nothing on build date, design, staffing or fires. The access level 'permission' is carried over from the record; no source states a visiting rule. The record's 'tribal' ownership is not stated in any source read. Agency correction proposed.

Build year 1941 rests on the register alone; the KINGFM CCC attribution is a hiking video's narration quoted second-hand and is unverified. The 'standing' status comes from the firelookout.org index, not the register text. The access level 'public' is inferred from the hiking account, not stated by any source. Brief record checked: name, county, elevation, agency and 2022 registration match the register, so no corrections. Not reached: Bridger-Teton lookout records or a Forest Service page on current status; a 2022 Wyoming fire report mentioning the Cabin Creek lookout cabin appeared in search but was not read. The story does not claim a current site check.

Could not fetch the bhpioneer.com newspaper article (HTTP 429, too many requests) within the read budget, so staffing/anecdote detail rests on NHLR and the brochure PDF plus firelookout.com's personnel list; worth a retry later for any additional staffing or incident detail. Did not verify current rental/public-access specifics (e.g. whether the tower cab itself is open to visitors) beyond the brief's existing 'public' access level. 2026-10-04 fact-check: the story originally said the lookout straddles the Wyoming-South Dakota line; no source supports that, and firelookout.com (source 2) instead places it in Crook County, Wyoming, about a mile from the state line. Fixed the story wording and citation accordingly.

Height_m taken from Wikipedia's 26.25 ft (8.00 m) structure height, not from ground elevation. Material conflict (wood vs concrete) flagged but not independently resolved beyond preferring the NRHP-sourced Wikipedia account.

Build date is disputed: NHLR circa 1940; county page and brochure 1941 (CCC role claimed on the county page, possible but undocumented per the brochure). The brochure says the cab was moved from Red Castles on Bare Pass before 1955, which the NHLR record does not mention. Restoration start: August 2015 (Pinedale) vs 2016-2019 (brochure). Unread leads: a 2020 Pinedale Online piece says built around 1941 by the CCC; a search snippet from npshistory.com (Lookouts, Latrines, and Lodgepole Cabins, hcs-2.pdf) says the lookout is recommended not eligible for the National Register; neither was read or verified. Road access is from a 2019 brochure; check current conditions with the Big Piney Ranger District before publishing visit advice.

The 1941 build year is supported by the register, firelookout.com and a 1941 newspaper item reprinted on West Lookouts, which is a secondary transcription. The 1940 telephone-line item calls the site a fire lookout before the 1941 build report; I could not settle whether an earlier structure stood there. The abandonment claim comes from a hiking listing, not an agency record. No staffing, fire or current access source was found, so none is stated. Brief record checked: the name, elevation, agency and 2022 registration match, so no corrections were needed. Not reached: Bridger-Teton or Bridger NF lookout records, and the NHLR nomination file for WY 21.

Sources conflict on whether the structure is a tower or a cabin. The 2007 fire item is quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; its original publisher, Teton Valley News, was not opened. The Buckrail article speaks of towers and may not cover this site. The brief's elevation (2596 m) was not checked against a source we read; 'Ground' matches the FFLA list. Do not confuse this with the Elk Mountain Fire Lookout in the Black Hills National Forest, South Dakota, which appeared in search results only and is not cited. Access and staffing are unknown.

Record was thin: the NHLR page is the only substantive source, and the other two are short. No staffing, fire or current-condition source was found. The brief's height_m 36.6 (120 ft) traces to the Stumpy Point, NC tower on the same ranch (westlookouts), so it is corrected to 30 ft from firelookout.com. Agency conflict is left unresolved. Two leads were not used: a Deadwood history Facebook post (search snippet only, page did not load) says the Moskee Fire burned more than 7,000 acres in 1936; and ghosttowns.com's Moskee page gives 1921 for Homestake's involvement, not 1922. Access is set to permission from both NHLR and westlookouts. No photos added: the NHLR credits Dixie Boyle but gives no license.

Build year 1938 is supported by three sources, but a 1942 newspaper item (quoted on westlookouts) calls Huckleberry a permanent station that year; not resolved. Current status is unconfirmed: the newest dated text read is the register entry (2011 registration; 'slated for restoration') and firelookout.com 'Standing'. Elevation conflict (7,209 ft register vs 9,615 ft nomination and firelookout) is proposed as a correction for human review. Page budget was used up before reading the Wyoming SHPO page, the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort page or the Hiking Project page; search snippets claim restoration and overnight use, but those were not read or cited, so check them before any access statement is changed. No new photos.

Elevation conflict left unresolved: register 9,395 ft (2,864 m, matches the record's 2863.6 m) vs Forest Service 9,477 ft. NRHP listing date: register says December 2016, Wikipedia says November 15, 2016. Footprint: register and Wikipedia give 14 ft square, the nomination gives a 20 ft exterior footprint. The Forest Service page spells the name 'James Torrey Saban'; the register says 'James T.', so the story keeps 'James T.' and does not expand it. Current staffing and access come from the Forest Service page (last updated May 13, 2025), not a site visit. A search snippet about an overnight rental concerned Sheep Mountain, a different lookout, and was not used. The nomination gives no date for the restoration work. No new photos.

The brief's 1969 build date is contradicted by three sources (1964); Wilma Perue's 1969-1971 tenure may be the source of the mix-up. Rental fee comes from a Forest Service page last updated June 6, 2025; confirm before publishing. The record's kind 'two_story' is not supported by any source read: the NHLR describes a single R-6 cab with an interpretive site on a lower level. No fire or move history found; the CCC-era cab is undated beyond the 1930s.

The 1941 CCC build and precut log method rest on the USFS survey (Volume II evaluations, cover photo credited to the USFS). Current status rests on firelookout.com's undated 'Still there'. Not read: a Flickr photo page (search snippet calls it abandoned; not used), and the Living New Deal page (403 Forbidden). The westlookouts 1941 item describes four CCC lookout houses, 12 feet square; the story does not tie those to this site, and the survey supports the 1941 build on its own. The record has no height_m for this site, and none was found in these sources. No staffing after 1954 was found. No photos added: the NHLR credits SingleTracks.com but gives no license.

Built year and register data are well sourced. The 1926 build date (Outside Bozeman) is unresolved and reported as a conflict. Jim McCown (1963-1987) rests on one listing and is not confirmed; the 1975 visitor's Jim is unnamed, so the story does not link them. Current condition is inferred from a standing listing and a photo caption; no recent condition report was read. A search summary attributed a 1991 removal to this lookout, but the Outside Bozeman article's 1991 removal concerns Divide Lookout, not Sheridan, so it is not used. Blueprint location conflicts: WillhiteWeb says the Montana State Library holds them; Montana History Portal item 93097 credits the Yellowstone National Park Heritage and Research Center. Access level is unknown; no source read says whether the cabin can be entered. Height is not stated in any source; elevation_m is from the register. The record's Park County is supported; the Teton County listing is the only conflict.

Build date is contested: the NHLR Built field and HABS say 1941, but the NHLR narrative says construction began June 1939 and was completed summer 1940. The record keeps 1941; the story reports both. The 1921 stone lookout (Willhite, HABS, NHLR) is treated as the predecessor. The NPS page is undated; its staffing statement is in the present tense. Drive-up status rests on HABS (a parking area north of the building; the lookout described as the only Yellowstone fire lookout facility accessible by vehicle) plus two NPS hiking trails. Road seasonality and whether the upper floors are open to visitors were not checked. No fire events beyond the staffing history and the 1980 modification appear in the sources read. No climbing advice is given.

NHLR is the main source for the 1939 build, the CCC help, the secondary-lookout purpose and the 2021 registration. Current use and public access are not stated in any source read: the NPS trail page covers the hike only, so the access level is left out of facts. Staffing is not documented; the slide-file captions only label the structure as a lookout (1964) and a lookout station (1975). Unread leads, from search snippets only and not used: a Parkwolf trail page calls the summit lookout 'historic (typically closed)', and a SummitPost Cascade Lake page says an old summit structure is 'apparently no longer in use'. Both should be checked before any statement about current use. Elevation 9,402 ft matches the record's elevation_m 2865.7. No height_m in any source read. No photos added: the NHLR photos lack licence terms and the NPS slide-file image URLs were not captured.

Built, staffing and registration rest on the NHLR page. The 1937 newspaper wording is quoted second-hand on the Forest Lookouts page; the newspapers themselves were not checked. Access and hike details come from one personal visitor account, which is undated, so treat them as indicative. No specific fires are named in the sources. The brief's access 'unknown' could become 'restricted' once the NPS status is confirmed. No photo URLs were added.

Build year (1941) and staffing are consistent across NHLR and the 1941 newspaper items as transcribed on Forest Lookouts; the original newspaper scans were not read. Current access, rental status and condition are not established beyond the July 2025 FFLA post. A June 2025 Pinedale Online / geolconsulting article on protecting the tower could not be read (SSL certificate errors from both fetch_text and WebFetch), so the wrap and fire details rest on the FFLA post alone. Elevation differs between NHLR (9,665 ft) and firelookout.com (9642'). Access is omitted because no level could be supported. No photos added.

A travel-blog page (roadtripryan.com) and the WebSearch AI summary both offered a vivid, specific narrative - an 1922 primitive fire watch predecessor and a 1938 lightning strike that set the lookout's bed on fire - that appears nowhere in the NHLR register, the FFLA register, or the Forest Service's own Bighorn lookouts history page. I did not use any of that material; it has the hallmarks of AI-generated filler rather than sourced history, and a human may want to track down the roadtripryan.com page's own citations if any exist. Note that the CCC-construction claim itself is NOT part of that invented narrative - Recreation.gov and the Rocket-Miner newspaper piece (sources 4 and 6, both used in the story) independently and directly state the lookout was 'Constructed in 1950 by the Civilian Conservation Corps,' so that part is sourced, just flagged in the story as doubtful because the CCC was disbanded in 1942. A footnote error was also fixed: the story had attributed the 'Emergency' staffing status to 'the Forest Fire Lookout Association's own register,' but that fact actually comes from firelookout.com, an independent reference site by Rex Kamstra, not from FFLA's own site (firelookout.org, source 3) - the FFLA page for Wyoming is just a name/county/status table with no staffing field for this lookout. Text corrected; footnote [^2] was already pointing at the right source. The record's elevation_m (2911.8m / ~9554ft) runs a little low against the 9600-9610ft the registers give; likely just rounding/survey differences, not flagged as a correction. No other conflicts found worth a formal correction.

Museum hours and the tower's presence at the museum come from undated tourism and visitor-tip pages; confirm with the museum (gemuseum.com) before publishing. Climbing status is not confirmed. Height 15.2 m converts the 50-foot figure from firelookout.com. The 1986 move year comes from the register alone. The record's agency is null; the Forest Service entry refers to the original site.

No new photos found beyond those already on the tower record. The exact abandonment year is unknown (NHLR hedges with 'most probably ... mid to late 1940's'); I used 1945 as a placeholder year for the 'abandoned' event rather than inventing precision. The kind correction (tower -> shelter) is worth a human look since 'tower' vs 'shelter' is partly a classification judgment, not a hard fact.

Height_m in the record (9.1 m / ~30 ft) likely describes the original 1930s pole tower rather than the current 41-55 ft structure; worth checking against a primary USFS record before correcting. Exact year of the tower replacement (after the original 1938 build) is not pinned down by any source consulted.

History is well sourced across the Forest Service, NHLR and Wikipedia. Access and restroom details rest on Hiking Project, a third-party listing that may be out of date. The brief's design L-4 most likely describes the 1938 cab, so it is corrected. The first lookout's name is unresolved: NHLR says Mert Ellsbury, firelookout.com says Lyman Ellsbury for 1939. The story reports both. Staffing source is NHLR undated text, so as_of is undated. Brief elevation 2028.7 m matches NHLR 6,656 ft; Wikipedia says 6,640 ft. Sundance AFS radar claim is from the Forest Service page and was not separately checked. No photos added.

Status is likely wrong in the tower record (see correction) and should be fixed by an editor, not auto-applied. Build year is fuzzy (1932 vs. ~1934) because NHLR's stated span and the Buckrail piece's '23 years of service ending 1957' don't quite agree; left unresolved rather than guessed. No NRHP nomination form or newspaper coverage was found for this one — the two non-register sources (firelookout.com, Buckrail) carried the real narrative detail (staff names, prior tent/stone camp). Fact-check correction (2026-10-04): a draft version of the story attributed a 2000 near-miss wildfire to Wyoming Peak, citing the Buckrail article; that passage in Buckrail is actually about Deadman Fire Lookout, a different lookout covered in the same article, and has been removed.
